evidence_text:
High-sensitivity pan-cancer AI assessment of lymph node metastasis via uncertainty quantification. The histological heterogeneity of primary tumors across the pan-cancer spectrum poses a formidable barrier to accurate lymph node metastasis assessment, often causing AI systems to make "overconfident errors" on rare variants that lead to missed diagnoses. To address this, we present UPATHLN, a unified diagnostic platform that synergizes a pathology foundation model-based encoder with a decoupled uncertainty estimation mechanism. We developed and validated the system using a large-scale multicentre dataset of 26,229 lymph nodes from 14 distinct primary origins. In internal validation, UPATHLN achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.986. Crucially, the uncertainty module functioned as a decisive fail-safe: by flagging potential false-negative predictions for mandatory pathologist review, it intercepted all missed diagnoses, securing 100% conditional sensitivity across both the development and independent test cohorts-even for tumors from seven unseen primary origins. Concurrently, this mechanism reduced the review burden on negative lymph nodes by 73.2%. Ultimately, UPATHLN sets a new benchmark for safety-critical AI, demonstrating that explicitly modeling uncertainty is key to unlocking reliable, workload-efficient diagnostics at the pan-cancer scale. Introduction  Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide  1  , primarily driven by metastasis  2 , 3  . Lymph nodes (LNs) are critical anatomical checkpoints in cancer progression  4  , serving as initial metastatic sites and immune regulatory hubs orchestrating host-tumor interactions  5  . Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) status is therefore paramount for prognostic assessment and therapeutic decision-making across diverse cancer types  6  . However, current clinical management relies primarily on crude quantitative approaches—predominantly pN staging  6  —which fail to capture crucial biological features such as lymph node ratio (LNR), metastatic tumor burden, and diverse spatial growth patterns of metastatic cells within LNs. Recent evidence explicitly links elevated LNR to decreased survival rates and shortened recurrence-free intervals  7  , while highlighting how spatial distributions of metastatic cells can modulate the immune microenvironment, potentially facilitating immune escape  8  . Despite these insights, pathologists now face an unprecedented surge in LN specimens due to rising cancer incidence  9  , rendering such detailed, multi-dimensional analysis practically unfeasible in routine workflows.  Deep learning has rapidly advanced pathological diagnosis, with numerous artificial intelligence (AI) systems gaining regulatory approval. However, existing AI approaches for LNM detection  10 – 15   typically follow cancer-specific paradigms. This fragmentation hinders widespread clinical adoption by necessitating multiple, disparate systems  16 , 17  , conflicting with the need for operational efficiency and unified diagnostic standards. Moreover, tumor heterogeneity manifests as a “long-tail distribution”  18 , 19  , where common metastatic patterns coexist with diverse rare variants. Standard deep learning models often struggle with these outliers, prone to “overconfident errors” where the system makes incorrect predictions with high certainty on out-of-distribution data. The reliable detection of these rare but clinically significant variants is crucial for patient safety  20 , 21  , yet remains challenging even with large datasets. While emerging foundation models  22 – 27   offer powerful representational capabilities, their effective application across the pan-cancer spectrum requires substantial annotation resources. Thus, there is an urgent need to transcend these limitations and establish a unified, robust, and safe diagnostic framework capable of not only high sensitivity but also reliable failure awareness across all cancer types.  To address these challenges, we developed UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware AI platform integrating a pathology foundation model with uncertainty-guided active learning and robust uncertainty estimation (Fig.  1 ). Trained and validated on an extensive multi-center, multi-cancer LN dataset, this study demonstrates UPATHLN’s capacity for highly sensitive and safe pan-cancer LNM detection with robust generalization. Ultimately, this study represents a critical step towards establishing a unified, trustworthy diagnostic standard for AI-assisted pathology.    Fig. 1   Development of clinically safe pan-cancer lymph node pathology diagnostic system.   a  Multi-center data composition: clinical samples from three hospitals of varying scales covering lymph nodes (LNs) from 14 primary sites.  b  Surgical case complexity: each case typically involves >10 LNs, increasing diagnostic workload compared to primary tumor assessment.  c  Representative HE examples of lymph node metastases illustrating morphological heterogeneity. Insets highlight thyroid-type colloid-like material and other non-specific patterns that may be prominent in metastases from the indicated primary sites, including mucin pools, stromal fibrosis/desmoplasia, and keratin pearls.  d  Uncertainty-guided active learning framework: system leverages clinical pathology database with iterative refinement where pathologists review high uncertainty (HU) predictions, verify challenging cases through IHC staining (CAM5.2, AE1/3), and exclude poor-quality samples. In clinical practice, uncertainty estimates guide pathologists' review to prevent rare subtype misdiagnosis and enable continuous system improvement.                     Results   Establishment of the UPATHLN platform and active learning optimization  To establish the UPATHLN platform, we curated a large-scale, multi-center pan-cancer dataset comprising 26,229 lymph nodes (LNs) from 8294 whole-slide images (WSIs) across 2738 patients, spanning tumors from 14 distinct primary organs. The dataset was rigorously partitioned into a development cohort and an independent test cohort, with seven rare primary origins strictly held out as unseen primary-origin holdouts to evaluate generalization to previously unseen origins (SFig.  1 ). To ensure high-quality input to the platform, our automated LN extraction pipeline achieved robust performance, with YOLOv8-s demonstrating a recall of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection and nnUNet achieving a Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for tissue segmentation, effectively excluding non-target tissues (Fig.  2a  and SFig.  2 ).    Fig. 2   Deep learning framework for lymph node metastasis detection with iterative refinement.   a  System architecture overview. The pipeline sequentially employs a detection model to localize lymph node regions and a segmentation model to delineate their contours. The core classification framework features a Multiscale Cross-Attention architecture that utilizes the UNI pathology foundation model as a feature encoder. By synthesizing features from multi-scale tissue patches, the model simultaneously outputs tumor confidence via the Classification Module and prediction uncertainty via the Uncertainty Estimation Module.  b – e  Performance metrics comparing original and high uncertainty (HU)-filtered predictions across training iterations: tile-level AUC ( b ), PPV ( c ), NPV ( d ), and lymph node-level sensitivity ( e ).  f ,  g  Lymph node-level metrics: average false positives (FPavg) and average high uncertainty regions (HUavg). At the lymph-node level, each LN was counted once regardless of the number of false-positive or high-uncertainty subregions within it. In bar charts ( b – g ), 95% confidence intervals were derived from bootstrapping (1000 iterations).                   Rather than relying on static training, we optimized the platform using an uncertainty-driven active learning strategy. Misclassified tiles were enriched in the high-uncertainty (HU) tail of the tile-level uncertainty-score distribution (SFig.  4a ). Accordingly, we summarized tile uncertainties into a slide-level ambiguity score and ranked candidate WSIs for expert review (SFig.  3 , “Methods”). Through five rounds of human-in-the-loop iterations, this active optimization substantially improved discriminative performance on the internal validation set, increasing the tile-level AUC from a baseline of 0.953 (95% CI: 0.932–0.974) to 0.986 (95% CI: 0.976–0.996), with consistent gains in both PPV and NPV (Fig.  2b–d ).  To rigorously attribute this high performance to architectural design rather than data accumulation alone, we benchmarked the final model against alternative architectures trained on the identical dataset generated from the final iteration. The multiscale architecture significantly outperformed both the single-scale UNI baseline (AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.910–0.946; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001) and the ImageNet-pretrained feature extractor (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.901–0.935; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001; SFig.  4b ).    Uncertainty-aware classification achieves high-sensitivity LNM detection  Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a clinical fail-safe. While the optimized multiscale classifier achieved a robust intrinsic sensitivity of 0.996 (95% CI: 0.985–1.000; Fig.  2e ), it erroneously classified three metastatic cases as negative when relying exclusively on diagnostic probability scores (false negatives, FNs). In the uncertainty-annotated confusion matrix (SFig.  5a ; HU-flag counts are shown in parentheses), all three FNs were flagged as high uncertainty and therefore routed for mandatory pathologist confirmation. This capability to “rescue” potential false negatives effectively neutralized the risk of missed diagnosis, underpinning the system’s 100% conditional sensitivity and ensuring that ambiguous but critical lesions were correctly routed for pathologist confirmation.  To evaluate clinical workload, we quantified the review burden at the LN level. Here, each LN was counted at most once, regardless of how many false-positive or high-uncertainty subregions it contained. Across iterations, both the LN-level false-positive (FP) rate and HU rate steadily declined (Fig.  2f, g ), reaching final values of 0.112 (95% CI: 0.070–0.155) and 0.156 (95% CI: 0.110–0.202), respectively. The model’s progressive refinement was visually corroborated by prediction heatmaps (Fig.  3a  and SFig.  6 ), and it precisely identified diverse metastatic burdens, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cell clusters (Fig.  3b ). Final validation by pathologists on the remaining development cohort confirmed a 100% positive detection rate with minimal review overhead (1% FP rate and 0.16% HU rate at the LN level).    Fig. 3   Visualization of iterative refinement and representative challenging cases.   a  Representative lymph node whole-slide images (WSIs) with prediction heatmaps from the first iteration and the final (fifth) iteration, showing progressive refinement across active-learning cycles. Right, a magnified example tile from the high-uncertainty (HU) regions identified in the first iteration.  b  Representative isolated LNM detection cases with immunohistochemical (IHC) validation. For each case, the HE slide, the registered IHC section, and the corresponding prediction heatmap are shown, with magnified tumor tiles from the boxed regions. In the magnified panels, orange arrowheads on HE indicate tumor cell foci, and the corresponding IHC images highlight tumor cells by brown chromogenic staining. In the heatmaps, yellow denotes HU regions, red denotes regions with high tumor confidence, and blue denotes lymph node tissue. Scale bars as indicated.                     Validation of pan-cancer robustness and safety  Performance evaluation on the independent test cohort confirmed the system’s robust discriminative power (Fig.  4  and SFig.  7 – 10 ). To establish a baseline, we first evaluated the standalone classification module without uncertainty intervention. Operating strictly on diagnostic probability scores, the module achieved a robust sensitivity of 98.7% and a specificity of 88.0% (SFig.  5b ). Although this represents a high level of diagnostic accuracy, relying solely on this conventional probability thresholding still resulted in 60 FN predictions (missed LNMs). Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a decisive fail-safe mechanism to address this residual risk. It successfully intercepted all 60 initially missed instances by classifying them as HU. This “rescue effect” secured a 100% conditional sensitivity across the entire test cohort, effectively neutralizing the clinical risk of missed diagnoses.    Fig. 4   Pan-cancer generalization performance across 14 primary origins.  The multi-center multi-cancer independent test cohort is stratified into common and rare origins. Primary sites are sorted by WSI count and color-coded: purple (Trained) and mint green (Unseen). Rows display: (1) Total WSI counts; (2) Metastatic status distribution (red: metastatic; blue: non-metastatic); (3) LN-level conditional sensitivity (maintaining 100% via uncertainty referral); (4) False Positive (FP) rate; and (5) High Uncertainty (HU) rate. Color intensity reflects numerical magnitude.                   The operational cost of this safety profile was quantified using the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N). Accounting for the union of FP and HU predictions, the effective RBR-N was 26.8% (3180/11,873). This indicates that 73.2% of negative LNs were safely excluded from manual review.  Subgroup analysis revealed remarkable consistency across organ origins, with a weighted average FP rate of 7.5% (SD: 2.1%) (Fig.  4 ). For the seven cancer types included in training, performance remained stable regardless of sample size. Notably, although Stomach cancer LNs were overrepresented in the training data (35.6%), their performance (HU rate: 5.2%; FP rate: 6.6%) closely mirrored the cohort average, indicating that the model maintained balanced discriminative power despite the non-uniform training distribution. While robust to sample size variations, the model exhibited sensitivity to specific non-neoplastic histological features. LNs from the lung and cervix exhibited higher HU rates (32.6% and 26.0%, respectively). Pathological audit confirmed that in lung cancer, these flags were predominantly triggered by anthracitic pigment, indicating that the model correctly identified non-malignant confounders as HU regions (SFig.  11 ).  Most notably, the system demonstrated exceptional adaptability to the seven cancer types entirely unseen during training. The fail-safe mechanism remained fully effective even in these out-of-distribution domains, with zero missed diagnoses recorded. Regarding efficiency, the model maintained consistently low LN-level FP rates for the majority of these unseen origins (6/7), ranging from 2.4% (kidney) to 10.8% (thyroid) without fine-tuning. The sole exception was penile cancer (SFig.  8 ), a rare type with complex morphology, where the system exhibited an adaptive increase in review rates (HU: 30.2%; FP: 20.0%). This reflects a cautious inference strategy that prioritizes diagnostic safety when encountering highly atypical histological patterns.    Interpretability and pathological characterization of uncertainty  To elucidate the interpretability underlying this robust performance, we deconstructed the uncertainty landscape. Multiscale feature fusion dimensionality reduction analysis (Fig.  5a, b ) clearly delineated tumor and normal regions, with HU areas concentrated at the boundaries in feature space. We were able to effectively extract these areas through uncertainty quantification.    Fig. 5   Visualization and interpretation of uncertainty estimation.   a ,  b  t-SNE visualization of tile-level feature embeddings from the internal validation dataset.  a  Binary prediction distribution (red: tumor; blue: normal), with triangles indicating misclassified samples.  b  Uncertainty level distribution (yellow: High Uncertainty [HU]; blue: Low Uncertainty [LU]), showing HU samples concentrating at the tumor-normal decision boundary.  c  Pathological categorization of HU clusters identifying four non-neoplastic confounders: dense connective tissue (orange), loose connective tissue (teal), bleeding (green), and low-quality regions (blue).  d  Representative heatmaps displaying spatial distributions of HU regions (yellow) alongside tumor (red) and normal (blue) predictions.  e  Clinical workflow illustration: HU predictions trigger pathologist re-review, with IHC confirmation reserved for challenging cases.                   Further analysis allowed categorization of HU regions into types such as dense connective tissue, loose connective tissue, low-quality image areas, and bleeding areas (Fig.  5c ). As shown in Fig.  5d , the model assigned high HU scores to two patients with distinct atypical cytomorphology: one with lymphocyte-like tumor cells featuring scant cytoplasm and naked nuclei, and another exhibiting plasmacytoid/histiocytoid features with moderate cytoplasm. This assessment mechanism enables pathologists to selectively focus on these challenging cases, thereby ensuring diagnostic accuracy and clinical safety while improving efficiency. As the system continues to be applied, manual review of uncertain regions will facilitate ongoing model optimization (Fig.  5e ).     Discussion  This study addresses the limitations of current organ-specific AI paradigms by presenting UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware framework for pan-cancer LNM diagnosis. While previous deep learning approaches have validated LNM detection in organ-specific cohorts, they often operate as “black boxes,” lacking the safety mechanisms required for broad clinical adoption  20  . By devising a specialized Multiscale cross-attention framework to effectively contextualize features from the pathology foundation model, UPATHLN establishes a robust clinical safety net. Notably, this architectural design demonstrated a definitive “fail-safe” capability in a large-scale independent cohort: the uncertainty mechanism successfully intercepted all initially missed metastases, securing 100% conditional sensitivity. This achievement marks a significant advancement: moving from algorithms that prioritize raw accuracy to safety-critical systems that effectively mitigate the risk of FNs in metastatic screening.  The parallel uncertainty estimation branch underpins the technical integrity of this safety profile. Classical uncertainty estimation methods—such as uncertainty-prediction model co-training  28 , 29  , multiple model ensembles  30  , or repeated dropout strategies  28 , 31  —increase computational burden and often flag large unnecessary regions for manual reassessment. By contrast, our independent bypass architecture provides precise localization of diagnostically uncertain regions without compromising inference speed. This decoupled mechanism acts as a reliable diagnostic filter, specifically designed to handle the inherent biological heterogeneity of metastatic disease. It respects the ambiguity of “long-tail” rare variants and non-neoplastic confounders (e.g., anthracotic pigment), routing these cases strictly within the system’s competence boundaries. This “rescue effect” ensures that algorithmic limitations do not translate into diagnostic errors, maintaining high reliability even when encountering complex morphologies that typically confound conventional models.  Furthermore, we successfully navigated the data annotation bottleneck that typically constrains the scalability of foundation models. By coupling high-level feature representations with an uncertainty-guided active learning framework, we efficiently captured a comprehensive spectrum of metastatic morphologies across 14 cancer types without necessitating exhaustive annotation. This strategy proved vital for addressing the diverse patterns of metastatic pathology. Consequently, the system maintained robust performance even on LNM samples from primary sites entirely unseen during training. This demonstrates that uncertainty-driven learning provides a practical, scalable pathway to generalize pathology AI, enabling adaptability to domain shifts and rare cancer types lacking large-scale training data.  UPATHLN reconciles the critical tension between rising diagnostic volumes and the demand for granular prognostic assessment. By safely automating the exclusion of 73.2% of negative LNs, the system liberates pathologists to focus on complex cases. Crucially, this efficiency renders detailed “multi-dimensional analysis”—specifically the precise quantification of tumor-to-lymph node area ratio  12   and spatial distribution patterns—feasible in routine practice. Moving beyond crude pN staging, UPATHLN provides the quantitative depth required for modern precision oncology that is practically impossible to achieve manually.  Despite these advances, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study is retrospective, and all training/validation data were sourced from hospitals in China; therefore, real-world deployment requires prospective multi-center evaluation and external validation across diverse populations, institutions, and scanning protocols. Second, although many artifacts are appropriately flagged as high uncertainty, future work could incorporate dedicated artifact-suppression or quality-control modules to further reduce review burden without compromising safety. Third, while the pipeline is designed to be compatible with different pathology foundation models, we only evaluated UNI and did not empirically compare performance against alternative encoders.  Collectively, UPATHLN advances pan-cancer LNM screening by introducing a risk-aware architecture that balances automation with expert oversight. The synergy between its decoupled uncertainty “fail-safe” and active learning framework ensures robust performance and scalability under heterogeneous clinical conditions. This approach not only streamlines routine triage but also provides a quantitative basis for assessing metastatic burden, potentially informing prognostic insights beyond standard pathological staging.    Methods   Dataset collection and cohort definition  We established a large-scale, pan-cancer dataset combining clinical data from three independent medical centers, with heterogeneous clinical workloads and patient populations, enabling evaluation across varied real-world settings. The primary clinical cohort included 2738 patients (8294 WSIs, 26,229 LNs) covering 14 distinct solid tumor types (SFig.  1a ). We applied specific exclusion criteria to ensure data quality: WSIs exhibiting severe artefacts—such as tissue folding covering >20% of the area, significant out-of-focus blurring, or extreme staining inconsistencies—were removed prior to analysis. In addition to the clinical cohort, we utilized an annotated gastric cancer dataset from our previous work  12   (GLN21) and the publicly available breast cancer dataset from the CAMELYON16 challenge  11   (BLN16) for model initialization.  Crucially, to prevent data leakage, we employed a strict patient-level splitting strategy, where all WSIs and LN sections from the same patient were assigned exclusively to a single cohort. As illustrated in the study design flow (SFig.  3 ), the clinical data were stratified into two independent cohorts. The development cohort consisted of 683 patients (2547 WSIs, 9729 LNs) from 7 common cancer types and was further subdivided to support the active learning workflow (SFig.  1b ). The multi-center multi-cancer test cohort comprised an independent set of 2055 patients (5747 WSIs, 16,500 LNs), serving as the held-out standard for final performance evaluation (SFig.  1c ). To rigorously assess the model’s generalization capabilities, the test cohort was stratified into two groups: the 7 cancer types encountered during training and a distinct set of 7 cancer types (thyroid, pancreas, bile duct, kidney, prostate, penis, and anus). Crucially, samples from these rare origins were strictly excluded from the training pipeline, ensuring that their evaluation represents a true test of the model’s ability to generalize to completely unseen primary origins. For LN counting, pathologists manually reviewed the slides to identify spatially distinct LNs; serial sections of the same node, if present, were identified based on morphological continuity and excluded from the total count to ensure each observation represented a unique LN.  This retrospective, multi-center study was conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Changhai Hospital (CHEC2024-276), the Ethics Committee of the Second People’s Hospital of Wuxi (2024Y-125), and the Ethics Committee of the 960th Hospital of the People’s Liberation Army (2024-087). The requirement for informed consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the use of anonymized data.    Lymph node contour recognition  To increase the training accuracy of LN metastasis detection models, we first developed an LN contour recognition model. The WSIs of LN tissue include not only LNs but also muscle, extraneous fat, and cancer nodules. The presence of these nontarget tissues can adversely affect the accuracy of metastasis detection.  Our model comprises two stages: initially, the YOLOv8-s model is employed for LN detection due to its high efficiency and rapid localization capabilities. The detected regions are subsequently input into the nnUNet  32   model for segmentation to remove impurities from the LN periphery.  We processed images using 1024 × 1024 pixel tiles at 1× magnification and utilized a 256-pixel sliding window for segmentation. The YOLOv8-s model was trained with default parameters, using the annotated contour coordinates as ground truth labels. The nnUNet model was similarly trained with default settings, using the bounding box of annotated regions to cut tiles at 0.25× magnification and employing annotated contours as masks.  During inference, a staged strategy was employed: YOLOv8-s model-predicted coordinates were used to cut local tiles, which were then input into the nnUNet model to obtain precise contour masks. These masks were mapped back to the full 0.25x thumbnail based on relative coordinates. For overlapping sliding windows, an averaging method was used to smooth boundaries.  We annotated 200 WSIs with 721 LNs from various tumor types for the YOLOv8-s model and nnUNet model training. After initial training, predictions of unannotated WSIs in the development cohort were manually reviewed. We reviewed 918 WSIs (comprising 3528 LNs) and reannotated 132 WSIs with incorrect predictions. Then, the YOLOv8-s model was retrained on a combined dataset of the initial 200 annotated WSIs and the 918 manually reviewed WSIs (total 1118 WSIs; randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing). Ultimately, the YOLOv8-s model achieved a recall rate of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection.  Since nnUNet requires contour-level annotations, we used the initial 200 WSIs along with the 132 fully corrected WSIs (comprising 1245 LNs) for retraining. Finally, the nnUNet model achieved a mean Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for LN contour segmentation. A manual review of inference results from the development cohort confirmed the ability of the two-stage model to accurately delineate LN contours and exclude non-LN tissues. This process provides high-quality input data for subsequent metastasis detection. As illustrated in SFig.  2a , we effectively identified and extracted LN contours from complex pathological images, facilitating high-quality input for further metastasis detection. Some missed LN diagnoses are due to atypical morphology (e.g., indistinct capsules) or small nodal size (SFig.  2b ). In clinical applications, missed LN identification is rare, so it does not increase the workload. Pathologists can easily add annotations during the review process. As missed diagnosis cases continue to be collected, this situation will become increasingly rare. The annotation and review process was conducted by two senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience: Y.C. and C.Q.    Data preprocessing for the classification model  Following the extraction of LN contour regions from WSIs, we tiled tumor metastasis areas on the basis of annotations to train the classification model. Given that accurate diagnosis of some LN metastases requires multiscale observations, we applied multiscale tiling to the annotated dataset. This process involved extracting image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both 10x and 4× magnification, as shown in Fig.  2a . The center coordinates of tiles at both scales were aligned to ensure consistent observation of the same region at different resolutions.  By integrating the LN contour mask with the tumor mask, we cropped regions of interest into tumor and nontumor areas. At 10× magnification, a sliding window of 64 pixels was used to divide the region into extractable tiles, with each grid classified on the basis of the proportion of the tumor area annotated by doctors. Specifically, if more than 25% of a grid area was annotated as a tumor, the tile was labeled positive; otherwise, it was labeled negative. To ensure category balance, if the number of tiles in any category exceeded 100 within a WSI, we randomly selected 100 tiles. This sampling strategy maintained balanced categories at the tile level.    Feature extractor  In this study, we utilized UNI  23  , a Vision Transformer (ViT-Large  33  ) foundation model pre-trained on over 100,000 HE-stained WSIs, as a frozen feature extractor. UNI was selected as it represented a leading solution for pan-cancer feature representation at the time of study implementation. Importantly, our proposed multiscale architecture is designed to be foundation-model agnostic. While UNI was employed here as a representative high-performance encoder to validate our framework, the system is compatible with and can readily incorporate other emerging pathology foundation models  22 , 24 – 27  . For feature extraction, we processed image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both the 10× and the 4× magnification levels and randomly cropped them to 224 × 224 pixels. The resulting feature matrix for each tile maintains a shape of (196 + 1, 1024), where 196 represents the length of the patch-tokens, and 1 represents the class token.    Multiscale feature fusion and classification module  By extracting features from the same local region at different magnification levels and then fusing them, the model can capture both global and local pathological morphological features, better locating and identifying tumor areas. Specifically, we adopted the cross-attention module proposed by Zhou et al.  34   to multiscale image feature fusion. As shown in Fig.  2a , the entire cross-attention module consists of two cross-attention blocks and two self-attention blocks. The cross-attention blocks learn the intrinsic connections of multiscale image features by dynamically weighting features from different spatial scales.  In the cross-attention block, the process of generating Q, K, and V for each scale image feature is as follows:   1      Q    4  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x    =  LP     Norm       X    4  x              2      Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    =  LP     Norm       X    10  x             where     LP     ⋅        denotes linear projection and     Norm     ⋅        denotes layer normalization. The forwards pass in the cross-attention block can be summarized as:   3      P    4  x    =  Attn  (    Q    4  x  ′      K    4  x  ,      V    4  x    )  +  Attn  (    Q    4  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )      4      P    10  x    =  Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )  +  Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x    )     where     Attn  (    Q    4  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x      ) and     Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )     capture the intra-scale feature relationships. The intermediate expression  P  represents the potential connections obtained through interaction between the 4x and 10× magnification images. The attention mechanism     Attn     Q  ,  K  ,  V        includes two matrices multiplication operations, a scaling operation, and a softmax operation:   5    Attn  (  Q  ,  K  ,  V  )  =  softmax         QK    T          d    k           V     where    T    denotes the matrix transpose operator and     d  k     is the scaling hyperparameter set to 64. Next, the residual learning approach incorporates the resulting  P   4x   and  P   10x   into the normalization layer and multiple layer perceptron (MLP):   6      X    4  x    ′  =  MLP  (  Norm  (    P    4  x    )  )  +    X    4  x        7      X    10  x    ′  =  MLP     Norm     P  10  x        +    X    10  x       where     X   4    x   ′       and     X   10    x   ′       represent the inputs fed into the next cross-attention block.  Subsequently, we merged the cross-attention features by concatenating the tokens directly, resulting in a new feature embedding with a shape of (197 + 197,1024).  Finally, we input the new feature embedding into two self-attention modules, followed by LayerNorm normalization. The class token from the feature embedding is then used as the overall feature  F , which is fed into a fully connected layer to predict the tumor probability of the 10x tile.  During training, the parameters of the UNI pretrained ViT-Large feature extractor were fixed, and no backpropagation optimization was performed. We used ColorJitter from Torchvision for transformation with the following parameters: maximum increments of 0.1 for brightness, 0.2 for contrast, 0.2 for saturation, and 0.15 for hue. The tiles were also randomly flipped and rotated by 15°. To address the imbalance between positive and negative samples, we perform balanced sampling of positive and negative samples at the initialization of each epoch. We calculated the loss via cross-entropy between the predicted probabilities and the true labels and optimized it via adaptive moment estimation with weight decay (AdamW) during training, with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate was managed via a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and ending at 1e-6 over 40 epochs. All training and testing were performed on six NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.    Uncertainty estimation module  Deploying deep learning models across multi-center pan-cancer cohorts inevitably introduces challenges related to histological heterogeneity, variable data quality, and out-of-distribution inputs that essentially differ from the training distribution. In such scenarios, enforcing deterministic predictions often leads to high-confidence errors. To address this, we incorporated a parallel uncertainty estimation module into our diagnostic framework. The primary objective of this module is to quantify the reliability of region-level predictions, serving a dual purpose: guiding model optimization through active learning during development and acting as a trigger for pathologist review during clinical inference.  Diverging from conventional approaches that rely on computationally expensive ensembles or require joint training with classification objectives (which may destabilize the primary task)  28 – 31  , we implemented a sequential optimization strategy. Specifically, the uncertainty branch is trained as an independent architectural bypass only after the multiscale classifier parameters are frozen. This design ensures that the uncertainty mechanism is specifically calibrated to the fixed decision boundary of the main model. Consequently, this approach enables precise confidence estimation without compromising the original diagnostic performance, while incurring negligible computational overhead.  Specifically, we implemented this module by adapting the uncertainty estimation algorithm for pretrained models proposed by Kirchhof et al .   35  . As shown in Fig.  2a , using the same feature  F  as the classification model input, we passed it through the uncertainty estimation module comprising three fully connected layers with 512 hidden units and LeakyReLU intermediate activations, outputting a single value normalized by the Softplus function to ensure positivity. We used mean squared error (MSE) loss, comparing the uncertainty module’s predictions with labels derived from the classification model’s forward propagation loss, computed at runtime with backpropagation disabled. Crucially, this design provides an intuitive measure of reliability: a high predicted loss indicates that the model anticipates a likely error on the input, thereby flagging it as a “High Uncertainty” (HU) region for pathologist review.  The loss function is defined as:   8     L  uncertainty   =   1  N    ∑   i  =  1   N        u  i   −   L   pred  i       2      where    u    is the uncertainty module’s predicted value and      L    pred      is the loss from the classification model’s forwards propagation.  The training process employed the same data and sampling strategy as those of the classification module. We used the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate followed a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and decreasing to 1e-6 over 10 epochs.    Uncertainty-driven active learning strategy  To address tumor heterogeneity and optimize annotation efficiency, we implemented a human-in-the-loop, uncertainty-driven active learning framework structured into five distinct iterations (Fig.  1d  and SFig.  3 ). To facilitate this process, the clinically derived development cohort (683 patients) was partitioned into two functional subsets via random patient-level sampling: a large unlabeled candidate pool of 594 patients (2245 WSIs, 8832 LNs) available for selection, and a strictly held-out internal validation set of 89 patients (302 WSIs, 897 LNs). Notably, the internal validation set was comprehensively annotated at the lesion level prior to the active learning process. This set remained fixed throughout the study and served as a reliable ground truth to monitor model convergence and determine hyperparameters without biasing the training process.  The training workflow commenced with an initialization phase (Iteration 1), where the baseline model was trained solely on the fully annotated initialization datasets (GLN21 and BLN16) to establish foundational detection capabilities. Subsequently, we conducted four consecutive rounds of uncertainty-driven refinement (Iterations 2–5). In each round, the model performed inference on the unlabeled candidate pool to compute tile-level uncertainty scores      u    i      (derived from the uncertainty module). WSIs were then prioritized for expert review according to a slide-level diagnostic ambiguity score. Specifically, for a given WSI with N tiles, we defined ambiguity as the mean uncertainty of the top K most uncertain tiles:   9    A   (   W  S  I   )   =    1    K      ∑    i  ϵ  T  o  p  −  K      u    i    ,  K  =   ⌈   0.05  ⋅  N   ⌉      Here,     Top  −  K     denotes the set of tiles with the largest uncertainty scores within that WSI, and ┌.┐ is the ceiling operator. WSIs were ranked by     A     WSI        in descending order and selected for pathologist review.  Specifically, the top 200 WSIs were selected in iterations 2 and 3, while the top 100 WSIs were selected in iterations 4 and 5. Senior pathologists reviewed these flagged samples to correct FPs and verify missed metastases. After each review phase, the corrected samples were incorporated into the expanded training set.    Data annotation and establishment of ground truth  To satisfy the distinct requirements of model development and independent validation, we implemented a two-tier annotation strategy conducted by senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience (Y.C., C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.).  For the development cohort, pathologists performed exhaustive region-level annotations on WSIs selected for the expanded training set and the internal validation set. This involved delineating precise boundaries for all LNs and contouring all internal metastatic foci. This process ensured that the model received high-granularity supervision for distinct metastatic morphologies, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cells (ITCs). During active learning iterations, regions flagged as HU were specifically reviewed and corrected (C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.) to provide high-quality supervision for challenging examples.  For the independent test cohort, we established a rigorous diagnostic standard to evaluate clinical safety. Instead of pixel-level contours, we focused on the definitive metastatic status of each LN. Two senior pathologists (Y.C. and C.Q.) independently reviewed all WSIs. Discrepant cases were adjudicated by a consensus panel. To resolve diagnostic ambiguity in morphologically challenging cases, we performed confirmatory immunohistochemical (IHC) staining (CAM5.2 and AE1/AE3) on 52 challenging cases to determine the final ground truth (SFig.  12 ). This process ensured a non-ambiguous “Positive/Negative” label for every LN in the test set.    Statistical analysis  The detection (YOLOv8-s) and segmentation (nnUNet) models were implemented with probability thresholds of 0.25 and 0.50, respectively. For the classification model, the binary decision threshold was set at 0.50. The uncertainty threshold for each iteration was determined empirically using the Internal Validation Set. To balance the trade-off between the volume of regions flagged for review and FP predictions, we selected the threshold at the intersection point where the average High Uncertainty area per slide (HUavg) equalled the average False Positive area per slide (FPavg) (SFig.  13 ). Isolated positive predictions approximately the size of one tile (3600 μm²) were excluded from analysis owing to resolution constraints.  To comprehensively evaluate the system, we defined detection and classification targets at three distinct levels. Tile-level performance measures the fundamental classification accuracy of individual 256 × 256 pixel image patches, where a tile is labeled positive if tumor tissue comprises >25% of its area. Lesion-level (Region) performance evaluates the model’s ability to correctly localize and classify contiguous metastatic areas (including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and ITCs) within the LN tissue, distinct from simple tile-level accuracy. LN-level performance serves as the primary clinical unit for N-staging; an LN is considered positive if the model identifies at least one metastatic lesion within the nodal area.  We defined specific metrics to assess the safety and efficiency of the proposed human-AI collaborative workflow. Conditional classification sensitivity evaluates the classification performance specifically on all LNs successfully localized by the detection module. For performance evaluation, regions flagged as HU (highlighted in yellow in the prediction heatmaps) were considered positive for sensitivity calculations, as these areas require pathologist review in clinical practice. To quantify workload, we defined the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N) as the proportion of true-negative LNs that required high-magnification manual review. An LN contributes to this burden if it contains any region predicted as False Positive (FP) or High Uncertainty (HU).  Bootstrap analysis (1000 iterations) was performed to calculate 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all performance metrics. AUCs were compared using DeLong’s test (two-sided). evidence_text: Calibration-Aware Patient-Level Prediction of Source-Defined MSIMUT Status in Colorectal Cancer from Whole-Slide Histopathology Images Using Foundation-Model Embeddings. Background/Objectives: Microsatellite instability (MSI) is clinically important in colorectal cancer, but definitive assessment requires molecular or immunohistochemical testing. This study developed a leakage-safe, calibration-aware patient-level framework for predicting a source-defined MSIMUT category from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide-derived patches using fixed Phikon foundation-model embeddings. Methods: The TCGA-derived colorectal cohort comprised 360 patients, including 65 source-defined positive and 295 MSS cases, represented by 192,312 pre-extracted patches. Patch embeddings were aggregated using mean, max, and mean-plus-max pooling, and downstream classifiers were evaluated under patient-level cross-validation with calibration, threshold, decision-curve, clinicopathological, source-provenance, and patch-count sensitivity analyses. Results: In the primary random patient-level evaluation, logistic regression with mean-plus-max pooling achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.915 and PR-AUC of 0.809. Fully nested Platt calibration yielded pooled out-of-sample ROC-AUC 0.913, PR-AUC 0.796, Brier score 0.073, calibration slope 1.037, and calibration-in-the-large 0.023. Within the internally cross-validated mean-plus-max framework, an exploratory sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point yielded sensitivity 0.969, specificity 0.393, and negative predictive value 0.983. Provenance reconstruction identified source-partition-dependent patch-count structure. In a source-TRAIN to source-TEST holdout, mean-plus-max ROC-AUC decreased to 0.788, while patch count alone was near chance in source-TEST (ROC-AUC 0.517) and explicit patch-count addition did not improve discrimination. Conclusions: These findings support the methodological feasibility of fixed foundation-model embeddings for internal MSI-related pre-screening research, while showing that apparent performance is sensitive to source structure. Independent multicenter validation with clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR endpoints remains necessary before clinical application. 1. Introduction Microsatellite instability (MSI) is a molecular phenotype resulting from deficient DNA mismatch repair and the consequent accumulation of insertion and deletion errors within repetitive genomic regions [ 1 , 2 ]. In colorectal cancer, MSI is associated with a distinct hypermutated tumor biology and has important implications for prognostic assessment, therapeutic stratification, and response to immune checkpoint blockade [ 1 , 3 ]. Although MSI is defined at the molecular level, MSI-high tumors may also exhibit recognizable histomorphological and immune-related characteristics on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections, including prominent lymphocytic infiltration, mucinous differentiation, architectural heterogeneity, and variation in the tumor microenvironment [ 1 , 3 , 4 ]. This relationship between molecular status and tissue morphology makes MSI a particularly relevant target for computational pathology, in which routinely acquired histological images can be analyzed as high-dimensional biomedical data. In current clinical practice, MSI or mismatch repair status is generally assessed using polymerase chain reaction-based microsatellite testing or immunohistochemistry for the mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 [ 1 , 3 ]. These established approaches remain essential for definitive biomarker assessment but require testing beyond routine morphological examination. By contrast, H&E-stained slides are already generated as part of standard histopathological workflows and may contain image-level correlates of the underlying molecular phenotype. Computational analysis of these routinely available images has therefore been investigated as a potential pre-screening approach for identifying patients who may benefit from prioritized confirmatory testing [ 4 , 5 ]. Such methods should not be considered replacements for validated molecular or immunohistochemical assays, but rather as complementary strategies that may support prioritization within existing diagnostic pathways. The digitization of histopathological slides has enabled artificial intelligence methods to extract clinically relevant information from whole-slide images. Landmark work by Kather et al. demonstrated that deep learning could predict MSI directly from H&E-stained histological images of gastrointestinal cancers, establishing an important proof of concept for image-based molecular biomarker inference [ 5 ]. Subsequent studies and reviews have expanded this evidence base and further demonstrated the potential of computational pathology for MSI prediction [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. However, the published literature also shows substantial heterogeneity in cohort composition, class prevalence, image preprocessing, model architecture, validation design, reference standards, and clinical framing [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. The central question has therefore progressed beyond whether MSI-associated information is present in histomorphology to how this information should be represented, validated, and interpreted to support reliable, transparently evaluated, and potentially transferable patient-level inference. Methodological rigor is particularly important in whole-slide image analysis because individual patients may contribute multiple slides and thousands of correlated image patches. If these observations are partitioned without preserving patient-level independence, related samples may occur in both the training and evaluation sets, creating information leakage and producing optimistically biased performance estimates [ 8 ]. Moreover, discrimination alone does not fully characterize the potential relevance of a biomarker prediction model. Although the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) summarizes the ability of a model to rank positive and negative cases, it does not establish whether predicted probabilities are appropriately calibrated, whether operating thresholds suitable for a proposed use can be identified, or whether model-guided action may offer net benefit relative to default strategies [ 9 , 10 , 11 ]. Evaluation should therefore extend to class-imbalance-sensitive metrics, uncertainty estimation, probability calibration, threshold-dependent performance, and decision-analytic assessment. Robustness to variation in the amount of available tissue information is also relevant because whole-slide images may differ substantially in tissue area and patch burden. Accordingly, an unresolved methodological need is a patient-level framework that combines strict leakage control with calibration, operating-point analysis, decision curve evaluation, and representation-robustness assessment. Task-specific end-to-end deep-learning pipelines can require substantial computational resources, extensive model optimization, and careful management of cohort-dependent effects [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. Pathology foundation models provide a modular alternative by learning transferable representations from large and heterogeneous histopathology collections [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. In an embedding-based workflow, image patches are processed using a fixed pretrained encoder, after which the resulting feature vectors can be aggregated into slide- or patient-level representations for downstream prediction. This separation of representation learning from task-specific classification reduces the need for repeated end-to-end retraining and allows the effects of representation design, classifier selection, calibration, and robustness to be examined within a common feature space. Within such a framework, deterministic mean and max pooling provide a transparent means of testing whether pretrained embeddings retain sufficient globally distributed and locally salient information without introducing an additional trainable attention mechanism. The resulting representations can then be evaluated using comparatively simple downstream models, improving analytical traceability and facilitating representation-level interpretation. Nevertheless, latent embedding dimensions should not be assumed to correspond directly to specific microscopic structures, and an embedding-based workflow does not eliminate the computational burden of patch extraction and foundation-model inference. Against this background, the present study developed and internally evaluated a calibration-aware, leakage-safe, and decision-support-oriented framework for patient-level prediction of the source-defined MSIMUT category using a publicly available TCGA-linked colorectal cancer patch archive derived from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images [ 15 , 16 ]. The source repository defines MSIMUT as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated; accordingly, this category was treated as the positive analytical endpoint and was not assumed to be equivalent to a uniformly assay-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR outcome. The verified cohort comprised 360 patients, and patch-level features were extracted using the fixed Phikon pathology foundation model [ 17 ]. Mean pooling, max pooling, and their concatenation were evaluated for constructing patient-level representations, and multiple downstream classifiers were compared under strict patient-level separation. Evaluation extended beyond conventional discrimination analysis by incorporating repeated patient-level validation, bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation, leakage-safe nested probability calibration, threshold-based screening assessment, decision curve analysis, pooling-strategy comparison, patch-burden sensitivity analysis, and representation-level interpretability. The objective was to determine whether fixed Phikon-derived histopathology embeddings could support informative patient-level prediction that remained stable across alternative internal patient-level partitions, without end-to-end retraining, while explicitly characterizing probability behavior, operating-point trade-offs, potential decision-analytic relevance, and representation robustness. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design, Data Source, and Cohort Assembly This retrospective computational pathology study investigated patient-level prediction of microsatellite instability-related status using a publicly available colorectal histopathology patch dataset derived from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images. The patient was prespecified as the fundamental analytical unit because individual cases could contribute multiple correlated image-derived observations. Maintaining patient-level independence was intended to preserve the clinical interpretation of the prediction task and to reduce the risk of information leakage and optimistically biased performance estimates [ 6 , 8 ]. Accordingly, patient-level separation was maintained throughout representation construction and model evaluation. The overall study workflow is summarized in Figure 1 . Figure 1 Overview of the patient-level MSI prediction workflow. Whole-slide-derived histopathology patches and their source-defined MSIMUT/MSS labels were obtained from a publicly available TCGA-derived colorectal cancer dataset. The pre-extracted image patches were encoded using the original Phikon pathology foundation model and aggregated into patient-level representations. Candidate classifiers were evaluated under patient-level validation, and the selected model subsequently underwent uncertainty estimation, leakage-safe nested probability calibration, threshold-based assessment, decision curve analysis, robustness evaluation, and representation-level interpretation. Whole-slide-derived colorectal histopathology patches were obtained from a publicly available colorectal-only JPEG derivative [ 18 ] of the FFPE image dataset originally published by Kather et al. [ 16 ] and generated from TCGA diagnostic slides. The distributed archive was organized into source-defined MSIMUT and microsatellite-stable (MSS) categories. TCGA patient identifiers encoded in the patch filenames were extracted programmatically to reconstruct patient-level groups and to preserve the association between each patch and its source case. The source-provided category labels were used as the reference outcome for supervised prediction; no local relabeling or additional pathological annotation was performed. Patient-level groups were retained when the archive contained image patches with an extractable TCGA case identifier and a corresponding source-defined category label. No new participants were recruited, no intervention or specimen collection was undertaken, and no identifiable patient information was analyzed. Following reconstruction and verification of the patient-level groups, the final analytical cohort comprised 360 patients, including 65 patients in the source-defined MSIMUT category and 295 patients in the MSS category. The positive category therefore represented 18.1% of the cohort, resulting in a class-imbalanced prediction problem. The approaches used to preserve class distribution during validation and to evaluate performance under class imbalance are described in the subsequent methodological sections. The verified cohort was held fixed throughout all representation construction, model evaluation, and robustness analyses, ensuring consistency between cohort definition and reported performance [ 6 , 8 ]. No independent external validation cohort was available for the present study. Accordingly, all discrimination, calibration, threshold, decision-analytic, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses should be interpreted as internal evaluations of the TCGA-derived cohort. Additional internal sensitivity analyses were designed to examine potential site- and clinicopathological confounding within this cohort, but they were not considered substitutes for independent multicenter validation across different institutions, staining protocols, scanners, specimen-processing workflows, or patient populations.
