Reconstructed Source-Partition Holdout Analysis The original source-defined TRAIN/TEST partition of the upstream Kather dataset was successfully reconstructed for all 360 patients and all 192,312 analyzed patches, with no patient overlap between the two partitions. The reconstructed source-TRAIN set comprised 260 patients (39 source-defined MSIMUT and 221 MSS), whereas the source-TEST set comprised 100 patients (26 MSIMUT and 74 MSS). At the patch level, source-TRAIN contained 46,704 MSIMUT and 46,704 MSS patches, whereas source-TEST contained 28,335 MSIMUT and 70,569 MSS patches. These values refer to image files reconstructed from the available source filename manifest and matched to the analytical cohort. The source-documented random reduction of the larger MSS training-patch set provides a direct mechanism for the class-dependent patch-count structure observed in source-TRAIN. This partition therefore provided a provenance-defined holdout that was distinct from the random patient-level folds used in the primary cross-validation analysis. When the prespecified logistic-regression pipeline was fitted exclusively on source-TRAIN and evaluated once on the untouched source-TEST cohort, the mean-only representation achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.794 (95% CI, 0.671–0.898), PR-AUC of 0.668 (95% CI, 0.511–0.843), and Brier score of 0.174 (95% CI, 0.111–0.243). Max-only pooling yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.766 (95% CI, 0.655–0.861), PR-AUC of 0.548 (95% CI, 0.408–0.716), and Brier score of 0.263 (95% CI, 0.195–0.335). The mean-plus-max representation achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.788 (95% CI, 0.679–0.881), PR-AUC of 0.593 (95% CI, 0.446–0.767), and Brier score of 0.259 (95% CI, 0.189–0.333). Thus, discrimination remained above chance under the reconstructed source holdout, but performance was attenuated relative to the original random-fold evaluation, and the numerical ordering of the pooling representations differed from that observed in the primary analysis. In paired bootstrap comparisons on the same source-TEST patients, the ROC-AUC difference between mean-only and mean-plus-max pooling was 0.0057 (95% CI, −0.0764 to 0.0852), whereas the difference between mean-only and max-only pooling was 0.0281 (95% CI, −0.0759 to 0.1289). Both confidence intervals included zero, providing no clear evidence of a pairwise ROC-AUC difference among these representations in the source-holdout cohort. Accordingly, the numerically higher mean-only performance in source-TEST should not be interpreted as demonstrating superiority over the combined representation. Patch-count discrimination was strongly dependent on the reconstructed source partition. Raw patient patch count yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.918 and PR-AUC of 0.815 within source-TRAIN but only a ROC-AUC of 0.517 and PR-AUC of 0.330 within source-TEST. The near-chance ROC-AUC in source-TEST contrasts with the stronger patch-count association observed in the pooled cohort and demonstrates that patch burden was not a stable discriminator across the predefined source partition. Explicitly adding log1p-transformed patch count to the image-derived representations did not materially improve source-TEST discrimination. The count-only logistic-regression model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.5169 and PR-AUC of 0.3301. Adding patch count changed ROC-AUC only minimally for mean-only pooling (0.7937 to 0.7957; paired ΔROC-AUC, 0.0021; 95% CI, −0.0218 to 0.0244), max-only pooling (0.7656 to 0.7640; Δ, −0.0016; 95% CI, −0.0078 to 0.0042), and mean-plus-max pooling (0.7879 to 0.7827; Δ, −0.0052; 95% CI, −0.0125 to 0.0000). Thus, explicit patch-count information did not provide a transportable improvement in the source-holdout setting. Taken together, the source-holdout analysis indicates that part of the apparent performance under random patient-level partitioning was sensitive to upstream source structure and patch-burden-related preprocessing history. Mean-only performance changed less across validation schemes, from ROC-AUC 0.820 in the primary fixed-fold analysis to 0.794 in source-TEST, whereas mean-plus-max performance decreased from 0.915 to 0.788. In this dataset, the more source-robust internal discrimination therefore appeared closer to the 0.79–0.82 range than to the primary random-fold mean-plus-max estimate. At the same time, image-derived representations retained moderate discriminatory information in the untouched source-TEST cohort despite the loss of patch-count discrimination and the lack of improvement after explicit patch-count addition. Because both source partitions originated from the same upstream TCGA-derived resource, these findings represent a source-structured internal robustness analysis rather than independent external validation. 3.7. Clinicopathological and Site-Related Sensitivity Analyses GDC linkage confirmed that the cohort contained both TCGA-COAD and TCGA-READ cases. Age, project identifier, broad pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, and primary diagnosis showed measurable associations with the source-defined outcome, indicating that clinicopathological structure was not independent of class assignment. TSS code also showed a non-negligible effect size, although its permutation-based association test did not reach the conventional 0.05 threshold. The clinical-only model achieved a mean fold ROC-AUC of 0.770 and PR-AUC of 0.433, whereas the image-only model achieved 0.915 and 0.809, respectively. Combining the available clinical variables with the image representation yielded mean ROC-AUC of 0.916 and PR-AUC of 0.808. In paired bootstrap analysis, the difference between the image-plus-clinical and image-only models was 0.0002 for ROC-AUC (95% CI, −0.0025 to 0.0031) and 0.0016 for PR-AUC (95% CI, −0.0059 to 0.0098), providing no clear evidence of incremental discrimination from these covariates under the evaluated pipeline. A TSS-only model showed limited discrimination, with a mean ROC-AUC of 0.586 and PR-AUC of 0.227. When all patients sharing a TSS were isolated entirely between training and test groups, mean ROC-AUC decreased to 0.867 ± 0.047 and mean PR-AUC to 0.714 ± 0.101. This attenuation indicates that source-site structure may contribute to the apparent predictive performance and should not be ignored; however, substantial discrimination remained under TSS-isolated internal validation. These internal sensitivity analyses reduce, but do not eliminate, concern regarding clinicopathological and site-related confounding. Detailed clinicopathological association, clinical-comparison, and TSS sensitivity results are provided in Supplementary Tables S16–S18 . 4. Discussion 4.1. Principal Findings This study developed a calibration-aware, patient-level framework for predicting the source-defined positive category from colorectal histopathology using fixed pathology foundation-model embeddings. Its principal contribution was not the introduction of another end-to-end image architecture, but the integration of leakage-safe patient-level modeling, uncertainty estimation, calibration assessment, threshold-dependent evaluation, decision curve analysis, representation testing, and interpretability within a single reproducible workflow. Within the internally evaluated cohort, this approach demonstrated that pretrained histopathology embeddings could support informative patient-level prediction without retraining the image encoder. Logistic regression provided the most favorable combined profile among the five prespecified classifier implementations, achieving a primary ROC-AUC of 0.915. Its selection reflected the predefined ranking procedure, probability quality, positive-class recovery, and model parsimony rather than formal statistical superiority over Linear SVM or MLP, which showed similar discrimination. Repeated cross-validation and bootstrap analyses indicated that performance was not narrowly dependent on a single random patient-level partition. However, the reconstructed source-partition analysis provided a more stringent provenance-based test: when the prespecified logistic-regression pipeline was trained on the reconstructed source-TRAIN cohort and evaluated on the untouched source-TEST cohort, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.915 in the primary random-fold analysis to 0.788 for the mean-plus-max representation. By contrast, the mean-only representation changed from 0.820 in the primary fixed-fold analysis to 0.794 in source-TEST. This pattern indicates that the magnitude of discrimination observed under random patient-level cross-validation, especially the apparent increment associated with adding max pooling, was partly sensitive to upstream source structure. The more source-robust internal discrimination observed here was therefore closer to approximately 0.79–0.82 than to the primary random-fold mean-plus-max estimate. Nevertheless, above-chance discrimination was retained in the source-defined holdout, supporting the presence of predictive information within the fixed embedding representation while arguing against interpreting the primary cross-validation estimate as source-independent performance. This substantially attenuated source-holdout performance was therefore treated as a central interpretive limitation of the framework rather than as a secondary sensitivity finding. The nested calibration analysis materially changed the interpretation of probability performance. When calibration-method selection was nested entirely within the outer-training data, Platt scaling was selected in all five folds. The uncalibrated predictions showed a calibration slope below 1 (0.403) with a CITL of 0.040. Because the primary logistic-regression model used a balanced-class objective and was evaluated within the present development cohort, these probability-scale characteristics were interpreted descriptively rather than attributed to a single source of calibration error. After leakage-safe nested Platt calibration, the calibration slope was 1.037 and CITL was 0.023, with the pooled Brier score improving from 0.076 to 0.073. The same-score audit further confirmed that Platt scaling preserved fold-specific ROC-AUC exactly, whereas isotonic regression could alter rank-based metrics through the introduction of tied probabilities. These results address the optimism inherent in the original post-hoc calibration comparison but remain internal estimates requiring external reassessment. The clinicopathological sensitivity analyses also qualify interpretation of the image-derived signal. Age, broad pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, project membership, and primary diagnosis were associated with the source-defined outcome, confirming that clinically relevant covariate structure is present within the cohort. Nevertheless, the clinical-only model discriminated substantially less well than the image model, and addition of the audited clinical variables produced essentially no incremental improvement over image-only prediction. TSS-group-isolated validation produced lower performance than the original fixed-fold analysis but retained substantial discrimination. The reconstructed source-holdout analysis showed a further attenuation of the primary mean-plus-max ROC-AUC from 0.915 under random patient-level cross-validation to 0.788 when training and testing followed the original source partition. Considered together, these analyses indicate that clinicopathological, site-related, and broader source-provenance structure can influence apparent model performance. At the same time, the persistence of above-chance discrimination under both TSS-isolated and source-holdout evaluation suggests that these measured source effects do not fully account for the predictive signal. Residual confounding by unmeasured morphological, specimen-related, preprocessing-related, or center-specific technical factors nevertheless cannot be excluded. Threshold analysis also showed that no single operating point was uniformly optimal. Lowering the threshold reduced missed source-defined positive cases but substantially increased the number of MSS patients prioritized for confirmatory assessment. At the sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point, 2 source-defined positive patients were missed, while 179 MSS patients were classified as positive. Decision curve analysis showed bootstrap-supported internal net-benefit superiority over the better default strategy only from approximately 0.055 through 0.30; the sensitivity ≥ 0.95 threshold of 0.0219 fell below this range. Moreover, these threshold and decision-curve analyses were derived from internally cross-validated mean-plus-max predictions and were not repeated in the reconstructed source-holdout setting. Together, these results support further investigation of the model as a candidate prioritization or pre-screening framework, but they do not justify withholding confirmatory testing or adopting the derived thresholds as clinical cutoffs. The representation analyses indicated that aggregation design was an important component of model performance. Within the original fixed-fold cross-validation analysis, mean-plus-max pooling provided the most favorable overall numerical profile, whereas max-only pooling outperformed mean-only pooling. This ordering was not preserved under the reconstructed source holdout: mean-only pooling yielded a numerically higher ROC-AUC than mean-plus-max and max-only pooling, although paired bootstrap confidence intervals for the representation-level ROC-AUC differences included zero. The change in numerical ordering across validation schemes indicates that the apparent advantage of a particular pooling strategy was partition dependent and should not be interpreted as evidence of intrinsic representation superiority. The predominance of max-pooled dimensions among the highest-ranked SHAP features is therefore not sufficient to support a morphological multiple-instance-learning interpretation. Because raw max-pooled embeddings strongly encoded patch count, highly ranked max-pooled SHAP dimensions may also capture patch-burden or source-preprocessing proxies. Within the primary fixed-fold analysis, the combined representation performed more favorably than max pooling alone, consistent with additional information being retained by the mean-pooled component. However, the lack of the same numerical ordering in the source-holdout analysis indicates that the relative value of the pooling components was not invariant to dataset partitioning. Because the explanations remained confined to latent dimensions, they cannot establish that the model detected specific tumor regions, lymphocytic infiltration, mucinous morphology, or other recognizable MSI-associated histopathological patterns. The patch-count analyses showed that interpretation of the max-pooled component requires additional caution. In the pooled cohort, source-defined positive patients had substantially more available patches than MSS patients, and patch count alone showed appreciable discrimination. The upstream source documentation indicates that the source TRAIN partition was patch-balanced by random reduction of the more numerous MSS training patches [ 16 ], providing a concrete provenance mechanism for at least part of the class-dependent patch-count structure. Because the probability of observing an extreme latent activation can increase with the number of available patches, part of the apparent advantage of max pooling may therefore reflect patch-burden or preprocessing structure rather than histopathological information alone. Consistent with this concern, performance was attenuated when a common fixed number of patches was imposed across eligible patients. Raw max-pooled embeddings also strongly encoded patch count in the out-of-fold decoding audit. After fold-contained residualization, useful multivariable patch-count decoding was substantially attenuated by R 2 and mean absolute error, although a small inverse rank association remained. In the original random patient-level folds, the mean-plus-residualized-max representations still outperformed mean-only pooling; however, the source-holdout analysis did not confirm a transportable incremental advantage of max-containing representations over mean-only pooling. These findings indicate that patch burden contributed substantially to the raw max-pooled signal and that residualized random-fold performance should be interpreted cautiously rather than as proof that patch-count effects were fully removed. The reconstructed source-partition analysis further showed that the pooled patch-count association was not stable across the original source structure. Patch-count discrimination was strong in source-TRAIN but approached chance level in source-TEST, consistent with the class-dependent patch-sampling history of the upstream training partition. Explicitly adding log1p-transformed patch count to the image-derived representations did not materially improve source-TEST discrimination. At the same time, image-derived representations retained moderate discrimination in source-TEST despite the loss of patch-count discrimination. These results argue against absolute patch burden alone explaining the source-holdout predictions, while also showing that the magnitude and pooling-specific pattern of performance under random patient-level cross-validation were sensitive to upstream source structure. Residual confounding by other source-associated technical, specimen-related, preprocessing-related, or morphological factors therefore remains possible. In the separate proportional patch-subsampling analysis, performance also remained comparatively stable when patient representations were reconstructed from reduced patch fractions, without a monotonic benefit from increasing patch availability. This finding suggests that the model was not critically dependent on exhaustive patch enumeration within the existing archive and may have implications for computational efficiency. It does not, however, demonstrate robustness to differences in specimen sampling, staining, scanning, institutional practice, or external patch-generation pipelines. Taken together, the findings support the methodological feasibility of a calibration-aware, embedding-based patient-level prediction framework while also demonstrating that validation design materially affects the estimated magnitude of performance. Random patient-level cross-validation yielded strong discrimination, whereas the reconstructed source holdout produced more moderate discrimination and revealed sensitivity to upstream dataset structure. Accordingly, the primary ROC-AUC of 0.915 should be interpreted as an estimate of performance under internal random patient-level partitioning rather than as evidence of source-independent generalizability. The source-holdout findings strengthen the rationale for independent multicenter validation rather than substituting for it. External multicenter validation, prospective workflow assessment, and spatially resolved pathological interpretation remain necessary before the framework can be considered for clinical integration. 4.2. Comparison with Previous MSI Prediction Studies As outlined in the Introduction, Kather et al. first established the feasibility of inferring MSI-related information directly from routine H&E-stained gastrointestinal cancer histology [ 5 ]. Subsequent studies extended this concept through larger colorectal cancer cohorts, alternative deep-learning architectures, and multi-cohort validation designs [ 33 ]. Systematic reviews and meta-analytic evidence have since confirmed that histology-based MSI-H/dMMR prediction can achieve strong discrimination, while also documenting substantial heterogeneity related to cohort composition, reference standards, image processing, model design, and validation setting [ 4 , 34 ]. In particular, the lower and more variable specificity observed across external validation settings reinforces that favorable internal discrimination does not by itself establish clinical transportability. Earlier MSI-prediction pipelines relied on task-specific convolutional training, patch-level classification, or trainable weakly supervised slide-level aggregation. The present study addressed a related but distinct question: whether a fixed pathology foundation model already encoded sufficient task-relevant information for patient-level prediction using deterministic pooling and comparatively simple downstream classifiers. Recent foundation-model benchmarks similarly suggest that performance depends not only on encoder capacity, but also on pretraining data, aggregation design, downstream adaptation, and validation strategy [ 23 , 24 , 35 ]. Consequently, neither increasing encoder scale nor using a more complex slide-level learner should be assumed to provide consistent improvements across cohorts and tasks. The predictive performance observed in the present study lies within the broad range reported for histology-based MSI prediction, but direct numerical ranking against previous models would be inappropriate. Published studies differ in cancer-site composition, specimen type, MSI prevalence, molecular reference standard, tissue selection, preprocessing, and whether testing was performed internally or on genuinely independent cohorts [ 5 , 23 , 33 , 34 ]. More importantly, many previous investigations used PCR-, immunohistochemistry-, or sequencing-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR outcomes, whereas the current analysis used the source repository’s MSIMUT category, defined as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated, as the positive class. The available source metadata do not permit the highly mutated component to be assigned to a more specific molecular subgroup. The analytical target should therefore not be treated as equivalent to a strictly assay-confirmed MSI-H endpoint. Because the patch archive was derived from a TCGA-linked resource also represented in earlier MSI studies, the present analysis constitutes an internally validated methodological investigation rather than an independent external replication [ 5 , 16 ]. More clinically advanced studies have evaluated whether histology-based models can function as high-sensitivity pre-screening systems. MSIntuit was blindly validated in an independent consecutive cohort and designed to identify patients for whom standard MSI testing could potentially be avoided while maintaining very high sensitivity [ 36 ]. This operational logic is conceptually aligned with the sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point examined in Section 3.4 of the present study. However, the distinction in evidentiary strength is important: the MSIntuit thresholds were evaluated in an independent cohort and across different scanners, whereas the operating points reported here were derived and assessed internally and remain exploratory. A subsequent multicentre blinded evaluation involving more than 1200 patients further illustrates the level of external evidence required to assess cross-site transportability and realistic workflow performance [ 37 ]. The contribution of the present study therefore lies less in claiming higher discrimination than in characterizing dimensions of model behavior that have not been reported consistently across the MSI literature. The framework evaluated PR-AUC and probability accuracy alongside ROC-AUC, quantified calibration intercept, calibration slope, and calibration-in-the-large, compared calibration strategies within a leakage-safe nested procedure, examined prespecified sensitivity targets, and estimated decision-analytic net benefit. It also treated pooling strategy and patch availability as explicit methodological variables. These analyses provide a more complete account of internal model behavior than discrimination metrics alone, but they do not place the model at the same evidentiary level as externally validated or prospectively specified clinical systems. The pooling and interpretability findings provide an additional point of comparison with trainable attention-based and multiple-instance-learning approaches. Rather than learning slide-level attention weights, the present framework compared deterministic mean, max, and mean-plus-max representations. The predominance of max-pooled dimensions among the highest-ranked SHAP features was compatible with predictive information being concentrated within a subset of patches, while the stronger overall performance of the combined representation within the random patient-level folds suggested that more distributed information remained complementary; however, this ordering was not preserved under the reconstructed source holdout. Because the analysis did not localize or pathologically annotate influential regions, it complements rather than replaces heatmap-based, attention-based, or pathologist-validated spatial interpretation used in previous studies. Overall, the present study does not demonstrate superiority over previously published end-to-end, weakly supervised, foundation-model-based, or clinically validated MSI systems. Instead, it shows that fixed pathology foundation-model embeddings, deterministic patient-level pooling, and a parsimonious linear classifier can support informative internal prediction when accompanied by explicit evaluation of uncertainty, calibration, operating thresholds, decision-analytic value, and representation robustness. The study is therefore positioned as a methodological complement to prior MSI-prediction research and as a foundation for subsequent external multicentre and prospective validation. 4.3. Methodological and Translational Implications The first methodological implication is that the analytical unit should correspond to the intended clinical unit of prediction. In patch-rich computational pathology datasets, the apparent number of image samples can obscure the fact that the effective number of independent observations is determined by patients. Maintaining patient-level separation throughout representation construction, model fitting, calibration, and evaluation was therefore essential to prevent correlated tissue fragments from producing optimistic estimates. Within this constraint, the combination of a fixed encoder, deterministic pooling, and a comparatively simple downstream classifier provided a modular framework in which representation, aggregation, and prediction could be examined separately. This modular design has implications for reproducibility and model maintenance. Keeping the Phikon encoder fixed avoids repeated task-specific image-model training and allows downstream components to be audited, recalibrated, or replaced without retraining the complete image-processing pipeline. Related work in computational pathology has also illustrated the broader value of modular representation-transfer strategies, including the transfer of information from multimodal training frameworks to models operating on a single histopathology modality [ 21 ]. Recent pathology foundation-model benchmarks indicate that downstream performance depends not only on encoder capacity, but also on representation quality, aggregation strategy, task adaptation, and validation design [ 24 , 35 ]. In the present cohort, the favorable performance of logistic regression indicated that task-relevant information was accessible to a linear downstream classifier within the fixed Phikon-derived representation space. This finding should not be interpreted as evidence that simple classifiers will be optimal across other datasets, encoders, aggregation strategies, or clinical endpoints. Rather, it supports evaluating representation quality and aggregation design before increasing downstream model complexity. An embedding-based workflow should nevertheless not be regarded as computationally cost-free. Whole-slide tiling, patch storage, and foundation-model inference may still impose substantial processing and infrastructure requirements. The principal efficiency advantage lies in avoiding repeated end-to-end task-specific training rather than eliminating whole-slide processing costs. Similarly, the stability observed under reduced patch fractions supports further investigation of predefined patch budgets, adaptive sampling, or sequential stopping strategies, but the present study did not measure execution time, storage requirements, energy consumption, or prospective turnaround time. The patch-burden findings therefore indicate the feasibility of resource-aware investigation rather than a demonstrated operational efficiency benefit. A further translational implication is that discrimination must be complemented by evaluation of probability behavior and intended clinical action. Calibration analysis showed that informative rankings may coexist with probabilities requiring adjustment, while threshold analysis demonstrated that the relative consequences of missed positive cases and unnecessary confirmatory assessments vary substantially across operating points. Calibration and threshold selection should therefore be repeated in the intended deployment population, accounting for disease prevalence, clinical consequences, and workflow-specific tolerance for false-positive and false-negative results. The source-defined positive prevalence was 18.1% in the present cohort and may differ materially from that of future screening populations, with corresponding effects on predictive values and testing burden. Decision curve analysis can support this assessment but does not replace prospective workflow evaluation, health-economic analysis, or direct measurement of clinical outcomes [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 38 ]. The most plausible translational role for the framework is not autonomous MSI diagnosis, but candidate pre-screening and prioritization of confirmatory testing. An H&E-based probability estimate could potentially help identify cases for earlier molecular or immunohistochemical assessment, whereas a high-sensitivity operating point could be investigated within a rule-out-oriented workflow. If validated prospectively, such an approach might reduce avoidable testing, shorten diagnostic pathways, and, particularly in tissue-limited specimens, contribute to tissue stewardship by preserving tumor material for other clinically indicated molecular or targeted biomarker analyses. These potential benefits were not measured in the present study. Moreover, because the modeled endpoint was the source-defined MSIMUT category rather than a uniformly assay-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR outcome, the current framework cannot support withholding or replacing established PCR- or immunohistochemistry-based testing [ 36 , 37 , 38 ]. Representation-level interpretability provides only a partial basis for translational transparency. The SHAP analysis characterized reliance on latent mean- and max-pooled dimensions but did not identify the tissue structures responsible for individual predictions. For the max-pooled component, the patch producing the maximum value in a specific embedding dimension is mathematically traceable through dimension-wise argmax tracking, provided that patch-level embeddings and provenance mappings are retained. This could support future spatially resolved analyses, but it would identify dimension-specific source patches rather than, by itself, establish a single causal or pathologically meaningful region for the patient-level prediction. Future studies should combine such tracing with patient-level attribution, spatial visualization, pathologist review, and validation against recognizable histopathological patterns. Clinical translation would additionally require external multicenter validation, locked preprocessing and calibration procedures, slide-quality control, assessment across scanners and staining protocols, evaluation of uncertain or non-evaluable cases, fairness analysis, and model-version governance. The present findings therefore support a transparent methodology for evaluating foundation-model embeddings in patient-level biomarker prediction, rather than a deployment-ready diagnostic system. Leakage control, modular representation design, probability calibration, operating-point analysis, decision-analytic assessment, and patch-burden testing address complementary requirements that should be considered before an embedding-based computational pathology model progresses toward prospective clinical evaluation. 4.4. Strengths and Limitations This study has several methodological strengths. First, the patient was maintained as the analytical and validation unit throughout the complete workflow. Patch-level embeddings derived from the same patient were not divided between training and testing subsets, reducing the risk of optimistic performance estimates caused by correlated tissue fragments. A single verified patient manifest, outcome vector, representation matrix, and set of validation partitions were retained across classifier comparison, repeated validation, calibration, threshold analysis, pooling comparison, patch subsampling, and interpretability assessment. This consistency strengthened the internal traceability of the computational workflow. Second, model evaluation extended beyond a single cross-validation estimate or discrimination metric. The primary five-fold analysis was complemented by repeated patient-level cross-validation, bootstrap uncertainty estimation, leakage-safe nested probability calibration, sensitivity-targeted operating-point analysis, and decision curve analysis with bootstrap-based uncertainty assessment. Additional sensitivity analyses examined clinicopathological and tissue-source-site structure within the cohort. Reporting ROC-AUC together with PR-AUC, Matthews correlation coefficient, Brier score, calibration parameters, predictive values, and confusion-matrix counts provided a broader characterization of model behavior under class imbalance. Pooling comparison and patch-burden experiments additionally evaluated assumptions concerning representation design and image availability, while SHAP analysis was explicitly restricted to representation-level interpretation. The use of a fixed encoder, deterministic pooling procedures, controlled random seeds, training-fold-contained preprocessing, and programmatically retained intermediate outputs further supported reproducibility and auditing. Several limitations nevertheless constrain the interpretation of the findings. Most importantly, all analyses were based on a single retrospective TCGA-derived cohort, and no independent external dataset was available. Patient-level internal validation reduces information leakage but cannot reproduce the domain shifts encountered across independent institutions, patient populations, specimen-processing protocols, staining conditions, scanners, or digital-pathology systems. Two complementary source-structure assessments were included: TSS-group-isolated validation based on TCGA/GDC metadata and a reconstructed holdout based on the original upstream TRAIN/TEST partition. Both analyses remained internal to the same TCGA-derived source resource. The attenuation from a primary mean-plus-max ROC-AUC of 0.915 under random patient-level cross-validation to 0.788 under the reconstructed source holdout demonstrates that internal random-fold estimates were sensitive to source partitioning and should not be interpreted as evidence of transportability. Neither the TSS-isolated analysis nor the reconstructed source holdout constitutes independent external multicenter validation. The present results therefore characterize performance across multiple internal validation structures within the available source cohort rather than demonstrating transportability across clinical settings. Performance, calibration, fairness, and operating characteristics across independent patient populations, laboratories, staining workflows, scanners, and acquisition systems remain unknown. The outcome definition also requires caution. The positive class remained the source repository’s MSIMUT category, formally defined as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated, rather than a uniformly clinically adjudicated PCR-, immunohistochemistry-, or sequencing-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR endpoint. GDC-derived MSIsensor2 status was available for all 360 cases. Among the 351 patients with an unambiguous GDC-derived MSI or MSS designation, agreement with the source archive label was 98.9%, with a Cohen’s κ of 0.959. Existing image-based out-of-sample predictions also retained strong discrimination when evaluated against this secondary GDC-derived endpoint. However, the GDC-derived MSIsensor2 annotation represents a bioinformatics-derived molecular annotation rather than a uniform clinical reference assay. The high concordance therefore supports consistency of the source labels but does not convert the primary outcome into a clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR endpoint. Accordingly, the model should continue to be interpreted as predicting the source-defined archive label. Detailed MSIsensor2 concordance and secondary-endpoint performance results are provided in Supplementary Table S19 . The study also depended on a previously processed JPEG patch archive rather than direct reconstruction from the original whole-slide repository. Although the derivative dataset title refers to TCGA colon adenocarcinoma, linkage of all 360 patient identifiers to GDC metadata confirmed that the analytical cohort contained both TCGA-COAD and TCGA-READ cases, supporting its description as a colorectal cohort. Nevertheless, the derivative archive was accessed through a community-hosted repository without a persistent dataset DOI or a peer-reviewed data descriptor. The complete upstream case-selection pathway used to create the derivative archive—including the initial number of TCGA cases considered, case-level exclusion criteria, the number of originating whole-slide images, and all preprocessing decisions—could not be reconstructed fully. Upstream tissue detection, patch selection, stain normalization, slide-quality control, tiling stride, and overlap therefore could not be independently modified or completely audited. These provenance limitations remain relevant despite successful patient-level linkage to the original TCGA case identifiers. The sample size was modest relative to the 1536-dimensional patient representation, and only 65 patients belonged to the source-defined positive class. Regularization, patient-level cross-validation, and repeated resampling reduced but did not eliminate risks related to high dimensionality and class imbalance. Regularization-sensitivity analysis further showed that discrimination remained similar across C = 0.01–1 but declined under substantially weaker regularization at C = 10–100, while no convergence warnings were observed across the evaluated configurations. Moreover, the candidate classifiers represented prespecified fixed implementations rather than an exhaustive or independently optimized comparison. Logistic regression and Linear SVM used class weighting, whereas the evaluated MLP, random forest, and gradient boosting implementations used unweighted objectives. Because imbalance handling was not harmonized across all candidate implementations, the classifier comparison should be interpreted as a comparison of the prespecified analytical pipelines rather than as an intrinsic ranking of the underlying algorithm families. The primary classifier was selected from five prespecified implementations using internal cross-validation within the same cohort. To examine potential classifier-selection optimism directly, a nested pipeline-selection sensitivity analysis restricted pipeline selection entirely to each outer-training set. Logistic regression was selected in all five outer folds, and the resulting nested-selected outer-test predictions were identical to those of the fixed logistic-regression reference, yielding no observed difference in ROC-AUC or PR-AUC. This finding supports the internal reproducibility of the original pipeline choice. Nevertheless, because both the original comparison and the nested sensitivity analysis were performed within the same cohort, model-selection uncertainty cannot be considered eliminated, and the results should not be interpreted as demonstrating intrinsic superiority of logistic regression over other algorithm families. Calibration and decision-oriented analyses remained internal, although the principal source of calibration-method selection optimism identified in the original analysis was addressed through the fully nested calibration procedure. Calibration-method selection was repeated within a fully nested procedure in which uncalibrated probabilities, Platt scaling, and isotonic regression were compared using cross-fitted predictions generated exclusively from the corresponding outer-training data. Outer-test observations were not used for calibrator selection or fitting, and Platt scaling was selected in all five outer folds. The resulting nested-Platt probabilities showed substantially improved calibration, with a pooled calibration slope of 1.037 and calibration-in-the-large of 0.023. Nevertheless, calibration performance remains specific to the present development cohort and requires reassessment in an independent population. Similarly, the Youden and high-sensitivity operating thresholds were derived and evaluated from internally generated out-of-sample probabilities and remain exploratory cohort-specific operating points. Decision-curve analysis was supplemented by paired bootstrap uncertainty assessment, but its results likewise do not establish prospective clinical utility. The bootstrap procedures resampled patient-level outcome–prediction pairs without repeating the complete sequence of representation construction, model fitting, calibration selection, and threshold derivation and therefore quantify uncertainty conditional on the generated predictions rather than all sources of model-development uncertainty. Interpretability remained confined to latent embedding dimensions. SHAP values characterized relative reliance on the mean- and max-pooled components but did not identify specific histopathological structures, cell populations, or causal biological mechanisms. The predominance of max-pooled dimensions among the top SHAP-ranked features should be interpreted cautiously because raw max-pooled embeddings strongly encoded patch count; these dimensions may therefore partly reflect patch-burden or source-preprocessing proxies. The interventional masker did not explicitly model correlations among embedding dimensions, and attribution magnitudes may differ under correlation-aware explanation methods. Dimension-wise max-pooling provenance could potentially permit tracing individual maximal activations back to source patches, but such tracing was not performed or validated through pathologist review. The original proportional patch-subsampling experiment represented repeated reductions within each patient’s existing archive and therefore assessed robustness to reduced patch availability, but it did not equalize absolute patch counts across patients and should not be interpreted as a control for patch-count confounding. Fixed-N, fold-contained patch-count-adjustment, source-holdout, and explicit patch-count-addition analyses demonstrated that absolute patch burden and upstream patch-generation history contributed to the raw max-pooled signal. Patch count itself may reflect a mixture of tissue area, tumor extent, source-image characteristics, and upstream patch-generation or tissue-selection processes; consequently, neither fixed-N subsampling nor statistical residualization can determine which biological or technical mechanism generated the observed patch-count difference. Metadata linkage allowed several potentially relevant clinicopathological and site-related factors to be examined, including age, pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, primary diagnosis, TCGA project membership, and tissue-source-site code. These variables showed measurable associations with the source-defined outcome. A clinical-only model nevertheless discriminated less well than the image-only model, whereas combining the audited clinical variables with the image representation produced essentially no incremental discrimination over the image-only pipeline. In addition, discrimination was attenuated but remained substantial when all patients sharing the same TSS were isolated between training and testing. These findings indicate that the measured clinical and site variables do not fully account for the image-model discrimination; however, they do not exclude residual confounding by unmeasured morphological, technical, or clinical factors. Important covariate limitations therefore remain. Sex/gender and a uniform clinical molecular MSI-test result were not included in the analyzable metadata extract used for the present sensitivity analyses, and the study did not incorporate pathologist-adjudicated histological subtype, detailed tumor-cell content, treatment information, complete pathology-report variables, or center-specific staining and scanner characteristics. Prospective turnaround time, computational cost, storage requirements, energy consumption, cost-effectiveness, tissue preservation, workflow acceptability, and effects on patient management were also not evaluated. A further reproducibility limitation is that the commit-specific revision of the Phikon encoder used during the original embedding-generation run was not pinned or retained; consequently, bitwise regeneration of the patch embeddings directly from the source images cannot be guaranteed across different hardware and software environments. This limitation is partly mitigated by the public release of the exact patient-specific embedding arrays used as fixed inputs for all downstream analyses. Collectively, these limitations indicate that the framework should be regarded as a transparent internally validated methodological investigation rather than a clinically validated or deployment-ready MSI decision-support system. 4.5. Future Directions The immediate priority for future research is independent multicenter validation using a prespecified and frozen version of the complete analytical pipeline. The pathology foundation-model revision, preprocessing procedures, pooling strategy, classifier parameters, calibration mapping, and operating thresholds should be locked before external evaluation. Direct transportability should first be assessed without site-specific refitting or retrospective threshold optimization. If discrimination or calibration deteriorates, recalibration or domain-adaptation strategies should be evaluated in a separately designed development phase and tested in data that were not used to select the adaptation procedure. Performance should be reported by institution, scanner, staining protocol, specimen type, and clinically relevant patient subgroup to distinguish genuine generalizability from average performance that conceals site-specific failure [ 35 , 37 , 38 , 39 ]. Where transfer of raw whole-slide images is restricted by data-governance, infrastructure, or privacy constraints, distributed validation and federated-learning strategies could be investigated. The modular separation between fixed embedding extraction and a lightweight downstream classifier may facilitate such designs. However, latent embeddings should not be assumed to be inherently anonymous or privacy preserving. Any distributed implementation would require explicit evaluation of information leakage, secure aggregation, institutional governance, and reproducibility across local computational environments. Future validation should also use clinically adjudicated reference standards. Cohorts with PCR-, immunohistochemistry-, or sequencing-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR status would determine whether the source-defined MSIMUT signal identified in the present study transfers to a more narrowly defined clinical endpoint. When multiple assays are available, discordant results should be reviewed explicitly rather than collapsed automatically into a binary label. Consecutive or population-based cohorts would additionally permit calibration, predictive values, testing burden, and operating thresholds to be evaluated under prevalence conditions that more closely reflect the intended clinical setting. Robustness assessment should extend beyond random patch reduction within a single preprocessed archive. Relevant evaluations include alternative tissue blocks and slide sections from the same patient, biopsy versus resection material, variable tumor content, staining perturbations, scanner platforms, tissue-detection procedures, and external patch-generation pipelines. The modular framework also permits controlled comparison of Phikon with alternative pathology foundation-model encoders. Such comparisons should use identical patient partitions, pooling strategies, downstream classifiers, calibration procedures, and evaluation metrics to separate encoder-related differences from variation introduced elsewhere in the pipeline. Encoder selection should be completed within development data rather than through retrospective comparison on the final external test cohort. Resource-aware processing should be evaluated concurrently with these robustness experiments. Predefined patch budgets, adaptive tissue sampling, uncertainty-guided patch selection, and sequential stopping criteria could be compared with exhaustive patch processing. These analyses should measure not only predictive performance but also inference time, storage requirements, computational cost, energy consumption, and diagnostic turnaround time. This would establish whether the observed internal tolerance to reduced patch fractions can produce a reproducible operational benefit. Spatially resolved interpretability represents another important research direction. Dimension-wise provenance tracking could identify the source patches responsible for individual max-pooled activations, after which these patches could be mapped back to their originating slide locations. Patient-level attribution would then need to be integrated with spatial visualization and independent pathologist assessment. Such studies could examine whether influential regions correspond reproducibly to immune-rich areas, mucinous differentiation, glandular irregularity, architectural heterogeneity, or other recognizable histopathological patterns. Attribution stability across tissue perturbations, agreement among pathologists, and comparison with correlation-aware explanation methods would be required before latent feature importance could support morphological or biological interpretation. Prospective studies should evaluate a clearly prespecified clinical role rather than generic deployment. A plausible initial setting would be model-assisted prioritization of confirmatory MSI testing, with molecular or immunohistochemical assessment remaining the reference procedure. A rule-out-oriented strategy would require externally validated sensitivity, a fixed operating threshold, and predefined management of uncertain, low-quality, and non-evaluable slides. Prospective outcomes should include missed positive cases, additional testing generated by false-positive predictions, turnaround time, tissue consumption, costs, workflow acceptability, and effects on clinical decisions. Retrospective threshold and decision-curve analyses can inform the design of such studies but cannot replace direct workflow evaluation [ 10 , 11 , 36 , 37 , 38 ]. Beyond their essential role in cohort description and subgroup assessment, clinicopathological variables should be further evaluated and expanded in independent external multimodal validation. In the internal sensitivity analysis, age, pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, primary diagnosis, TCGA project membership, and tissue-source-site information were examined, and combining the audited clinical variables with image-derived embeddings did not provide clear incremental discrimination over the image-only model. Future multimodal studies should therefore incorporate broader and prospectively collected variables that were unavailable or incompletely represented in the present cohort, including sex/gender, pathologist-adjudicated histological subtype, specimen type, structured pathology-report information, and center-specific technical factors. The incremental value of such multimodal integration should be tested against both image-only and clinical-only baselines in independent external cohorts using prespecified analytical pipelines, with particular attention to transportability, calibration, and clinical utility rather than model complexity alone. Taken together, these directions define a staged translational pathway: first, they externally validate the locked image-based framework; second, assess clinically confirmed endpoints and domain robustness; third, connect latent representations with pathologist-recognizable morphology; and finally, evaluate a prespecified role within prospective clinical workflows. This sequence would determine whether foundation-model-derived histopathology embeddings can contribute safely, reproducibly, and efficiently to MSI pre-screening or confirmatory-test prioritization in colorectal cancer. 5. Conclusions This study demonstrates the methodological feasibility of leakage-safe, patient-level prediction of a source-defined MSIMUT category in colorectal cancer histopathology using fixed Phikon foundation-model embeddings. Deterministic pooling of patch-level embeddings, followed by a comparatively simple logistic-regression classifier, supported strong internal discrimination under random patient-level cross-validation with the primary mean-plus-max representation (ROC-AUC, 0.915), but the same representation showed more moderate discrimination under the reconstructed source holdout (ROC-AUC, 0.788; PR-AUC, 0.593), indicating that the primary random-fold estimate was optimistic relative to source-holdout performance. Leakage-safe nested Platt calibration improved probability behavior without using outer-test outcomes for calibration-method selection, and the resulting calibrated predictions supported exploratory threshold and decision-curve analyses within the internally evaluated TCGA-derived cohort. However, the additional provenance-based analyses materially qualify the interpretation of these findings. Reconstruction of the original source TRAIN/TEST partition showed that performance was attenuated under a source-structured internal holdout, with the mean-plus-max ROC-AUC decreasing to 0.788. Patch-count analyses further showed that absolute patch burden and upstream source-preprocessing history contributed to the raw max-pooled signal and to the magnitude of performance observed under random patient-level partitioning. Although image-derived representations retained moderate discrimination in source-TEST and explicit patch-count addition did not improve source-holdout performance, the results should not be interpreted as evidence of source-independent generalizability. The lower source-holdout performance was therefore considered a key limitation of the current framework and a major reason for restricting the interpretation to internal methodological feasibility. The model should therefore be viewed as an internally evaluated methodological framework for MSI-related pre-screening research rather than as a clinically validated diagnostic tool. The predicted endpoint was the source-defined MSIMUT archive label, not a uniformly clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR reference standard. All performance, calibration, threshold, decision-analytic, clinicopathological, source-provenance, and patch-count sensitivity results remain internal to the TCGA-derived cohort. Independent multicenter validation using clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR outcomes, heterogeneous acquisition conditions, locked preprocessing and calibration procedures, and prespecified operating thresholds is required before any clinical application, confirmatory-testing decision, or workflow integration can be considered. title: FTU-Seek: Foundation Model-Guided Hard-Negative Learning for Sparse Functional Tissue Unit Segmentation.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: FTU-Seek: Foundation Model-Guided Hard-Negative Learning for Sparse Functional Tissue Unit Segmentation. Background/Objectives: Functional tissue units (FTUs), including tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs), blood vessels, and glands, encode localized immune, vascular, and epithelial organization in histopathology. Accurate quantification of these structures is important for studying tissue architecture and disease-associated tissue organization. However, FTUs are frequently sparse, heterogeneous, and surrounded by large amounts of morphologically similar background tissue, making automated segmentation in whole-slide images (WSIs) challenging. We therefore developed FTU-Seek, a pathology foundation model-guided framework that treats morphology-aware negative-patch selection as a key component of sparse FTU segmentation. Methods: FTU-Seek uses frozen multi-depth features from the UNI pathology foundation model to train a patch-level classifier that distinguishes FTU-containing from FTU-absent tissue. Target-absent patches are subsequently ranked according to their predicted target-containing probabilities, and the highest-scoring hard negatives are selected through a static TopK strategy to construct compact segmentation training sets. The framework was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and internal test cohorts across TLS, blood-vessel, and gland segmentation tasks, with an additional independent 30-WSI held-out cohort for TLS. Positive-only, all-tissue, random-negative, and matched random TopK sampling strategies served as comparators. Segmentation-derived phenotypes were further explored in external TCGA cohorts. Results: The patch-level classifiers achieved mean validation AUCs of 95.92%, 90.11%, and 98.16% for TLS, blood vessel, and gland classification, respectively. For TLS segmentation, the pre-specified Top1000 configuration retained 27.6% of the all-tissue training workload and achieved a slide-level Dice of 76.69 ± 11.89% on the independent 30-WSI held-out cohort. Compared with matched random Top1000 sampling, it improved Dice by 3.72 percentage points (95% CI, 2.05-5.38). Blood vessel and gland segmentation achieved performance approaching all-tissue training while reducing the retained training workload by approximately one-half and one-third, respectively. Compared with matched random sampling, classifier-guided hard-negative selection produced the greatest improvements for sparse and morphologically ambiguous FTUs. Exploratory TCGA analyses further showed associations of TLS phenotypes with overall survival, vascular phenotypes with overall survival and microvascular invasion, and glandular phenotypes with clinicopathological characteristics. Conclusions: FTU-Seek demonstrates that pathology foundation models can support sparse FTU segmentation not only through feature representation but also through morphology-aware construction of segmentation training sets. By prioritizing informative hard negatives, the framework reduces redundant segmentation-training workload while maintaining competitive segmentation performance and supporting quantitative tissue phenotyping from routine histopathology.

title: A weakly supervised deep learning model for OSCC diagnosis and lesion highlighting in histopathology images.

evidence_text:
A weakly supervised deep learning model for OSCC diagnosis and lesion highlighting in histopathology images.

Background

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the predominant histopathological subtype of oral malignancies, and histopathology-based diagnosis remains central to clinical management. With the rapid development of digital pathology and deep learning, automated analysis of histopathology images has shown considerable potential for improving screening efficiency and reducing inter-observer variability. However, in both public datasets and real-world research settings, only image-level labels are commonly available, whereas region-level annotations are often lacking. This limitation makes weakly supervised modeling necessary and also restricts rigorous validation of spatial interpretability.

Methods

To address these challenges, we developed a weakly supervised deep learning framework based on patch-level representation learning and multiple-instance aggregation for image-level OSCC diagnosis with exploratory heatmap visualization. Specifically, histopathology images were divided into patches and encoded into feature embeddings. UNI 2, a recently developed pathology foundation model with highly competitive performance in contemporary computational pathology benchmarks, was adopted as the primary feature extractor to obtain informative patch representations. ResNet-50 was additionally implemented as a conventional baseline encoder for comparative evaluation. A self-attention-based multiple-instance aggregation module was then introduced to capture dependencies among instances within each patch set and to generate binary OSCC predictions.

Results

In five-fold cross-validation, the UNI-2-based model achieved a mean area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9919, compared with 0.9899 for the ResNet-50 baseline. On the independent external validation cohort, UNI 2 further achieved an AUC of 0.9992, outperforming ResNet-50, which achieved an AUC of 0.9564. As an exploratory interpretability analysis, attention responses were visualized as heatmaps to inspect model focus patterns and support qualitative error review, without assuming verified lesion-level correspondence in the absence of region-level annotations.

Conclusions

This framework demonstrates strong image-level diagnostic performance for OSCC and provides exploratory visualization for qualitative model review without requiring additional fine-grained annotations, offering a reusable technical pathway for weakly supervised OSCC histopathology modeling and future multicenter validation.

title: Knowledge-enhanced pretraining for vision-language pathology foundation model on cancer diagnosis.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Knowledge-enhanced pretraining for vision-language pathology foundation model on cancer diagnosis. Vision-language foundation models have shown great promise in computational pathology but remain primarily data-driven, lacking explicit integration of medical knowledge. We introduce knowledge-enhanced pathology (KEEP), a foundation model that systematically incorporates disease knowledge into pretraining for cancer diagnosis. KEEP leverages a comprehensive disease knowledge graph encompassing 11,454 diseases and 139,143 attributes to reorganize millions of pathology image-text pairs into 143,000 semantically structured groups aligned with disease ontology hierarchies. This knowledge-enhanced pretraining aligns visual and textual representations within hierarchical semantic spaces, enabling a deeper understanding of disease relationships and morphological patterns. Across 18 public benchmarks (over 14,000 whole-slide images) and 4 institutional rare cancer datasets (926 cases), KEEP consistently outperformed existing foundation models, showing substantial gains for rare subtypes. These results establish knowledge-enhanced vision-language modeling as a powerful paradigm for advancing computational pathology.

title: Tissue as Landscape: An Interpretable Ecological Framework for Quantifying Whole-Slide Spatial Architecture and Cancer Prognosis

evidence_text:
Tissue as Landscape: An Interpretable Ecological Framework for Quantifying Whole-Slide Spatial Architecture and Cancer Prognosis Abstract

Background Accurate risk stratification remains essential for guiding cancer management, yet conventional clinicopathological factors and many whole-slide image (WSI)-based deep learning models incompletely capture interpretable tissue-level spatial heterogeneity. We developed Tissue Ecological Landscape (TEL), a scalable and interpretable computational pathology framework that converts routine hematoxylin and eosin-stained WSIs into quantitative spatial biomarkers for cancer prognosis. Methods We analysed H&E-stained WSIs and matched clinical data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) cohorts across clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), glioblastoma (GBM), and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC). Tile-level features were extracted using a pathology foundation model, grouped into data-driven tissue communities, and mapped back to slide coordinates. Landscape ecological indices were then used to quantify fragmentation, size heterogeneity, boundary complexity, aggregation, connectivity, and diversity. TEL-based Cox survival models were trained in TCGA cohorts and externally validated in the corresponding CPTAC cohorts. Model performance was compared with CLAM, and biological relevance was explored using SHAP-based interpretation, immune infiltration analysis, and gene set enrichment analysis. Results TEL achieved external validation C-indices of 0.669, 0.573, and 0.632 in ccRCC, GBM, and LSCC, respectively, with a mean C-index of 0.625 and a mean time-dependent AUC of 0.660. TEL showed prognostic performance comparable to CLAM while providing explicit spatial descriptors of tissue architecture. The TEL risk score significantly stratified patients into high- and low-risk groups in both training and external validation cohorts and remained independently associated with overall survival after adjustment for available clinicopathological variables. SHAP analysis revealed cancer-type-specific spatial determinants of prognosis, with fragmentation and size heterogeneity predominating in ccRCC, aggregation-related features in GBM, and boundary complexity in LSCC. In ccRCC, a low-patch-density/high-patch-area-variation phenotype identified a high-risk subgroup associated with poor survival, inflammatory pathway enrichment, reduced metabolic activity, and distinct immune infiltration patterns. Conclusions TEL enables interpretable quantification of whole-slide tissue spatial architecture from routine H&E images and provides externally validated prognostic information across multiple cancer types. By linking spatial disorganization patterns with survival and tumor microenvironmental features, TEL may serve as a complementary spatial biomarker framework for translational cancer risk stratification.

title: An interpretable cell-centric representation of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma matches multiple-instance learning for clinical outcomes and leads to novel pathologist-driven histological biomarkers

evidence_text:
An interpretable cell-centric representation of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma matches multiple-instance learning for clinical outcomes and leads to novel pathologist-driven histological biomarkers

ABSTRACT

Current state of the art computational pathology foundation models attain satisfying accuracy most general pathology tasks including detection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) but fail to provide sufficient explainability, operating as “black boxes”. Some interpretability effort has been made, with models providing attention maps that project back on the slide the models high attended areas that pushed for the given prediction result, without further naming or reasoning explanation which can limit pathologists trust toward the prediction. We developed C3PRO, a cell-centric framework attempting to provide deeper understanding and explainability, by using embeddings extracted using a pathology foundation model, from cell centered tiles containing both the cell and its close neighborhood, which were then clustered into recurrent morphological phenotypes. A spatial graph was additionally constructed on top of the back-projected vocabulary to account for recurrent motifs. The evaluation of the model performance involved a cohort of 809 patients (825 diagnostic biopsies) using nested cross validation. C3PRO was benchmarked against four different multiple instance learning frameworks and achieved on-par performance for diagnostic (0.958 AUC), survival (0.617) and resectability (0.696) prediction, while providing additional insights compared to the strongest baseline models. Each clustered phenotype was probed and extracted as a representative tile mosaic and annotated by two expert pathologists, constituting a phenotype vocabulary available for statistical analysis. These phenotypes were scored by pathologists with physical brightfield microscopy and replicated the independent statistical significance impact on overall survival prediction from diagnostic biopsies.

STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

Pathology foundation model multiple-instance-learning frameworks cannot be audited by the pathologists. We demonstrate that a representation constructed from identifiable cell phenotypes is on par with state-of-the-art models for diagnosis, prognosis, and resectability in pancreatic cancer. This approach also uncovers prognostic stromal states that expert observers cannot differentiate using light microscopy.

title: Geranium: Multimodal Retrieval of Genomics Data Visualizations.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Geranium: Multimodal Retrieval of Genomics Data Visualizations. Effective visualization is essential for interpreting genomics data, yet researchers often face challenges in finding relevant, reusable examples. Existing tools offer limited support for searching the vast landscape of genomics visualizations, making the process of authoring new visualizations time-consuming and inefficient. To address this gap, we introduce Geranium, a data visualization retrieval system for searching and authoring genomics visualizations. Geranium supports multimodal retrieval, enabling users to query with images, text, or grammar-based specifications. Retrieved examples serve as scaffolds for authoring, providing templates that researchers can adapt with their own data, thereby streamlining the mechanics of visualization construction. Geranium integrates three embedding methods to combine specialized and general knowledge: grammar-based embeddings tailored to genomics visualizations, multimodal embeddings from a biomedical vision-language foundation model, and text embeddings from a fine-tuned large language model. For each visualization, we construct a multimodal representation that includes a Gosling specification, a pixel-based rendering, and natural language descriptions. We evaluate embedding strategies to maximize top-$k$k retrieval accuracy and conduct user studies with domain collaborators to gather feedback on usability. Our collection comprises 3,200 visualizations across 50 categories, ranging from single-view to coordinated multi-view designs and supporting applications from single-cell epigenomics to structural variation analysis.

title: A vision-language foundation model for precision oncology.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: A vision-language foundation model for precision oncology. Clinical decision-making is driven by multimodal data, including clinical notes and pathological characteristics. Artificial intelligence approaches that can effectively integrate multimodal data hold significant promise in advancing clinical care<sup>1,2</sup>. However, the scarcity of well-annotated multimodal datasets in clinical settings has hindered the development of useful models. In this study, we developed the Multimodal transformer with Unified maSKed modeling (MUSK), a vision-language foundation model designed to leverage large-scale, unlabelled, unpaired image and text data. MUSK was pretrained on 50 million pathology images from 11,577 patients and one billion pathology-related text tokens using unified masked modelling. It was further pretrained on one million pathology image-text pairs to efficiently align the vision and language features. With minimal or no further training, MUSK was tested in a wide range of applications and demonstrated superior performance across 23 patch-level and slide-level benchmarks, including image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval, visual question answering, image classification and molecular biomarker prediction. Furthermore, MUSK showed strong performance in outcome prediction, including melanoma relapse prediction, pan-cancer prognosis prediction and immunotherapy response prediction in lung and gastro-oesophageal cancers. MUSK effectively combined complementary information from pathology images and clinical reports and could potentially improve diagnosis and precision in cancer therapy.

title: A multimodal whole-slide foundation model for pathology.

evidence_text: A multimodal whole-slide foundation model for pathology. The field of computational pathology has been transformed with recent advances in foundation models that encode histopathology region-of-interests (ROIs) into versatile and transferable feature representations via self-supervised learning. However, translating these advancements to address complex clinical challenges at the patient and slide level remains constrained by limited clinical data in disease-specific cohorts, especially for rare clinical conditions. We propose Transformer-based pathology Image and Text Alignment Network (TITAN), a multimodal whole-slide foundation model pretrained using 335,645 whole-slide images via visual self-supervised learning and vision-language alignment with corresponding pathology reports and 423,122 synthetic captions generated from a multimodal generative AI copilot for pathology. Without any fine-tuning or requiring clinical labels, TITAN can extract general-purpose slide representations and generate pathology reports that generalize to resource-limited clinical scenarios such as rare disease retrieval and cancer prognosis. We evaluate TITAN on diverse clinical tasks and find that it outperforms both ROI and slide foundation models across machine learning settings, including linear probing, few-shot and zero-shot classification, rare cancer retrieval, cross-modal retrieval and pathology report generation.

evidence_text: A Unified Information Bottleneck Framework for Multimodal Biomedical Machine Learning. Multimodal biomedical machine learning increasingly integrates heterogeneous data sources (including medical imaging, multi-omics profiles, electronic health records, and wearable sensor signals) to support clinical diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response prediction. Despite strong empirical performance, most existing multimodal systems lack a principled theoretical foundation for understanding why fusion improves prediction, how information is distributed across modalities, and when models can be trusted under incomplete or shifting data. This paper develops a unified information-theoretic framework that formalizes multimodal biomedical learning as an information optimization problem. We formulate multimodal representation learning through the information bottleneck principle, deriving a variational objective that balances predictive sufficiency against informational compression in an architecture-agnostic manner. Building on this foundation, we introduce information-theoretic tools for decomposing modality contributions via conditional mutual information, quantifying redundancy and synergy, and diagnosing fusion collapse. We further show that robustness to missing modalities can be cast as an information consistency problem and extend the framework to longitudinal disease modeling through transfer entropy and sequential information bottleneck objectives. Applications to multimodal foundation models, uncertainty quantification, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection are developed. Empirical case studies across three biomedical datasets (TCGA breast cancer multi-omics, TCGA glioma clinical-plus-molecular data, and OASIS-2 longitudinal Alzheimer's data) show that the framework's key quantities are computable and interpretable on real data: MI decomposition identifies modality dominance and redundancy; the VMIB traces a compression-prediction tradeoff in the information plane; entropy-based selective prediction raises accuracy from 0.787 to 0.939 at 50% coverage; transfer entropy reveals stage-dependent modality influence in disease progression; and pretraining/adaptation diagnostics distinguish efficient from wasteful fine-tuning strategies. Together, these results develop entropy and mutual information as organizing principles for the design, analysis, and evaluation of multimodal biomedical AI systems.

evidence_text: Deep Learning Image Processing Models in Dermatopathology. Dermatopathology has rapidly advanced due to the implementation of deep learning models and artificial intelligence (AI). From convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformer-based foundation models, these systems are now capable of accurate whole-slide analysis and multimodal integration. This review synthesizes the most recent advents of deep-learning architecture and synthesizes its evolution from first-generation CNNs to hybrid CNN-transformer systems to large-scale foundational models such as Paige's PanDerm AI and Virchow. Herein, we examine performance benchmarks from real-world deployments of major dermatopathology deep learning models (DermAI, PathAssist Derm), as well as emerging next-generation models still under research and development. We assess barriers to clinical workflow adoption such as dataset bias, AI interpretability, and government regulation. Further, we discuss potential future research directions and emphasize the need for diverse, prospectively curated datasets, explainability frameworks for trust in AI, and rigorous compliance to Good Machine-Learning-Practice (GMLP) to achieve safe and scalable deep learning dermatopathology models that can fully integrate into clinical workflows.

title: Leveraging Multimodal Foundation Models in Biliary Tract Cancer Research.
