In brief, all hearts underwent in situ cardioplegia and were kept in cold cardioplegia or saline until transmural samples were snap frozen in liquid nitrogen (within 4 hours) and stored at −80 °C until processing for mRNA analysis.      Participant demographics  Bulk RNA-seq included 142 participants: NF  n  = 29 (11 male, 18 female; mean age 51.8 ± 16.1 years, range 18−75), pressure-loaded  n  = 78 (61 male, 17 female; mean age 53.6 ± 11.0 years, range 20−69) and RV failure  n  = 35 (21 male, 14 female; mean age 55.0 ± 8.7 years, range 27−69). Single-nucleus RNA-seq included 11 participants: NF  n  = 4 (two male, two female; mean age 55.5 ± 12.1 years, range 39−65), pressure-loaded  n  = 4 (two male, two female; mean age 54.2 ± 1.3 years, range 53−56) and RV failure  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 47.7 ± 20.0 years, range 27−67). Xenium spatial transcriptomics included nine participants: NF  n  = 3 (one male, two female; mean age 61.0 ± 6.1 years, range 54−65), pressure-loaded  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 54.3 ± 1.5 years, range 53−56) and RV failure  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 47.7 ± 20.0 years, range 27−67). Per-participant sex, age and underlying diagnosis are given in Supplementary Tables  1 ,  4  and  6 . The pediatric single-nucleus cohort comprised 14 participants from two institutions (Colorado  n  = 9, Washington University in St. Louis  n  = 5): NF donors  n  = 4 (two male, two female; mean age 4.9 ± 3.3 years, range 1.3−8.0), single-ventricle participants with protein-losing enteropathy or plastic bronchitis  n  = 5 (three male, two female; mean age 9.6 ± 5.1 years, range 4.8−16.0) and single-ventricle participants with systolic heart failure  n  = 5 (four male, one female; mean age 10.5 ± 8.3 years, range 3.8−23.0). One participant in the systolic heart failure group was 23 years old at collection. All others were under 18.    Bulk RNA-seq: sample stratification  Diseased RVs were stratified into two groups: pRV (right atrial pressure and right atrial to pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ratio—that is, RA ≤ 8 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≤ 0.37) and RVF (RA ≥ 9 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≥ 0.63) based on validated clinical predictors of RVF or death after left ventricular assist device placement  17 , 18  .    Bulk RNA-seq: human sample preparation  Snap-frozen cardiac tissues from the RVs of explanted donors were pulverized in a liquid nitrogen-cooled cryomill. Total RNA extraction was performed using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen) with poly(A) selection. RNA quality was assessed using RNA 6000 Nano Kit (Agilent Technologies) and 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies), targeting an RNA integrity number (RIN) score >7.0. RNA-seq libraries were prepared using TruSeq mRNA Stranded Kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturerʼs recommended protocol.    Bulk RNA-seq: transcriptome pseudo-alignment  Libraries were sequenced to a depth of more than 20 million reads per sample. Reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic  58  . Trimmed reads were pseudo-aligned to the human transcriptome (GRCh38) using Kallisto  59  . Transcript-level abundances were converted to gene-level counts with tximport, which weights transcripts by length to correct for the length dependence of read counts under the 2 × 150 sequencing configuration  60  . The resultant gene-level count matrices were then used for downstream analysis.    Bulk RNA-seq: differential gene expression  DEGs were detected using DESeq2 (ref.   61  ). To account for inter-subject differences including sex, race, other clinical variables and batch effects, SVA  62   was used to estimate 21 surrogate variables and remove sequencing batch effects—that is, with the model Expression ~ Group + SV1 +…+ SV21, where the tilde represents ‘distributed as’. A joint model was fit over all contrasts, and then pairwise comparisons (for example, NF versus pRV) were conducted for disease states using the Wald test at an  α  value of 0.1. The surrogate variables were fit from demographic and clinical covariates (sex, age, race, body surface area, height, weight, body mass index, thyroid disease, pacemaker status and sequencing and library preparation batch). Those covariates are not released, as they are indirect identifiers. The fitted surrogate variables are deposited with the count matrix so that the published models can be reproduced without patient-level characteristics.    Bulk RNA-seq: WGCNA  The R packages WGCNA  20   and hdWGCNA  45   were used for all WGCNA analysis. Only genes expressed in more than 5% of subjects (or nuclei for EC snRNA-seq) were retained for analysis. For bulk analysis, WGCNA was run on DESeq2 normalized counts and was used to identify gene modules that co-varied among subjects, agnostic of disease state.  The key of EC hdWGCNA module identities is as follows: ecM1 core/capillary identity ( n  = 1,139 genes); ecM2 sarcomeric/cardiomyocyte ambient signature ( n  = 836); ecM3 constitutive RNA splicing/processing ( n  = 647); ecM4 arterial identity ( n  = 125); ecM5 AP-1/NR4A immediate-early stress ( n  = 120); ecM6 peri-vascular/mural-like ECM ( n  = 115); ecM7 venous/inflamed program ( n  = 91). Hubs are in Supplementary Data  18 .  For the bulk WGCNA module catalog (nomenclature), the module identities used were as follows (29 in total; full hub gene lists in Supplementary Data  4 ): M1 resident-macrophage identity (hubs  VSIG4 ,  CD163 ,  MRC1 ,  LAPTM5 ,  HCLS1 ,  FCN3 ); M2 cytoskeletal/focal adhesion + structural/ECM (contractile, multi-lineage); M3 late chromatin/epitranscriptomic ( METTL3 ,  INO80 ,  KANSL1 ,  PHF8 ,  MBD1 ); M4 myeloid/T cell antigen presentation; M7 polycomb/developmental ( EZH2 ,  HOXB8 ,  ITGA4 ,  POLE2 ); M8 MHC-II master,  CIITA -enriched; M10/M25/M26 nuclear-encoded ETC/OXPHOS (M10/M26 also complex III/ATP synthase/ MCUR1 ); M12 cardiomyocyte ( TNNI3 ,  TNNI3K ,  BMPR2 ,  MYH7 ); M13 immunoglobulin repertoire ( IGHG/IGKC ); M14 cardiac transcriptional regulators ( CASZ1 ,  RARA ,  KDM5A ,  MED13L ,  TLE4 ,  DDR1 ); M15 endothelial activation (95 genes, chemokine signaling); M21 TGFβ/Notch/Wnt suppressors ( SKI ,  AXIN1 ,  MIB2 ,  CTBP1 ,  MTA1 ,  ALKBH5 ); M24 complex I/IV hubs; M27 splicing/RNA processing ( SRSF7 ,  SF3B1 ); and M28 mtDNA-encoded ETC ( MT-ATP6 ,  MT-CO2 ,  MT-CO3 ,  MT-CYB ,  SOD1 ). Modules M5, M6 and M16 are referenced descriptively without standalone identities.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sample selection  Diseased hearts were selected from patients with DCM who had no high-impact variants identified on whole-exome sequencing. To maximize the probability of capturing transcriptional changes, the RVF samples were enriched for severity, possessing decreased diastolic function (RA ≥ 14 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≥ 0.7), decreased systolic function (TAPSE ≤ 1.7) and at least moderate tricuspid regurgitation; pRV samples were comparatively enriched for normal diastolic function (RA ≤ 4 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≤ 0.33), systolic function (TAPSE ≥ 2.2) and trivial or less tricuspid regurgitation. RVF and pRV samples were otherwise well balanced for other clinical and demographic variables (Supplementary Tables  4  and  5 ). For the pediatric HLHS cohort, Fontan/Glenn single-ventricle physiology differs fundamentally from adult LVF secondary pressure overload in onset timing, ventricular morphology and load history; pediatric comparisons, therefore, test molecular convergence rather than direct replication.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: human sample preparation  Samples were prepared as described previously  12  . In brief, frozen cardiac tissues from the RV of explanted donors (approximately 100 mg) were sectioned to 100 µm (Leica, CM1950 cryostat) and then transferred into a 2-ml Dounce homogenizer containing 1 ml of chilled lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 250 mM sucrose, 25 mM KCl, 3 mM MgCl 2 , 1 µM DTT and 0.05% IGEPAL-630 in nuclease-free water). Samples were homogenized with 10 passes of a coarse pestle and then 10 passes of a fine pestle and then incubated on ice for 15 minutes. Large debris was removed by centrifugation at 40 g  for 1 minute (Beckman Coulter, Allegra X-15R swinging bucket centrifuge) before sequentially being filtered through a 50-µm and then a 10-µm filter (puriSelect Life Science) into a 50-ml conical tube. The filters were washed with 6 ml of wash buffer (0.01% BSA, 5 mM MgCl 2 , PBS), and the resultant suspension was pelleted at 550 g  for 5 minutes at 4 °C. The pelleted nuclei were resuspended in 150 µl of cold nuclei resuspension buffer (0.01% BSA, 5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.4 U µl −1  murine RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs), PBS) and counted on a hemocytometer before dilution to 1,000 nuclei per microliter.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: mouse sample preparation  Samples were prepared similarly as above for the human samples, with the notable exception of an additional fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) step at the end. DAPI (1 µg ml −1 ) was added into the lysis buffer. Instead of resuspension in nuclei resuspension buffer, nuclei were resuspended in FACS buffer (1% BSA, 0.4 U µl −1  murine RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs), PBS). Nuclei were flowed at the lowest flow rate on a FACSAria III (BD Biosciences) with a 100-µm nozzle. In total, 100,000 DAPI +  singlets were collected. Nuclei were recovered by spinning at 500 g  for 5 minutes and then resuspended in nuclei resuspension buffer before quantification and dilution to 1,000 nuclei per microliter.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: 10x Chromium single-cell gene expression  Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Genomics Chromium microfluidic platform (Single Cell 3′ solution, v3) for an estimated recovery of 6,000 cells per device. Processing of libraries was performed according to the manufacturerʼs instructions.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sequencing and alignment  Complementary DNA libraries were multiplexed and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 S4 chip (Azenta) to a goal of approximately 75,000−100,000 reads per nucleus. Raw base call files for each sample were demultiplexed and converted to FASTQ files using the 10x Genomics toolkit Cell Ranger 7.1.0 (cellranger mkfastq)  63  . FASTQ files were then uploaded to the 10x Genomic Cloud where Cell Ranger Count 7.1.0 was run on each sample to map them to the human (GRCh38) 2020-A transcriptome or the mouse (GRCm39) 2020-A transcriptome with the include-introns flag set to true. Resultant raw feature matrices were then used for downstream analysis.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: ambient RNA and noise removal  To remove ambient and background RNA contamination, we used CellBender  64  , running remove-background with hyperparameter tuning (primarily of learning rate) to ensure smooth convergence during model training. CellBender-denoised count matrices were then further processed with DecontX  65   to estimate and subtract residual per-cell ambient contamination, and the DecontX-corrected counts were carried forward for all downstream analyses. Some residual cytoplasmic RNA contamination during nuclear isolation can nevertheless produce low-level off-target detection of canonical cell type markers (for example,  RYR2  in non-cardiomyocyte populations); cell type assignment, therefore, relies on relative enrichment over a panel of cluster-defining markers rather than presence/absence of any single gene.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: filtering and quality control  All further analysis was conducted in Seurat  66  . Nuclei with more than 5% mitochondrial transcripts, with fewer than 200 transcripts or with more than 100,000 transcripts were discarded. For each nucleus, the entropy (using the Python package ndd and its entropy function) and the exonic percentage (using scR-Invex) were calculated. Nuclei with entropy below Q1 − 1.5×IQR (first quartile (Q1), interquartile range (IQR)), exon percentage above Q3 + 1.5×IQR (third quartile (Q3)) or mitochondrial read percentage above Q3 + 1.5×IQR were flagged as outliers and removed. For secondary outlier detection, nuclei were then clustered using Seuratʼs built-in graph-based clustering approach (FindNeighbors and FindClusters). Each cluster was fit with an ellipsoid using the sklearn EllipticEnvelope function, and the 5% of nuclei farthest from the cluster centroid were labeled as outliers and also removed. For doublet removal, we elected to utilize a semi-supervised approach, as has been done previously  11  , which was based upon identifying nuclei that simultaneously had gene expression signatures consistent with two (or more) cell populations  11  . Practically, this was done by iteratively clustering nuclei at high resolution, generating  z -score expression profiles for each expected cell population and visualizing the nuclei clusters colored by  z -score using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding. Clusters that demonstrated high expression profiles for multiple cell types were deleted, and then the entire above process was repeated until no further clusters were removed (six rounds).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: myeloid subtype marker rationale  Myeloid subtype assignments were supported by markers with established functional roles:  F13A1  (coagulation factor XIII) is required for post-infarction cardiac integrity  67  .  MARCO  and  HPGDS  define scavenger populations implicated in non-inflammatory clearance of damage-associated molecular patterns and prostaglandin D 2 -mediated inflammation resolution, respectively  36  .  VSIG4 ,  CD163  and  LYVE1  mark self-renewing tissue-resident macrophage subsets associated with complement-mediated immune quiescence  36   and hyaluronan-dependent maintenance of arterial tone  68  . Initial high-resolution subclustering of CCR2 −  resident macrophages identified three transcriptionally distinguishable subsets (enriched for  HPGDS , a broader  F13A1 / CD209 / VSIG4  signature or  RBPJ ), but these subsets showed no disease-specific expansion (all differences <10% of total resident macrophages) and were combined into a single CCR2 −  resident macrophage population for downstream analyses.  CCR2  transcript itself is sparsely detected in droplet-based snRNA-seq of human heart  10  , a well-described dropout effect that disproportionately affects modestly expressed transcripts. Populations were, therefore, defined by combinatorial marker expression rather than by  CCR2  expression alone.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sample integration  The 11 single-nucleus datasets were integrated using the R Harmony package  69  . Specifically, the 11 preprocessed (as above) and normalized/scaled (via SCTransform) datasets were first combined via Seurat merge, and then the RunHarmony command was utilized to generate batch-corrected PCA components (50 dimensions). These Harmony-corrected dimensions (rather than raw PCA) were used for all downstream neighbor graph construction (FindNeighbors), clustering (FindClusters) and UMAP embedding (RunUMAP).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: reference mapping  Reference mapping was conducted using the Seurat version 4 reference mapping pipeline. In brief, both the reference and query datasets were initially preprocessed via SCTransform. The reference dataset was then integrated using canonical correlation analysis (CCA) integration rather than Harmony integration as used elsewhere. Anchors between the reference and query dataset were then identified and used to map query data to the integrated reference dataset.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: differential gene expression  Differential gene expression at the single-nucleus level was performed using the FindMarkers function. The default Wilcoxon rank-sum method was used for statistical testing. Only genes with log 2 FC > 0.1 were retained, and those with adjusted  P  < 0.05 were considered significant.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: pseudobulk differential gene expression  Pseudobulk dataset generation was done by summing counts (from the ‘counts’ slot of the SCTransform assay) for each major cell type using the AggregateExpression function. Differential gene expression analysis was then conducted via DESeq2. For both snRNA-seq and Xenium pseudobulk analyses, multiple-testing correction was performed using Benjamini−Hochberg FDR within each DESeq2 run (per subtype × contrast); no global correction was applied across the full subtype × contrast matrix, in keeping with standard pseudobulk practice where each cell type is treated as a distinct experiment. DEG counts reported throughout this paper use the unified threshold adjusted  P  < 0.05, |log 2 FC| > 0.5 and baseMean > 50 unless otherwise stated.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: enrichment analysis  Pathway enrichment analysis was conducted using the web interface for Enrichr  70   and the R enrichR package. Inputs were genes upregulated or downregulated in the cluster of interest (log 2 FC > 0.1, adjusted  P  < 0.05). Combined score was calculated as  c  = log( p ) ×  z , where  c  is the combined score,  p  is Fisherʼs exact test  P  value and  z  is  z -score for deviation from expected rank.    Bulk RNA-seq: PAH comparison  To compare RVF transcriptional programs across etiologies, we reanalyzed the published PAH RV bulk RNA-seq dataset from Khassafi et al.  19  . Raw count matrices were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus ( GSE240941 ) and processed using the same DESeq2 pipeline as our adult RV bulk data. DEGs from PAH RVF versus PAH NF were compared with our RVF versus NF DEGs to identify concordant and discordant genes. Pathway enrichment analysis (EnrichR) was performed separately on concordant genes (same direction in both datasets) and discordant genes (opposite direction).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: mitochondrial transcription factor analysis  We assessed mitochondrial biogenesis transcriptional regulators across three analytic axes (per-patient pseudobulk DESeq2 expression, CollecTRI/decoupleR  71   transcription factor activity inference and MitoCarta3.0 (ref.   72  ) module scoring) to disentangle transcription factor transcript level, downstream regulon activity and aggregate mitochondrial program output.   Mitochondrial transcription factor panel  A literature-curated panel of nine mitochondrial biogenesis regulators was analyzed:  ESRRA ,  ESRRG ,  PPARA ,  PPARGC1A  (PGC-1α),  NRF1 ,  NFE2L2  (NRF2),  TFAM ,  POLRMT  and  TFB2M , covering the PGC-1α/ERR/PPAR/ NRF1 / TFAM  axis governing nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene expression and mtDNA transcription.    Per-patient pseudobulk expression  For each subtype and lineage, raw RNA counts were aggregated per patient × disease state with Seurat AggregateExpression; counts were then modeled by DESeq2 (design = ~group) with apeglm log 2 FC shrinkage and Benjamini−Hochberg correction. Pairwise contrasts (NF versus pRV, pRV versus RVF, NF versus RVF) used the Wald test. Per-patient violin plots show pseudobulk variance-stabilized transformation (VST) expression, with pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum  P  values reported between disease states. Pseudobulk treats each patient as the unit of replication, avoiding the inflated significance produced by treating individual nuclei as independent observations.    Transcription factor activity inference via CollecTRI/decoupleR  Transcription factor activities were inferred from the cardiomyocyte snRNA-seq using the decoupleR R package with the CollecTRI regulon network (decoupleR::get_collectri, organism = ‘human’, split_complexes = FALSE). Per-cell transcription factor activity was estimated by univariate linear modeling (decoupleR::run_ulm) on SCTransform-normalized expression with default minimum regulon size. Per-patient mean activity per disease group was computed and visualized as a heatmap for the curated mitochondrial transcription factor panel; this approach captures downstream regulon-level activation independent of transcription factor transcript abundance. Pairwise group differences were tested by Wilcoxon rank-sum on per-patient mean activities.    MitoCarta3.0 module score  The MitoCarta3.0 inventory of human mitochondrial-localized genes was used to score aggregate mitochondrial program output. Seurat AddModuleScore was applied to the full MitoCarta3.0 gene set on the SCTransform-normalized snRNA-seq cardiomyocyte data; per-cell scores were aggregated per cardiomyocyte subcluster × disease state.    Bulk RNA-seq cross-validation  DESeq2-VST expression values for the same nine-transcription-factor panel were extracted from the bulk RNA-seq cohort ( n  = 142 patients). Disease-state differences were tested by Wilcoxon rank-sum.     Spatial transcriptomics: 10x Xenium  The Xenium protocol was completed using the Xenium Slides and Sample Prep Reagents Kit (10x Genomics, PN-1000460) and associated consumables. The procedure itself was done using the manufacturerʼs suggested protocol ( CG000578 ; 10x Genomics) without modifications. In brief, 5-µm sections of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) RV samples were mounted onto a Xenium slide (10x Genomics) prior to deparaffinization, decrosslinking, fixation and permeabilization. We specifically chose nine RV samples (three NF, three pRV and three RVF) based on RNA quality and sample geometry (variable sizes but typically 10 × 10 mm) for Xenium analysis. Probes were hybridized, washed, ligated and amplified prior to autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining. Custom probes were designed based on a manually curated list of 100 cluster-specific marker genes from the snRNA-seq data (using the Seurat FindAllMarkers function). The prepared slides were then loaded onto the Xenium Analyzer (10x Genomics), which was run following the recommended protocol. A total of 477 target genes (377 predesigned from the Human Multi-Tissue and Cancer Panel and 100 custom genes) plus 64 negative control probes (541 total) were included on the panel (design ID: 44Z7X8; Supplementary Data  10 ). Output was visualized via Xenium Explorer (10x Genomics). Default Xenium segmentation recovered fewer cells than transcript-level methods, and Baysor  73   produced visually apparent over-segmentation of large cardiomyocytes. Proseg  74   (version 0.3.0) was, therefore, used for resegmentation with the ‘–xenium’ preset, which leverages nucleus boundary overlap for transcript-to-cell assignment. Transcripts with quality value <20 were excluded prior to resegmentation. Each tissue section was divided into overlapping spatial patches using SpatialData/Sopa  75  , and Proseg was run independently on each patch with default parameters (10 components, initial voxel size 10 µm). Patch-level results were merged with global cell ID remapping to avoid collisions across patches. Cell type annotation was performed using RCTD  76   (spacexr R package) in full mode, using our snRNA-seq dataset as the reference. The snRNA-seq reference was constructed from the 12 major cell type annotations with downsampling to a maximum of 500 nuclei per cell type. RCTD was run with UMI_min = 10 and UMI_min_sigma = 100. RCTD weights were used to assign each spatially resolved cell to its most likely cell type. SPLIT  77   ambient RNA correction was applied to the Proseg-resegmented count matrices. To validate cell type frequency estimates against segmentation-dependent cell size variation, nucleus-level proportions were computed by mapping Xenium DAPI nucleus boundaries to Proseg cell boundaries using polygon intersection, with each nucleus inheriting the RCTD annotation of its maximally overlapping Proseg cell. This provides an orthogonal frequency estimate where each nucleus counts as one unit regardless of cell body size. SpaGE  21   imputation was used to impute the expression of genes not included in the Xenium panel but present in the snRNA-seq reference. Subclustering of spatially resolved cells was performed within each of the 12 major cell types using Seurat (version 5). For each cell type, the SPLIT-corrected count matrix (supplemented with SpaGE-imputed genes) was normalized via SCTransform, reduced to 30 principal components and clustered using the Louvain algorithm at a resolution selected to maximize biological interpretability while minimizing over-splitting. Subtype annotations were manually assigned based on marker gene expression and concordance with snRNA-seq subtypes. Pseudobulk differential gene expression analysis was performed within each spatial cell type using DESeq2. To preserve biologically meaningful transcript abundance differences that SPLIT over-corrects, pseudobulk aggregation was performed on the raw, uncorrected Proseg-resegmented count matrix. Genes with |log 2 FC| > 0.5 and adjusted  P  < 0.05 were considered significant. Spatial niche identification was performed using Seurat’s BuildNicheAssay function with  k  = 100 nearest spatial neighbors. To prevent patient-specific cardiomyocyte subtype variation from dominating niche definitions, all cardiomyocyte subtypes were collapsed into a single label prior to niche computation. Centered log ratio (CLR) transformation was applied to niche proportion vectors to amplify differences in rare cell type fractions, followed by  z -scoring. Mini-batch  k -means clustering ( k  = 15) was performed on the CLR-transformed vectors. Clusters sharing similar compositions were merged into 14 final niches. Niche proportions were compared across disease groups (NF, pRV, RVF;  n  = 3 per group) using Kruskal−Wallis tests with Benjamini−Hochberg correction.    Spatial transcriptomics: CellChat cell−cell communication analysis  To infer intercellular signaling within RV myocardium while retaining spatial context, we combined single-nucleus expression with Xenium spatial coordinates. Because the Xenium panel measured only 477 genes, single-nucleus expression was first imputed onto Xenium cells per patient, using each patientʼs own matched snRNA-seq dataset as the reference, so no expression information was shared across individuals. Cell type annotations were consolidated into 13 broad groups from subclustered labels: ECs, cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, macrophages, pericytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, lymphocytes, myeloid cells (monocytes, dendritic cells and proliferating myeloid cells), adipocytes, epicardial cells, neural cells, lymphatic endothelial cells and mast cells. CellChat  29   was run separately for each patient. For each sample, the imputed expression matrix, lineage annotations and Xenium cell centroids were used to construct a spatial CellChat object with spatial scale factors derived from the Xenium coordinate system. Ligand−receptor interactions were drawn from CellChatDB.human. Overexpressed genes and interactions were identified, and communication probabilities were computed under spatial constraints using the truncated mean method (trim = 0.25). Interactions supported by fewer than five cells were removed. Pathway-level probabilities were aggregated across constituent ligand−receptor pairs. For aggregate network visualization, per-patient CellChat objects restricted to the myocardium niche were averaged across patients within each condition (NF,  n  = 3; pRV,  n  = 3; RVF,  n  = 3) to prevent dominance by any single individual. Edge weights were normalized by the product of sender and receiver cell type proportions to control for compositional differences across conditions. For pathway ranking, summed communication probability across all ligand−receptor pairs was computed per pathway per condition and normalized to sum to 1 within each condition. Analyses were performed in R with CellChat version 3.    PAB procedure  All animal studies were approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocols 805255 and 805309). Mice were housed on a normal light/dark cycle (light on from 7:00 to 19:00) with constant access to normal chow and water. PAB was performed in 9-week-old C57BL/6J mice. The anesthetic procedure included induction with ketamine (100 mg kg −1  body weight) and xylazine (10 mg kg −1  body weight) cocktail (intraperitoneal injection), tracheal intubation with a 20-gauge needle and ventilation with a Harvard rodent ventilator (Harvard Apparatus) at a rate of 120−180 breaths per minute and tidal volume of 10 µl g −1  body weight. The main pulmonary artery trunk was dissected from surrounding tissues and constricted with a 7-0 suture tied against a 25-gauge needle to generate a severe RVF. The same procedure including dissection was performed for sham mice apart from pulmonary artery ligature. Close monitoring was performed during procedure and recovery. Meloxicam was administered preoperatively and postoperatively for 48 hours for analgesia, and mice were evaluated daily for 3 days after surgery. The skin sutures were removed 7−10 days postoperatively to avoid irritation and infection. RV remodeling was confirmed by echocardiography at 2-week and 2-month post-surgery timepoints (Supplementary Table  8 ).    PAB resident macrophage bulk RNA-seq  Heterozygous  Cx3cr1 -CreER; Rosa26 -tdTomato mice were fed tamoxifen chow (Inotiv, TD.130856) starting at 3 weeks of age for 1 week. At 8 weeks of age, mice underwent PAB (or sham surgery). Two weeks after surgery, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation, and their hearts were perfused with 20 ml of cold PBS. The hearts were then dissected, atria were removed and the left and right ventricles were harvested for single-cell isolation. The ventricles were digested as previously described to generate a single-cell suspension  78 , 79  . In brief, ventricles were finely minced in ice-cold PBS until a smooth consistency was achieved. Minced tissues were transferred to Eppendorf tubes containing digestion buffer (RPMI supplemented with 450 U ml −1  Collagenase I, 60 U ml −1  DNase I and 60 U ml −1  hyaluronidase enzymes) and digested at 37 °C on a shaker for 45 minutes. After digestion, samples were briefly vortexed and immediately placed on ice to stop the reaction. Then, the cell suspensions were mechanistically dissociated by pipetting with a 1,000-µl pipettor. The digested solution was filtered through a 40-µm cell strainer and rinsed with neutralization buffer (HBSS without Ca 2+ /Mg 2+ , 2% heat-inactivated bovine serum and 0.2% BSA) to obtain a single-cell suspension. Red blood cells were lysed using ACK lysis buffer. Single-cell suspensions were stained for  CD45  (clone 30-F11; BioLegend, 103132), CD11b (clone M1/70; BioLegend, 101223) and  CD64  (clone X54-5/7.1; BioLegend, 139323). Resident macrophages (CD45 + CD11b + CD64 + tdTomato + ) were sorted by FACS, pelleted and then sent to Azenta for ultra-low-input RNA-seq.    Right ventricular cardiomyocyte mitochondrial isolation from frozen tissue  Mitochondria were isolated from flash-frozen tissue as done previously with modifications  80 , 81  . In brief, frozen right ventricular cardiac muscle was thawed on ice in mitochondrial isolation medium (Buffer A, 50 mM MOPS, 100 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgSO 4 , pH 7.1) for 10 minutes. Thereafter, the cardiac tissue was minced on ice for 3 minutes and then subjected to a 15-minute digestion in Buffer A supplemented with 0.25 mg ml −1  Collagenase II (Worthington,  LS004176 ) while rocking at room temperature. After collagenase digestion, cardiac tissue was centrifuged at 300 g  for 5 minutes at 4 °C. The pellet was then resuspended in Buffer B (50 mM MOPS, 100 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgSO 4 , 2 g l −1  BSA, pH 7.1) and homogenized via a glass-Teflon homogenizer (Wheaton) for approximately five passes and subsequently centrifuged at 800 g  for 10 minutes at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant containing the mitochondrial fraction was collected in a separate pre-chilled tube and centrifuged at 10,000 g  for 10 minutes at 4 °C to pellet mitochondria. The final mitochondrial pellet was washed with Buffer A to remove damaged mitochondria on the exterior of the pellet and then was resuspended in Buffer A. Protein concentration was determined using a bicinchoninic acid protein assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225). For mouse PAB and pediatric human samples, mitochondria were similarly isolated from flash-frozen RV tissue using the protocol described above. Pediatric samples were obtained from pediatric patients with HLHS (with and without RVF) and from non-diseased pediatric donors with normal cardiac anatomy.    Assessment of mitochondrial electron transport capacity using high-resolution respirometry  Mitochondria isolated from freeze/thawed tissue are fully uncoupled and have been suggested to lose components of the TCA cycle throughout processing; however, they still maintain electron transport capacity  80  . Using high-resolution respirometry (Oroboros O2K), oxygen consumption (     J      O    2       ) was measured in isolated mitochondria from human right ventricular muscle in Buffer D (105 mM K-MES, 30 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 10 mM K 2 HPO 4 , 5 mM MgCl 2 -6H 2 O, 2.5 mg ml −1  BSA, pH 7.2) supplemented with 20 mM creatine at 37 °C. Alamethicin (10 µg ml −1 ) was supplemented to Buffer D during the experiment to ensure complete membrane permeabilization and access to substrates. Then, 5−15 mg of right ventricular tissue homogenate was added to the respiratory chambers at an oxygen concentration of approximately 200 µM. Once a baseline steady-state rate was established, substrates were injected as follows: NADH (1 mM) and cytochrome c (Cyt C) (5 µM), succinate (10 mM), rotenone (5 µM), antimycin A (5 µM), N,N,N′,N′-tetramethyl- p -phenylenediamine (TMPD, 0.5 mM) and ascorbate (1 mM). The mean      J      O    2        after each injection was measured and obtained once a steady-state flux was maintained for 5 minutes. Primary measurements included complex I (NADH + Cyt C), complex I + II (after succinate addition; coupled maximal OXPHOS capacity), complex II (rotenone-resistant respiration; succinate-driven with complex I inhibited) and complex IV (ascorbate + TMPD) maximal electron transfer capacity. Residual oxygen consumption (ROX) was defined as the      J      O    2        remaining after antimycin A addition (complex III inhibitor) and was subtracted from each preceding respiratory state to yield mitochondrial-specific values, in keeping with MITOEAGLE consortium conventions. All respiratory rates were normalized to the mass of starting mitochondrial protein (pmol O 2  s −1  mg −1  mitochondrial protein) for cross-cohort consistency. Inter-group differences were assessed by Kruskal−Wallis test with Mann−Whitney pairwise post hoc comparisons (NF versus pRV, NF versus RVF, pRV versus RVF). Non-mitochondrial respiration (ROX) was independently tested across groups to confirm that observed mitochondrial deficits were not confounded by NADPH oxidase (NOX)-mediated changes in non-mitochondrial O 2  consumption. The same O2K inhibitor titration protocol was applied to pediatric human samples. The pediatric respirometry cohort consisted of pediatric NF controls (non-diseased pediatric donors with normal cardiac anatomy,  n  = 7) and pediatric HLHS-palliated failing RVs ( n  = 9), forming a within-pediatric NF-versus-failing comparison matched for age, ventricular morphology (single-ventricle physiology in the failing arm) and load history.  Mouse PAB respirometry used a different, FAO-focused protocol on intact RV tissue fiber bundle preparations (rather than freeze/thaw-isolated mitochondria), reflecting the smaller available tissue mass and the goal of profiling β-oxidation capacity in the same run. Substrate addition was sequential: pyruvate + malate (complex I leak respiration in the absence of adenosine diphosphate (ADP)), ADP (complex I-driven coupled phosphorylating respiration), Cyt C (outer mitochondrial membrane integrity check; intact outer membrane defined as Cyt C / ADP ratio < 1.10), octanoyl-carnitine (complex I + FAO substrates) and succinate (complex I + II + FAO maximal coupled capacity). Respiratory control ratio (RCR) was calculated as ADP/pyruvate + malate. Inter-group differences (sham versus PAB-mild-RVF versus PAB-severe-RVF) at each timepoint (2 weeks, 2 months) were assessed by Kruskal−Wallis test with Mann−Whitney pairwise post hoc comparisons, in keeping with the adult and pediatric statistical framework.    Immune repertoire profiling  Mouse RV cardiac single-cell suspensions were stained with the following anti-mouse antibodies: CD45-BUV395 (clone 30-F11; BioLegend, 103191), CCR2-BV421 (SA203G11; BioLegend, 150605), Ly-6G − PerCP-Cy5.5 (1A8; BioLegend, 127615), CD11b-PE (M1/70; BioLegend, 101207), CD64-PE-Cy7 (X54-5/7.1; BioLegend, 139313), TREM2-APC (237920; R&D Systems, FAB17291A) and I-A/I-E (MHC-II)-APC-Cy7 (M5/114.15.2; BioLegend, 107627). Antibodies were used at the manufacturer-recommended amounts in a 100-µl staining volume: CD45-BUV395, CD11b-PE and I-A/I-E (MHC-II)-APC-Cy7 at 0.25 µg per 10 6  cells; CCR2-BV421, Ly-6G − PerCP-Cy5.5 and CD64-PE-Cy7 at 0.5 µg per 10 6  cells; and TREM2 − APC at 10 µl per 10 6  cells. Samples were acquired on an LSRFortessa (five-laser: 355 nm, 405 nm, 488 nm, 561 nm and 640 nm) using FACSDiva version 9.1 (BD Biosciences) and were analysed in FlowJo. Compensation was calculated from single-stain controls acquired in the same run. After exclusion of doublets (forward scatter area (FSC-A)/forward scatter height (FSC-H)), populations were gated as follows: leukocytes (CD45 + ); myeloid cells (CD45 + CD11b + Ly-6G − ; Ly-6G −  excluding neutrophils); and macrophages (CD64 +  within the myeloid gate). Macrophage residency was defined by CCR2 alone: CCR2 −  cells as resident macrophages and CCR2 +  cells as recruited and monocyte derived. TREM2 +  macrophages were gated within the macrophage gate. Surface MHC-II was quantified as the geometric mean fluorescence intensity (gMFI) of I-A / I-E on the CCR2 −  resident gate. MHC-II gMFI was analyzed on a log scale (fluorescence intensity is log distributed). Trends across sham, mild-RVF and severe-RVF groups were tested with a batch-adjusted linear model on the per-animal (log transformed for gMFI) values. One sham was excluded for quality control. Gates were drawn separately for each of the two staining cohorts, on the internal negative population of each bivariate plot, and applied identically to every sample within a cohort. The complete gating cascade for a representative animal from each cohort is shown in Extended Data Fig.  9 .                      Histology  Full-thickness human RV and mouse hearts were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, serially dehydrated in ethanol and paraffin embedded (FFPE). FFPE blocks were sectioned at 10 μm, mounted onto slides and stained with either trichrome or Sirius Red according to the manufacturerʼs instructions. Widefield brightfield microscopy was performed on a Keyence BZ-X810 microscope at ×10 with image stitching using BZ-X800 software. Image processing was performed in Fiji. For mouse slides, a region of interest (ROI) was manually drawn to isolate the RV free wall from the septum. Tissue borders and fibrosis-positive regions were identified using color deconvolution to generate binary masks. Statistical analysis was performed in Prism using Kruskal−Wallis with two-stage linear step-up Benjamini−Krieger−Yekutieli correction for pairwise comparisons.  For cardiomyocyte cross-sectional analyses, slides were stained with Alexa Fluor 488 WGA (Cell Signaling Technology, 1:100) and α-actinin (Abcam, ab68167, 1:200) and DAPI. Donkey anti-rabbit IgG Alexa Fluor 568 was used as secondary antibody (Invitrogen/Thermo Fisher Scientific, A10042, 1:500). Three representative stitched ×40 tile-scan images were acquired per subject in RV regions where cardiomyocytes were predominantly oriented in cross-section. Regions containing predominantly longitudinally oriented cardiomyocytes were manually excluded. Cellpose  82   was used for cell segmentation on processed WGA images using the following settings: diameter 100, flow threshold 0.5, cell probability threshold 0.0, normalization percentiles 1.0−99.0 and dynamic Niter iterations 200. Generated images were subsequently analyzed in CellProfiler  83  . Cardiomyocytes were identified by filtering segmented objects based on α-actinin intensity, size and eccentricity to exclude non-cardiomyocytes, cell aggregates and obliquely sectioned cells. Minimum Feret diameter (MinFerDia) was extracted for each cardiomyocyte as a proxy for cross-sectional cell size (17,864 cardiomyocytes total across the 12 patients). For visualization (Extended Data Fig.  2i ), per-patient median minimum Feret diameter was used. The full per-cell dataset is provided in Supplementary Data  16 .  Statistical analyses were performed in R using linear mixed-effects models to account for the hierarchical structure of the data. Experimental group (NF/pRV/RVF for human studies and sham/mild-RVF/severe-RVF for mouse studies) was modeled as a fixed effect. Subject identity was included as a random intercept for all analyses, and slide was additionally included as a random intercept for mouse studies to account for repeated measurements obtained from the same specimen and histologic section. Pairwise group comparisons were performed using estimated marginal means with Benjamini−Hochberg correction for multiple testing.    Clustering parameters  All clustering analyses used the following parameters unless otherwise specified. For bulk RNA-seq WGCNA, a soft-thresholding power was selected using the pickSoftThreshold function to achieve approximate scale-free topology. For snRNA-seq analysis, SCTransform normalization was applied with mitochondrial read percentage regressed out. PCA was computed using the top 3,000 variable features, and 50 principal components were retained for downstream analysis. Nearest neighbor graphs were constructed using FindNeighbors with  k  = 20. Clustering was performed using FindClusters with the Louvain algorithm. Clustering resolution was selected in a semi-supervised manner: nuclei were clustered at a range of resolutions (0.1−2.0), and the resolution yielding biologically interpretable clusters with distinct marker genes was selected. For the 12 major cell types, the default Seurat resolution of 0.8 was used. For subclustering, a resolution of 0.5 was used for fibroblast, endothelial, myeloid, mural and natural killer/T lineages. Cardiomyocyte subclustering used a resolution of 0.3. For EC hdWGCNA, seven modules were identified using a soft-thresholding power automatically selected via the pickSoftThreshold function to approximate scale-free topology. For Xenium subclustering, 30 principal components were used with resolutions of 0.3 (cardiomyocytes) to 0.5 (all other cell types). UMAP was computed using RunUMAP with n.neighbors = 30 and min.dist = 0.3.   Quantification and statistical analysis  Details of specific statistical analyses for each section, sample sizes and statistical tests used are given in the  Methods  and in the corresponding figure legends. All analysis was done in R using primarily custom-written scripts, which are available with deposited data, and the Seurat package. For pseudobulk DE, DESeq2 was run independently for each cell subtype, and pairwise disease comparison and  P  values were adjusted for multiple testing within each analysis using the Benjamini−Hochberg procedure. Cross-subtype correction was not applied, as each subtype−comparison pair tests an independent biological question.     Software and versions  Analyses were performed in R version 4.3.3. Bulk RNA-seq processing used Trimmomatic version 0.39, kallisto version 0.51.1, tximport version 1.30.0, DESeq2 version 1.42.1 with apeglm version 1.24.0 shrinkage, sva version 3.50.0, edgeR version 4.0.16 and WGCNA version 1.73. Single-nucleus data were processed with Cell Ranger version 7.1.0, CellBender version 0.3.0 and decontX (celda version 1.18.1) and analyzed with Seurat version 5.1.0 (SeuratObject version 5.0.2, SeuratWrappers version 0.3.5), harmony version 1.2.3, hdWGCNA version 0.3.01, monocle3 version 1.3.7, decoupleR version 2.9.7 with CollecTRI, fgsea version 1.28.0, enrichR version 3.3, presto version 1.0.0 and glmGamPoi version 1.14.3. Xenium data were processed with Proseg version 1.1.9 and Sopa version 2.2.10 and analyzed with spacexr (RCTD) version 2.2.1, SPLIT version 0.1.3, SpaGE (GitHub commit edd0fb70; no tagged releases) and CellChat version 3. Histology was analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ version 1.54p, Cellpose version 3.1.1.2 and CellProfiler version 4.2.8. Flow cytometry was acquired with FACSDiva version 9.1, gated in FlowJo version 11.1.0 and reanalyzed with flowWorkspace version 4.14.3 and ggcyto version 1.30.2. Figures were produced with ggplot2 version 3.5.2, patchwork version 1.3.0, cowplot version 1.1.3, EnhancedVolcano version 1.20.0, Nebulosa version 1.12.1 and scCustomize version 3.0.0. Anthropic Claude was used to assist with the implementation and debugging of analysis code and to improve the clarity and readability of author-written text. Genotype-driven tumor ecosystems drive immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in melanoma.

Background

Genetic and transcriptional alterations in cancer cells shape their interactions with immune and stromal compartments, thereby influencing tumor progression, immune evasion, and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Yet, how these interactions are spatially organized within melanoma and how they relate to clinical outcome remains incompletely understood.

Methods

We used spatial multi-omic profiling on melanoma tissues from patients, compared those with loss-of-function mutations in the Neurofibromin 1 (NF1) tumor suppressor gene to those with intact NF1, and integrated these results with functional studies and subsequent gene expression changes observed in patient-derived melanoma models and an immunotherapy-resistant syngeneic mouse model.

Results

Spatial multi-omic analysis of melanoma tissues from patients identified 12 meta-niches composed of distinct cell populations with unique molecular features. Although all tumors contained these meta-niches, those enriched in immunosuppressive cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and macrophages were significantly more common in tumors with NF1 loss. Conversely, niches enriched in cytotoxic CD8+ T cells were significantly reduced. In both human and mouse melanoma, NF1 loss was associated with impaired antigen-presentation programs and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. Mechanistically, EGFR signaling emerged as a prominent feature of NF1-deficient melanoma ecosystems and correlated with reduced expression of antigen-presentation genes and T cell exclusion. EGFR inhibition restored the expression of antigen-presentation programs and enhanced antitumor immune responses in a syngeneic Nf1 knockdown model resistant to ICIs.

Conclusions

These findings define spatially organized, functionally distinct meta-niches enriched in NF1-mutant melanoma that may contribute to their aggressive disease features and poor ICI response. Our study links an understudied melanoma driver to specific immune-evasion mechanisms and identifies EGFR inhibition as a candidate strategy to improve outcomes in patients with NF1-mutant melanoma resistant to immunotherapy. Introduction Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have improved clinical outcomes and survival for many patients with cancer. However, more than 50% of tumors do not respond to these treatments, suggesting that they deploy immune-evasive mechanisms not targeted by ICIs [ 1 , 2 ]. Although cancer-driving genetic mutations, tumor cell intrinsic transcriptional programs, and features of the tumor immune microenvironment have been linked to histopathology [ 3 ], immune evasion [ 4 ], and resistance to ICIs [ 5 ], it remains unclear how the spatial organization of tumor cells and their local interactions with surrounding stromal and immune cells shape specific mechanisms of ICI resistance. Melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer due to its high metastatic potential and resistance to therapy [ 6 , 7 ], is a valuable model for studying immune evasion and resistance to ICIs. Despite its high neoantigen load, transcriptional heterogeneity, and diverse oncogenic driver mutations, fewer than 50% of patients achieve durable responses to ICI, underscoring a critical gap in our understanding of tumor-intrinsic mechanisms of immunotherapy resistance. Neurofibromin 1 ( NF1 ) loss-of-function mutations are observed in up to 27% of melanomas and in up to 45% of BRAF- and NRAS-wild -type tumors [ 8 ]. Despite being associated with worse disease-specific and overall survival [ 9 ], NF1 -mutant ( NF1 Mut ) melanomas lack effective targeted therapies [ 8 , 10 , 11 ]. Moreover, co-occurring NF1 mutations with alterations in BRAF or NRAS confer resistance to BRAF and MEK inhibitors [ 8 , 10 – 12 ]. As a result, clinical management of NF1 Mut melanoma remains particularly challenging. NF1 Mut melanomas have the highest tumor mutational burden, and NF1 loss has been linked to increased programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) cell-surface expression, suggesting that these tumors might respond to ICIs [ 5 , 9 , 10 , 13 , 14 ]. Paradoxically, more than half of NF1 Mut melanomas fail to respond to ICIs [ 8 , 14 ]. These data suggest that NF1 Mut tumors may employ alternative, immune checkpoint-independent mechanisms to evade immune surveillance and resist treatment, highlighting the need to define these mechanisms in order to improve clinical responses. Here, we used spatial multi-omic approaches to characterize cellular neighborhoods composed of melanoma cells in distinct transcriptional states together with cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), endothelial cells, myeloid cells, T cells, and other immune and stromal populations in human NF1 Mut and NF1 wild-type ( NF1 WT ) melanoma tissues. We define recurrent cellular neighborhoods across tumors as meta-niches (MNs) and show that their abundance, composition, and immune regulatory functions are associated with NF1-loss-linked transcriptional programs. Finally, using patient tissues and a preclinical Nf1 knockdown melanoma model, we identify EGFR inhibition as a therapeutic strategy to overcome resistance to PD-1 blockade in NF1 Mut melanoma. Materials and methods Study cohort Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor samples were prospectively collected from melanoma patients enrolled in the Interdisciplinary Melanoma Cooperative Group Database (IMCG) at NYU Langone Health (IRB #10362). Inclusion criteria for this clinicopathological database included patients who presented to the Laura and Isaac Perlmutter Cancer Center (2002–2018) with melanoma and were accrued within two months of diagnosis. All patients signed NYU Langone Health Institutional Review Board-approved consent authorizing the use of their specimens for research and follow-up. A board-certified dermatopathologist (G.J.) reviewed H&E-stained tumor sections from 32 patients and selected two representative areas per patient specimen, one at the tumor center and another at the tumor margin. These areas were used to assemble two tissue microarrays (TMAs). Xenium spatial analysis Processing, integration, and annotation of Xenium spatial transcriptomics data Xenium analyses were performed on 42 cores from 32 patients contained in two tissue microarrays. Data from multiple cores were acquired on the same Xenium Slide and imported into Seurat (v5.0.0) [ 15 ] running on R (v4.3.2). Tissue coordinates of individual cores were imported as CSV files using the Xenium Explorer. For each core, a segmentation object was generated with CreateSegmentation(), and the core-specific field of view (FOV) was overlaid onto the full-region FOV using Overlay(). Core-specific counts were extracted to create Seurat objects, filtering out cells with zero or low transcript counts (< 50). Spatial features were reconstructed using centroid-based FOVs CreateCentroids() and CreateFOV() and molecule overlays CreateMolecules() for visualization within core boundaries. Individual core Seurat objects were first merged using the merge() function, with orig.ident retained to track the core of origin. The merged dataset was normalized and variance-stabilized using SCTransform() (selecting the top 5,000 variable features). Batch effects across patients were corrected using Harmony [ 16 ] (HarmonyMatrix), with core ID specified as the grouping variable. Harmony-corrected embeddings were then used for downstream dimensionality reduction, including principal component analysis (PCA) and UMAP, as well as neighbor graph construction and clustering. Cell identities were assigned by identifying cluster-specific marker genes using FindAllMarkers() and manually annotating clusters based on canonical marker expression. Differential abundance of clusters and cell types between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT samples was calculated as the fraction of cells per patient in each cluster, and differences were assessed using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with stat_compare_means() ggpubr (v0.6.2) [ 17 ]. Spatial neighborhood mapping and meta-niche characterization To characterize local cellular neighborhoods, tissue coordinates for each cell were retrieved, and the composition of neighboring cell types within a 40 μm radius was computed for each cell using a fixed-radius nearest neighbor search (frNN function, dbscan package) [ 18 ]. Cells with fewer than three neighbors were excluded. The resulting neighborhood compositions were represented as vectors of cell-type fractions and clustered across all cells to identify 12 MNs using k-means clustering [ 19 ]. MN labels were mapped back to the original Seurat objects, allowing for per-patient and per-cell assignment. Frequencies of MNs per patient were calculated, and differences between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT samples were assessed using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Niches that varied significantly between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanoma tissues were visualized using the ImageDimPlot function of Seurat with custom color schemes. CellChat [ 20 ] was used to infer cell-cell communication within spatially defined MNs or on each individual tissue core. Cells were grouped by cell type and NF1 genotype, and interactions were predicted using the Human ligand–receptor database. Comparative network analyses identified shared, unique, and differential signaling between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT cells, with circle plots and heatmaps summarizing interaction strength and signaling roles across cell types. Spatial proximity analysis of cell types To quantify spatial relationships between cell types, tissue coordinates were extracted from each Seurat object. Spatial proximity was evaluated independently within each tissue core. For each source–target cell-type pair, the Euclidean distance from every source cell to its nearest target cell was calculated using the get.knnx() function from the FNN package (v1.1.3), and distances were summarized within each core before comparison by NF1 genotype. Cores lacking either the source or target cell population were excluded from the corresponding cell-pair analysis. To assess whether tissue-level sampling characteristics could influence the spatial-distance measurements, we quantified the total number of cells analyzed, estimated the analyzed tissue area, and overall cellular density for each core. The analyzed area was estimated from the spatial coordinate range of each core, and cellular density was calculated as the total number of cells divided by the estimated area analyzed. We also calculated the average number of melanoma-cell neighbors per tissue. These parameters were compared between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT tissues using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Transcriptional profiling of spatial meta-niches and association with EGFR Following MN identification, transcriptional programs were mapped by aggregating gene expression across cells assigned to each spatial MN. Average expression profiles were computed and used to characterize niche-specific transcriptional signatures. EGFR expression was quantified across meta-niches and summarized at the patient–niche level. Genotype-dependent differences between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT samples were assessed using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. To resolve MN-specific mechanisms, we quantified both the fraction of EGFR-positive cells and the mean EGFR expression in EGFR-positive cells, stratified by the dominant cell types within each MN. EGFR-associated transcriptional programs were assessed at the pathway level rather than by single-gene correlation. Specifically, activity scores were calculated for Gene Ontology and Hallmark gene sets, and these pathway scores were correlated with EGFR expression using Spearman’s correlation. This approach identified niche-specific pathways whose activity increased or decreased in association with EGFR expression. Cell type–specific differential expression and pathway enrichment independent of spatial niches Differential expression analyses were performed on melanoma cells, CD8 + T cells, CAFs, and myeloid cells independently of spatial niche assignment using Seurat. Cells were subset by cell type and stratified by NF1 genotype. The RNA assay was normalized using NormalizeData(), and differential expression between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT cells was assessed using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests implemented in FindMarkers(). Genes with an adjusted P -value < 0.05 were considered significant and were separated into genotype-specific up- and downregulated sets. Functional enrichment analyses were conducted using clusterProfiler (v4.10.1) with gene identifier mapping via org.Hs.eg.db (v3.18.0). Gene Ontology Biological Process enrichment was performed using enrichGO(), and pathway-level enrichment was evaluated by ranking genes by log fold change, followed by GSEA using gseGO(). In parallel, Hallmark pathway enrichment was performed using Hallmark gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB; collection H, release 2025.1), accessed via msigdbr (v25.1.1). Core enrichment genes were converted to gene symbols to facilitate biological interpretation. Data were visualized using ggplot2 [ 21 ]. Bulk RNA-Seq RNA-Seq data were analyzed as previously described [ 10 ]. Briefly, total RNA was extracted and treated with DNase using the RNeasy Plus Micro Kit (Qiagen, Cat. No.74034) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were prepared with the Illumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Ribo-Zero H/M/R Gold kit and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 at the NYU Genome Technology Center (RRID: SCR_017929). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and converted to FASTQ files using Illumina bcl2fastq. Reads were aligned to the human genome (hg19/GRCh37) or mouse genome (mm10) with the splice-aware STAR aligner, and PCR duplicates were removed using Picard ( http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/ ). Gene-level counts were generated with HTSeq, and DESeq2 was used to normalize counts and identify differentially expressed genes via negative binomial generalized linear models. Alignment, differential expression, and pathway analyses were performed using the Seq-N-Slide pipeline (RRID: SCR_021752, https://igordot.github.io/sns/ ). CODEX spatial proteomics 45-plex immunofluorescent (IF) imaging was performed on 56 archived FFPE tissues isolated from 32 melanoma patients. This 45-plex IF panel includes markers from Akoya Biosciences Phenocycler panel to classify melanoma cells (SOX10, S100b, GP100, NGFR, CSPG4, b-catenin, Axl), immune cells (CD20, CD3e, CD8, CD4, CD57, CD68, CD14, CD11c, CLEC9a, CD1c, Mac2, CD103, Foxp3, CD45RO, TCF-1, CD21, TOX, tryptase, CD169, CD66), endothelial cells (CD31, PDPN, LYVE1, AQP1, PNAd), epithelial cells (pan-cytokeratin) and stromal cells (PDPN, SMA, Collagen IV). This panel also includes markers for proliferation (Ki67), activation (IL-33, Granzyme B, IFNɣ), antigen presentation (HLA-DR), and immune inhibition (PD-1, ICOS, PD-L1, IDO1). 7 μm FFPE tissue was stained and scanned using PhenoCycler-Fusion 2.0 (Akoya Biosciences) according to Akoya’s commercial protocol. HALO Image Analysis Platform (Indica Labs, Albuquerque, NM, USA), an AI-assisted image segmentation software, was used for quantitative image analysis. We trained the software to accurately segment cells based on their nuclear staining and identify tumor mass. This tumor classifier is trained by manually annotating tumor and non-tumor regions. The software considers both the structure and morphology of each pixel, as well as the intensities of our selected markers (DAPI, SOX10, S100b, GP100, and CSPG4), to automatically segment cell borders and annotate tumor regions. Cells within tumor nests (i.e. CD8 + T cells) are then annotated using markers threshold defined by pixel intensity and percent positive pixels within the cell borders. The final exported matrix contains the cell ID, tumor/non-tumor classification, average marker intensities, and the annotated cell phenotype. From this matrix, the cell densities (cells/mm2) and cell frequencies (cell count/total cells) are calculated for downstream analyses. A nonparametric Mann-Whitney test was used to calculate p-values. Cell culture A375 (RRID: CVCL_0132), 08-175 [ 10 ], SK-MEL-28 (RRID: CVCL_0526) and RIM3 [ 22 ] cell lines were utilized in this study [ 23 ]. A375 and Sk-MEL-28 cells were obtained from ATCC [ 24 ] and were cultured in Corning™ RPMI 1640 Medium (Mod.) 1X with L-Glutamine (Life Sciences, 10-040-CV). RIM-3 cells were obtained from the Sommer lab and cultured in DMEM (Corning, 10-017-CV). All culture media were enriched with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), L-glutamine from Invitrogen, sodium pyruvate solution (Sigma, S8636), non-essential amino acids (Sigma, M7145), GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco, 25050061), and normocin (Invivogen, NC9273499). All cell lines were maintained at 37 °C in 7% CO2 and were periodically tested for mycoplasma. Human cell lines NF1 and EGFR knockdowns were previously described [ 10 ]. All Lentiviral and piggyback vectors were designed and purchased from Vector Builder (Chicago, USA). shNF1 target sequence: GCCAACCTTAACCTCTCTAAT, and shEGFR target sequence: GCATAGGCATTGGTGAATTTA. NF1 ectopic expression was performed by using a piggyback vector that expresses a flag-tagged, tetracycline-inducible NF1 full-length gene (Vector builder: VB250317-1543ver), and an empty flag (VB250319-1011vbt) was used as a control. Plasmids were transfected using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen, L3000015) and expression was induced by adding 1ug/ml doxycycline (Gold-Bio, D-500-1) Western blotting and qPCR were performed as previously described [ 10 ] using antibodies against NF1 (Abcam, Cat. No. ab17963; RRID: AB_444142), EGFR (Abcam, Cat. No. ab52894; RRID: AB_869579), HSP90 (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. No. 4877; RRID: AB_2233307), and HLA class I ABC (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. 15240-1-AP; RRID: AB_1557426). Horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies were from Cell Signaling Technology (Cat. Nos. 7074 and 7076; RRIDs: AB_2099233 and AB_330924, respectively). qPCR primers were ordered from Invitrogen, USA. Primers used were: NF1: F: AACTTCTTCCTGCGACTGCG, R: CTCTGCGACAGACGTCAACA. EGFR: F: ACCTCTCCCGGTCAGAGATG, R: TGTGCCTTGGCAGACTTTCT. Live-cell imaging was performed using the Incucyte (Essen BioScience) as described previously [ 10 ]. Flow cytometry analysis was performed on cells treated with Human IFN-gamma Recombinant Protein (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat No. 300-02-100U). Cells were stained with PE-conjugated anti-human HLA-A/B/C antibody (BioLegend, Cat. No. 311406; RRID: AB_314875) or APC-conjugated anti-human HLA-DR/DP/DQ antibody (BioLegend, Cat. No. 361714; RRID: AB_2750316) at 4 °C for 30 min in the dark. Flow analysis was performed using BD FACS Symphony A5 analyzer and analyzed using FlowJo V10.10.0. Mouse models All animal-related procedures were conducted strictly following the guidelines and approvals set forth by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC# 202300101) at New York University Langone Health. RIM3 melanoma cells expressing shSCR or shNf1 were injected subcutaneously into the flank of six-week-old nude mice (Jackson Laboratory, RRID: IMSR_JAX:002019) or syngeneic C57BL/6J mice (Jackson Laboratory, RRID: IMSR_JAX:000664). Male mice were used because the sex of the mouse from which the RIM3 cell line was originally derived was not reported. For tumor-growth studies, mice were injected with1 × 10⁶ cells, whereas 2 × 10⁵ cells were used for treatment studies. Tumor dimensions were measured using digital calipers, and tumor volume was calculated as V = (π/6) x L x W 2 ), where L represents tumor length and W represents tumor width. For longitudinal tumor-growth studies, treatment was initiated when tumors reached approximately 100–200 mm³. Mice were then randomly assigned to vehicle control, afatinib, anti–PD-1, or combined afatinib plus anti–PD-1 treatment groups, with 12 mice per group, and treated for up to four weeks. For flow-cytometric endpoint studies, tumors were allowed to reach approximately 500 mm³ before mice were randomly assigned to the same treatment groups. 5–7 mice were treated for one week, after which tumors were collected for flow-cytometric analysis. Afatinib (MedChemExpress, BIBW 2992, Cat. No. HY-10261) was administered by oral gavage at 20 mg/kg five days per week. Anti–PD-1 antibody (Bio X Cell, anti-mouse CD279, Cat. No. BE0146) was administered by intraperitoneal injection at 10 mg/kg twice weekly. Mice were monitored for changes in body weight, general condition, and other signs of treatment-related toxicity daily. Animals were excluded only according to predefined criteria, including severe weight loss, and six animals were excluded. Tumor-growth curves are presented as mean ± SEM. For each mouse, the area under the tumor-growth curve (AUC) was calculated using the trapezoidal rule, and differences in AUC between treatment groups were assessed using two-sided unpaired t-tests. Mice were euthanized when tumor volume exceeded 2,000 mm 3 or when a predefined experimental endpoint was reached. Overall survival was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier analysis, and survival curves were compared using the log-rank test. A two-sided P  < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. To stain for immune markers, tumor masses were measured at the endpoint. Resected tumors were digested at 37 °C for 25 min with agitation by Collagenase D (1 mg/mL): (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. 11088866001) and DNase I (80 U/mL) (Roche Cat. No.04536282001) and passed through 70 μm cell strainers to generate single cell suspensions. Each tumor was divided into two wells and stained with a T cell panel or a Myeloid panel in addition to Ghost Dye live/dead stain (CYTEK Cat. No.130865T100). The T-cell panel included antibodies against CD45 (BD Biosciences, Cat. No. 564279; RRID: AB_2651134), CD4 (BD Biosciences, Cat. No. 612844), CD8α (Cytek, Cat. No.65-0081-U100), CD44 (Cytek, Cat. No. 60-0441-U100), granzyme B (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. MHGB04; RRID: AB_10372671), Ki-67 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. 48-5698-80; RRID: AB_11151155), FOXP3 (BioLegend, Cat. No. 126407; RRID: AB_1089116), PD-1 (BioLegend, Cat. No. 135225; RRID: AB_2563680), and TIM-3 (BioLegend, Cat. No. 75833-230). The myeloid-cell panel included antibodies against NK1.1 (BioLegend, Cat. No. 108710; RRID: AB_313397), CD11b (BioLegend, Cat. No. 101243; RRID: AB_2561373), CD11c (BioLegend, Cat. No. 117333; RRID: AB_11204262), Ly-6 C (BioLegend, Cat. No. 128012; RRID: AB_1659241), Ly-6G (BioLegend, Cat. No. 127618; RRID: AB_1877261), I-A/I-E (BioLegend, Cat. No. 107632; RRID: AB_2650896), and F4/80 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. 12-4801-82; RRID: AB_465923). Tumors were stained for 1 h at 4 °C in the dark. After washing, tumors were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and stored at 4 °C until analysis. Immune-cell populations were quantified as frequencies of live CD45⁺ cells, and absolute cell numbers were additionally normalized to tumor mass to account for differences in tumor size. Comparisons between groups were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed with Microsoft Excel, GraphPad Prism (version 10.2.0, RRID: SCR_002798), or R statistical software (RRID: SCR_001905 version 4.3.1). Results Melanoma tissues are organized into 12 spatially defined meta-niches To determine whether and how NF1 loss affects immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance, we used two tissue microarrays (TMAs) comprising samples from 32 patients with melanoma, including 17 NF1 Mut and 15 NF1 WT tumors (Fig.  1 A, Table S1). Because each patient contributed two tissue cores, these TMAs contained 64 cores (34 NF1 Mut and 30 NF1 WT ). We profiled 42 of these cores using the 10X Genomics 5 K Xenium platform. After image processing, cell segmentation, and rigorous quality control, we excluded cells with fewer than 50 transcripts and cores with fewer than 5000 cells. We batch-corrected and normalized the data across independent tissues, creating an integrated data set of 1,003,604 high-quality cells from 39 cores (20 NF1 Mut and 19 NF1 WT ). Louvain clustering separated melanoma cells from B cells, T cells, myeloid cells, plasma cells, epithelial cells, and other stromal cell types (Fig.  1 B), which were then annotated based on lineage-defining marker gene expression (Fig.  1 C). Although these cell populations were detected across most melanoma samples, their spatial distributions varied markedly between tumors (Fig.  1 D), suggesting that each tumor contains multiple specialized niches whose composition and organization may influence pathological features and therapy response. Fig. 1 Distinct spatial niches and cellular neighborhood architectures of melanoma. A Schematic representation of the study workflow, starting from isolating 64 melanoma tumors from 32 patients, generating TMAs, performing Xenium spatial transcriptomics on 42 samples and CODEX spatial proteomics on 56 samples to perform single-cell analysis, and testing of identified targets in preclinical models. B Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot of major cell types identified in the Xenium dataset. C Dot plot showing canonical marker genes for each cell type identified in (B). D Representative field of view (FOV) of a Xenium image, showing major cell types in multiple melanoma samples. E UMAP of lineage sub-types identified in the Xenium dataset. F Representative FOV of a Xenium image showing lineage sub-types identified in (E). G Stacked-bar plot showing the composition of each meta-niche (MN) across all cell types. Melanoma cell states are abbreviated as melanocytic (Melan), proliferative (Prol), neural-crest-like (NC), and mesenchymal (Mes). H Bar plot showing the number of patients included in each MN. I Representative FOV images of MNs identified in melanoma patients To characterize these niches in greater detail, we re-clustered cells within each major lineage based on gene expression, identifying 18 distinct cell types, including five melanoma cell states (Fig. 1 E-F, Figure S1A). We identified melanoma cells with melanocytic, proliferative, intermediate, neural crest (NC)-like, and mesenchymal (MES) features, consistent with previous reports [ 25 ]. Immune populations included cytotoxic CD8 + T cells and CXCL13 + CD8 + T cells, regulatory T cells (Treg), M2-like macrophages, interferon (IFN)-stimulated macrophages, activated myeloid cells, B cells, and plasma cells. Stromal populations included cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) with myofibroblastic (myCAF) or inflammatory (iCAF) features, as well as pericytes, endothelial cells, and epithelial cells. We mapped cell-type identities and transcriptional programs back to each tissue core, retrieved each cell’s centroid, and analyzed their neighborhoods within a 40-µm radius using a fast radius-based nearest-neighbor search (frNN) [ 18 ]. K-means clustering [ 19 ] grouped these neighborhoods into 12 frequently occurring meta-niches (MNs), which we defined as cellular spatial neighborhood patterns observed across multiple independent tissue samples (Fig. 1 G). Each MN was annotated according to its most prevalent cell types and broadly categorized as melanoma-rich, immune-rich, stromal-rich, or vascular-rich. Notably, each cell type appeared across multiple MNs (Figure S1B), indicating that cell identity alone does not determine niche architecture. Although individual patients exhibited significant variability in MN composition (Figure S1C), with some tissues dominated by melanoma-rich niches, the identified MNs were generally consistent across the cohort. Several MNs were found in all samples, while others appeared in more than 50% of cases (Fig.  1 H-I). These results suggest that, despite differences in niche abundance among patients, the main spatial MN programs reflect recurring TME states rather than isolated, patient-specific patterns. Overall, these data demonstrate that melanoma tissues are highly compartmentalized, with distinct cell types forming recurring MNs, and that each tumor contains multiple MNs in proportions unique to each patient. NF1-loss links meta-niche remodeling to immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance To determine whether variation in MN composition was associated with cancer-driving mutations, we compared NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanoma tissues. Although these tissues contained the same major cell populations (Figure S2A), NF1 Mut melanomas contained significantly more NC-like melanoma cells (Figure S2B-C). NF1 Mut melanomas were also significantly enriched in MNs dominated by NC-like melanoma cells, immune-suppressive M2-like macrophages, immune-suppressive iCAFs, and regulatory T cells (Fig.  2 A-B, S2D-F). Conversely, NF1 Mut melanomas were depleted of MNs enriched for cytotoxic T cells, Tregs, and IFN-activated macrophages, as well as MNs enriched in pericytes and endothelial cells (Fig.  2 A, C, S2D-F). These results suggest that NF1 loss reshapes the assembly of cells into specific MNs, potentially contributing to immune evasion. NC-like melanoma cells communicated more extensively with melanoma cells in other states, stromal and immune cells within MN2 (NC + M2 + CAF) of NF1 Mut than NF1 WT melanoma (Fig. 2 D). Myelin protein zero (MPZ), which has been associated with tumor progression, invasion, and metastasis [ 26 ], was the predominant and most characteristic signaling pathway active within MN2 (Figure S2G). Cell-cell communication within MN6 (iCAFs+M2) was generally much stronger in NF1 Mut than in NF1 WT melanoma (Fig. 2 E). Furthermore, interactions between mesenchymal melanoma cells and CAFs were consistently stronger in MN2, MN6, and MN3 of NF1 Mut than NF1 WT melanoma tissues (Fig. 2 D-F). In contrast, melanoma-immune cell interactions, especially those between activated macrophages and pericytes or endothelial cells, were stronger within the immune-active MN3 (IFN-myeloid + T cell) in NF1 WT than in NF1 Mut tumors (Fig.  2 F). Differential cell-cell communication analyses within this immune-active MN3 revealed a greater number of receptor-ligand interactions among cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, regulatory T cells, and activated macrophages in NF1 WT than in NF1 Mut tumors (Fig.  2 G). Conversely, signaling interactions between melanoma cells and CAFs in MN3 were higher in NF1 Mut than in NF1 WT tumors. CXCL signaling was significantly elevated in MN3 of NF1 WT tumors, whereas MPZ, Cell Adhesion Molecule (CADM), Protease-Activated Receptor (PAR), and Heparan Sulfate Proteoglycans (HSPG) signaling were increased in MN3 of NF1 Mut tumors (Figure S2H). These data are consistent with a more angiogenic and immunosuppressed tumor microenvironment (TME) in NF1 Mut compared to NF1 WT melanoma. Some differences in cell-cell communication between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanomas were not restricted to specific meta-niches; instead, they were evident globally across tissues. NC-like melanoma cells signaled extensively to iCAFs and mesenchymal melanoma cells, while myCAFs engaged in collagen and laminin signaling with NC-like melanoma cells, in NF1 Mut but not NF1 WT melanoma (Figure S3A-B). Conversely, myCAFs showed fewer interactions with cytotoxic CD8 + T cells and CXCL13 + CD8 + T cells in NF1 Mut than in NF1 WT tumors. These differences in cell-to-cell communication were accompanied by broader signaling changes across NF1 Mut compared to NF1 WT melanoma. NF1 Mut melanoma exhibited increased EGF signaling in mesenchymal melanoma cells and iCAFs; significantly higher levels of collagen, laminin, TGFβ, KIT, prostaglandin, VEGF, PDGF, and L1CAM signaling in the TME, where CXCL signaling was decreased (Figure S3C-E). It also showed increased signaling for PDGF, EGF, TGFβ, KIT, VEGF, ADGR-A, ADGR-D, tenascin, and laminin in myCAFs and iCAFs. Overall, these findings indicate that NF1 Mut melanoma is characterized by heightened stromal and growth factor signaling, a more fibrotic microenvironment, reduced vascular signals, and diminished immune-cell interactions. The immunosuppressive TME in this NF1 Mut melanoma cohort indicated that some tumors could be resistant to ICIs. To determine whether the spatial composition of MNs correlates with anti-PD1 or other ICI response data, we stratified our NF1 Mut melanoma cohort into 7 responder (R) and 11 non-responder (NR), and our NF1 WT melanomas into 9 R and 9 NR tissues. By comparing the fraction of each MN between R and NR we uncovered distinct response-associated patterns in NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanomas (Fig. 2 H). The MN2 (NC + M2 + CAF) was highly enriched in NF1 Mut but not NF1 WT tumors that didn’t respond to ICI or anti-PD1 (Fig. 2 I). myCAFs and mesenchymal melanoma cells were also enriched in the NF1 Mut NR group. In contrast, MN3 (IFN-myeloid + T cell) and MN9 (Inter+Prol+Melan) were enriched in the NF1 WT NR group. MN4 (vasc+perivascular) was more abundant in the R group. These data suggest that NC-like melanoma cells, as well as myCAFs, M2-like macrophages, and Tregs, may contribute to ICI resistance in NF1 Mut melanoma, consistent with their well-established immunosuppressive functions [ 27 – 29 ]. They also suggest that MNs orchestrated by melanoma cells that lost NF1 may function as spatially organized, immunosuppressive microenvironments that become enriched in NF1 Mut melanoma tissues that don’t respond to PD-1 or other ICIs. NF1 mutant tumors accumulate dysfunctional CD8 + T cells The selective enrichment of immune-suppressive MNs suggests that NF1 loss could alter the spatial structure of the tumor microenvironment, broadly impairing anti-tumor immunity. To test this idea, we examined global differences in immune cell organization and CD8 + T cell function in NF1 Mut melanoma by measuring distances between melanoma cells and nearby cell types. This neighborhood analysis showed that NF1 Mut melanoma cells are closer to CAFs, Tregs, M2-like macrophages, and pericytes, but are farther from cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, CXCL13 + CD8 + T cells, or endothelial cells compared to NF1 WT melanoma cells within tumors (Fig.  3 A-B). To rule out the impact of tissue sampling differences on the spatial results, we compared the total cell counts, tissue area, cellular density, and the average number of melanoma neighbors between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT tissue samples and found no differences in these parameters (Figure S4A). These findings suggest that the microenvironment surrounding NF1 Mut melanoma cells is depleted of immune cells but rich in CAFs, while NF1 WT melanoma tissues are more infiltrated by CD8 + T cells and other immune cell types.
