Graphical abstract Keywords Antibody-drug conjugate Breast cancer Spatial transcriptomics Single-cell analysis HER2 TROP2 Tumor microenvironment pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY Introduction Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women, with approximately 2.3 million new cases and 670,000 deaths worldwide in 2022 [ 1 ]. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) link a target-specific antibody to a cytotoxic payload and are now central to breast-cancer treatment [ 2 ]. Trastuzumab emtansine established the class in HER2-positive disease [ 3 ], extending median progression-free survival from 6.4 to 9.6 months and median overall survival from 25.1 to 30.9 months relative to lapatinib plus capecitabine. Trastuzumab deruxtecan and the TROP2-directed agents Sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan have since broadened their use across breast cancer subtypes [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. In the long-term DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, investigator-assessed median progression-free survival was 8.8 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio, 0.36), and median overall survival was 22.9 versus 16.8 months (hazard ratio, 0.69), with trastuzumab deruxtecan versus treatment of the physician's choice in HER2-low advanced breast cancer [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, Sacituzumab govitecan improved median progression-free survival to 4.8 versus 1.7 months (hazard ratio 0.41) and median overall survival to 11.8 versus 6.9 months (hazard ratio 0.51) in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer [ 5 ]. HER3, NECTIN4 , folate receptor-α, B7-H3, MUC1 and CEACAM5 are among the additional targets in clinical development [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]; the molecular alterations of MUC1 and their therapeutic exploitation have been reviewed recently [ 11 ]. For an ADC, tissue-level abundance is not enough. The target must also be located on the relevant cells. Expression in stroma, vasculature or normal epithelium can contribute to target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity, but ADC toxicity is multifactorial and also reflects payload cytotoxicity, platform-related properties, and host factors [ 12 ]. The clinical burden can nonetheless be substantial. In the updated DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 12.1% of patients receiving trastuzumab deruxtecan, including 1.1% grade 5 events [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, the most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events with Sacituzumab govitecan included neutropenia (52%) and diarrhea (12%) [ 5 ]. Conversely, target-negative tumor cells may escape direct binding, although a membrane-permeable payload can affect neighboring cells through a bystander effect [ 13 ]. Bulk assays and tissue-averaged immunohistochemistry do not resolve the cellular source of a target signal. The broader importance of tissue architecture extends beyond ADCs to other tumor-directed delivery platforms, including nanocarriers influenced by vascular permeability and retention, as well as stimuli-responsive nanoparticles under development for breast cancer [ 14 , 15 ]. Cell-resolved target assessment is already used in the chimeric antigen receptor T-cell field to anticipate on-target/off-tumor effects [ 16 ]. For ADCs, bulk surveys have catalogued target expression across tumors and normal tissues, including a 54-target pan-cancer analysis [ 17 ]. A post-mortem breast cancer series also compared metastases with matched normal organs [ 18 ]. In high-grade serous ovarian cancer, dissociated single-cell RNA sequencing identified clinical ADC targets that were most often restricted to cancer cells [ 19 ]. Spatial profiling has therefore been proposed as a means of interpreting target availability in tissue context [ 20 ]. Breast single-cell atlases have examined heterogeneity in ERBB2 and TACSTD2, but primarily within the malignant epithelial compartment [ 21 ]. Few studies have spatially identified multiple ADC targets across malignant and non-malignant compartments in breast cancer. Imaging-based transcriptomics can provide this information while preserving histological structure [ [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] ]. We therefore mapped 11 ADC targets in a publicly available whole-transcriptome breast cancer specimen, examined the recurrence of selected patterns in two public Xenium specimens, and compared the findings with TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes. The study is descriptive. Its purpose is to identify which cells contribute to each target transcript and to show where tissue-level abundance may obscure that source. Materials and methods Single-cell spatial dataset We used the public CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (Bruker Spatial Biology, "breast discovery" release, sample S0) [ 22 ]. The dataset contains one tumor specimen, which served as the discovery sample. Selected findings were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens (the cross-specimen Xenium analysis). We obtained the cell-by-gene matrix, cell metadata, and cell polygons from the public repository. The complete dataset contained approximately 645,000 cells. To make the analysis tractable using standard hardware, we drew a reproducible random subsample (seed = 1) and retained cells with at least 50 detected RNA molecules. This yielded 154,816 cells. Removing negative-control and system-control probes left 18,934 genes. Global coordinates were converted from pixels to micrometers using a scale of 0.12028 µm per pixel. We also split the retained cells into two random halves and compared cell-type mean target-expression matrices to assess sensitivity to subsampling. Clustering, annotation and differential expression Analyses were performed in R 4.5.2 with Seurat 5.5.1 [ 26 ]. Counts were log-normalized to counts per 10,000, then subjected to a natural-log transformation. We scaled the 2,000 most variable genes and used 30 principal components to construct a shared-nearest-neighbor graph. Louvain clustering was run at resolution 0.5, followed by UMAP embedding. Clusters were assigned to seven lineages using module scores for canonical markers and established breast cell-type signatures [ 27 ]. The lineages were tumor epithelial, fibroblast/stromal, myeloid, B/plasma, T, myoepithelial, and endothelial. One-versus-rest Wilcoxon rank-sum tests identified positive cell-type markers, with at least 10% detection, a minimum log2 fold-change of 0.25, and at most 500 cells per group. P values were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg method. These cell-level tests treat cells from one specimen as independent observations. We therefore used them to describe within-sample marker specificity and placed greater weight on effect sizes than on nominal P values. ADC-target analysis We examined eleven clinically relevant ADC targets: ERBB2 (HER2), TACSTD2 (TROP2), ERBB3 (HER3), NECTIN4, FOLR1 (FRα), CEACAM5 (CEA), CD276 (B7-H3), MUC1, MET, EGFR and FOLH1 (PSMA). For each cell type, we calculated mean log-normalized expression and the number and fraction of cells with detectable expression. Per-cell expression was also mapped in tissue coordinates. Cross-platform single-target detection comparison To describe cross-platform differences in single-target detection, we compared ERBB2 and TACSTD2 between the whole-transcriptome CosMx dataset and a 313-gene Xenium breast panel [ 23 ]. For each dataset, we calculated the fraction of tumor cells with zero counts for the target gene. The assays were applied to different specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes; this descriptive comparison was not designed to isolate a platform or panel-design effect. Receptor subtype, spillover control and spatial organization For each target, we report the number and fraction of expressing cells, along with the mean expression. This provides cellular support for findings in low-abundance microenvironments. To assess whether FOLH1 and CD276 enrichment could reflect transcript spillover across cell boundaries, we built a k-nearest-neighbor graph (k = 10) from cell centroids. We calculated the proportion of tumor-epithelial neighbors for each cell, then compared expression in the enriched lineage between cells with few (<25%) and many (>50%) tumor neighbors. The receptor phenotype was inferred from tumor-cell expression of ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 , with GATA3 and MKI67 as context. This RNA-based classification is not equivalent to immunohistochemical receptor status. Cell-type neighborhood enrichment followed the approach implemented in Squidpy [ 28 ]. For each ordered cell-type pair, we compared the observed number of graph edges with a null distribution from 100 permutations of cell-type labels and expressed the result as a z-score. Bulk transcriptomic contextualization (TCGA-BRCA) TCGA-BRCA gene-level expression (log2(normalized count + 1)) and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub [ 29 , 30 ]. Sample barcodes identified 1,097 primary tumors and 114 solid-tissue normals. In this dataset, NECTIN4 is recorded under its alias PVRL4 and was mapped accordingly. Tumor-versus-normal differences were tested for each target by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. Overall survival was derived from vital status and time to death or last follow-up. The full survival cohort contained 1,080 patients. For each target, we fitted a univariable Cox model using continuous expression and performed a median-split log-rank test. We interpreted these P values in the context of the 11 tested targets and did not search for additional endpoints and subgroups. Multivariable Cox models were fitted separately in the 808 patients with complete data for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 intrinsic subtype. Cross-specimen validation on Xenium We analyzed two additional public Xenium breast cancer specimens: the Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma sample and the breast cancer reference block [ 23 ]. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient. Public metadata did not establish patient-level independence of the reference block. We used the vendor-supplied graph-based clusters and assigned cells to the same lineages by marker scores. Four ADC targets were represented in the Xenium panel: ERBB2, TACSTD2, MUC1, and EGFR . For each target, we compared detection fractions between tumor epithelial and non-tumor cells. Detection fraction was chosen because absolute expression is not directly comparable across platforms with different panel sizes and sequencing depths. Results A seven-lineage single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor Unsupervised clustering produced 15 clusters, which were assigned to seven cell types ( Fig. 1 ). Tumor epithelium was the largest compartment (95,803 cells; 61.9%). Fibroblast/stromal and myeloid cells each accounted for 10.3%, followed by B/plasma cells (6.9%), T cells (5.3%), myoepithelial cells (2.7%), and endothelial cells (2.6%). Quality-control distributions are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. These populations occupied coherent tissue regions, with tumor epithelium forming contiguous fields and glandular structures ( Fig. 1 B). One-versus-rest testing identified 4,449 positive markers. The leading markers matched the assigned lineages, including PIP, SERHL2, and MLPH in the tumor epithelium; COL1A1, LUM, and POSTN in the stroma; and EGFL7, PLVAP, and FLT1 in the endothelium ( Fig. 2 ; Supplementary Table S4). The same correspondence was seen for myeloid ( APOE, LYZ, C1QC ), B/plasma ( IGKC, IGHA1, JCHAIN ), T ( GNLY, GZMA, ITGAE ) and myoepithelial cells ( ACTA2, MCAM, CSPG4 ). Fig. 1 Single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor. (A) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of 154,816 analyzed cells from one CosMx breast tumor specimen, colored by seven annotated cell types. (B) Spatial distribution of the same cells using tissue coordinates in micrometers. Each point represents a cell centroid. The same cell-type color key is used in both panels. Fig. 2 Cell-type marker expression in the discovery specimen. The five positive one-versus-rest markers with the largest average log2 fold change are shown for each of seven cell types. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in the indicated lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count. The size-key values are fractions: 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 correspond to 25%, 50% and 75%, respectively. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). Marker-test results are provided in Supplementary Table S4. ADC targets show tumor-enriched and microenvironment-enriched patterns The eleven ADC targets followed two broad patterns ( Fig. 3 ). MUC1 (mean log-normalized expression 0.82), HER2/ ERBB2 (0.68), NECTIN4 (0.60), TROP2/ TACSTD2 (0.52) and HER3/ ERBB3 (0.39) were highest in tumor epithelium. Their mean expression in non-malignant compartments was 0.14 or lower. Spatial maps showed that HER2 and TROP2 expression were associated with the tumor-epithelial regions of the section ( Fig. 4 ). Fig. 3 ADC-target expression across cell types. Dot plot of 11 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targets in the CosMx discovery specimen. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in each lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count; size-key values of 0.1-0.4 correspond to 10%-40%. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). MUC1, HER2, NECTIN4, TROP2 and HER3 had their highest mean expression in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, and PSMA was highest in endothelium. Cell counts and detection fractions are provided in Supplementary Table S1. These measurements concern RNA expression. Fig. 4 Spatial expression of representative ADC targets. Per-cell expression of HER2 (ERBB2, upper left), TROP2 (TACSTD2, upper right), PSMA (FOLH1, lower left) and B7-H3 (CD276, lower right) in the CosMx discovery specimen. Each point represents a cell centroid. The four panels use the same tissue coordinates and a common expression color scale. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). The maps show transcript localization and do not establish surface-protein abundance. Other targets were expressed preferentially outside the tumor compartment. B7-H3/ CD276 was highest in endothelial (0.35) and myoepithelial cells (0.31), followed by fibroblast/stromal and tumor cells (both 0.16). PSMA/ FOLH1 was concentrated in endothelium (0.47), whereas mean tumor-cell expression was 0.05. This distribution agrees with the reported localization of PSMA to tumor-associated neovasculature rather than breast carcinoma cells [ 31 ]. FOLR1 and CEACAM5 remained low across all cell types in this specimen (≤0.10). The microenvironmental findings were supported by the number of cells expressing (Supplementary Table S1). PSMA was detected in 20.0% of endothelial cells (817 of 4,076) and 3.2% of tumor cells. B7-H3 was detected in 16.0% of endothelial cells, 12.9% of myoepithelial cells, and 9.5% of tumor cells. Low PSMA expression in tumor cells argues against tumor-derived transcript spillover as the main explanation for endothelial enrichment. In the neighborhood analysis, endothelial cells with fewer than 25% tumor neighbors still had a mean PSMA expression of 0.39 (n = 2,282), compared with 0.05 in tumor cells. B7-H3 enrichment in stroma, endothelium and myoepithelium was also retained in cells located away from tumor epithelium (Supplementary Table S2). Single-target detection differed between platforms and specimens In the CosMx whole-transcriptome specimen, 60% of tumor cells had zero ERBB2 counts, and 68% had zero TACSTD2 counts. In the targeted 313-gene Xenium specimen, the corresponding fractions were 3.5% and 11%. Because the assays were applied to different tissue specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes, these differences cannot be attributed solely to assay design. They nevertheless caution against interpreting a zero count as absence of target expression over spatial transcriptomic platforms. Tumor receptor phenotype and spatial organization Among tumor cells, ERBB2 was the most highly expressed receptor gene (mean 0.68; detected in 36.6% of cells). ESR1 (0.09; 5.8%) and PGR (0.04; 2.7%) were low. This RNA profile is compatible with, but not diagnostic of, a HER2-enriched or hormone-receptor-negative phenotype. The HER2 and TROP2 findings should therefore be interpreted in the context of these receptors. Neighborhood analysis showed strong self-association of the tumor epithelium (z = 507) and negative associations with all non-malignant cell types. The largest negative values were observed in myeloid cells (z = -308) and fibroblast/stromal cells (z = -294). Among non-malignant populations, fibroblasts co-localized most strongly with myeloid cells (z = 131), whereas endothelial cells co-localized most strongly with myoepithelial cells (z = 137; Supplementary Fig. S3). Subsampling had little effect. Two random halves of the retained cells produced nearly identical cell-type mean target-expression matrices (Pearson r = 0.998). HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurs in additional Xenium specimens Both Xenium specimens were public datasets distinct from the CosMx discovery sample, although only the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen was known to come from a different patient. We therefore assessed cross-specimen recurrence without treating the reference block as a separate patient-level replicate (Supplementary Fig. S4, Supplementary Table S3). Because panel content and sequencing depth differed, the comparison used detection fractions. Ranking cell types by mean expression gave the same ordering. Tumor epithelium had the highest HER2/ ERBB2 and TROP2/ TACSTD2 expression in all six specimen-by-target comparisons. In the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen, for example, TROP2 was detected in 84% of tumor cells and 26% of non-tumor cells. MUC1 showed the same pattern where it was included in the panel. EGFR differed. In both Xenium specimens, EGFR was detected as often as or more often in non-tumor cells, with the highest levels in myoepithelial cells. Bulk tumor-versus-normal expression In TCGA-BRCA (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues), six targets were higher in tumor tissue: CEACAM5 (log2 fold-change +4.1), MUC1 (+2.1), CD276 (+0.85), ERBB3 (+0.85), NECTIN4 (+0.75) and ERBB2 (+0.54). All adjusted P values were below 0.001 ( Fig. 5 ; Supplementary Table S5). TACSTD2 did not differ between groups (log2 fold-change -0.29; P = 0.06). Four targets were lower in tumors: FOLR1 (-3.8), EGFR (-3.5), MET (-2.4) and FOLH1 (-1.6). These bulk contrasts are influenced by tissue composition and do not identify the cell type expressing the gene. B7-H3 illustrates the distinction, as it was higher in bulk tumor tissue but arose mainly from endothelial, myoepithelial and stromal cells in the spatial data. Fig. 5 ADC-target expression in TCGA-BRCA tumors and normal tissues. Box plots show log2(normalized count + 1) expression of 11 ADC-target genes in primary tumors (n = 1,097; red) and solid-tissue normal samples (n = 114; blue). The center line is the median, boxes span the 25th-75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Points beyond the whiskers are outliers. The y-axis range differs between gene panels. Two-sided Wilcoxon comparisons and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P values are reported in Supplementary Table S5. No ADC target shows a strong association with overall survival Among the 1,080 patients with survival data, no univariable association remained significant after correction for eleven targets. The lowest nominal P values in this full cohort were observed for NECTIN4 in the continuous Cox model (P = 0.040) and the median-split log-rank test (P = 0.053; Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Table S6). The complete-covariate subset contained 808 patients. In this subset, CEACAM5 had a nominal univariable association (P = 0.019), which weakened after adjustment for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 subtype (hazard ratio 1.22; P = 0.071; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P = 0.478). No target was associated with overall survival after covariate adjustment (Supplementary Table S7). These analyses do not support a strong single-gene prognostic effect, although the unselected cohort and limited event count constrain the inference. Discussion At the RNA level, the eleven ADC targets separated into two expression patterns in the discovery specimen. HER2, TROP2, HER3, NECTIN4 and MUC1 were concentrated in tumor epithelium. Among these, MUC1 had the highest mean expression, consistent with its long-standing status as a tumor-associated antigen and with continuing efforts to exploit MUC1 alterations therapeutically [ 11 ]. B7-H3 and PSMA were more prominent in stromal or vascular compartments. Bulk and tissue-averaged assays cannot resolve this difference in cellular source. Recovery of the established PSMA neovascular pattern provides an internal check on the cell assignments. These data do not estimate the therapeutic index, which also depends on surface protein abundance, internalization, expression in vital normal tissues, and payload and linker chemistry. Localization alone does not indicate whether a compartment contains sufficient antigen to affect treatment. PSMA is a useful caution. We detected FOLH1 in 20% of endothelial cells, but quantitative immunohistochemistry found PSMA staining in only a small minority of breast-cancer neovessels [ 32 ]. Those authors questioned the viability of PSMA-directed theranostics in this disease. A cell type can therefore be the dominant source of a low-abundance transcript without presenting a clinically meaningful antigen burden. Our study locates the RNA signal but does not quantify surface protein or predict efficacy or toxicity. The bulk and spatial examinations answered different questions. TCGA-BRCA identified targets whose total expression differed between tumor and normal tissue. It could not show whether the signal came from malignant cells. B7-H3 was higher in bulk tumor tissue but mapped mainly to endothelium, myoepithelium, and stroma in the spatial specimen. This is not a contradiction. Tumor-versus-normal contrasts are influenced by tissue composition, so we do not interpret bulk upregulation as evidence of tumor-cell specificity. Prior work defines the limits of the study's novelty. Single-cell surveys have already been used to identify non-malignant expression of CAR-T targets [ 16 ]. ADC-target catalogues are available for pan-cancer and breast cancer tissues [ 17 , 18 ], and dissociated single-cell data have been used to assess ADC target restriction in ovarian cancer [ 19 ]. B7-H3 expression in tumor endothelium and fibroblasts has been reported [ 33 ], as has PSMA expression in breast cancer neovasculature [ 31 , 32 ]. Our contribution is narrower. We assign 11 ADC-target transcripts to cell types in intact breast tissue, including the myoepithelial compartment, and assess selected targets in 2 additional specimens using another platform. The recovery of the known B7-H3 and PSMA localizations supports the approach but does not constitute a new biological discovery. Tumor epithelium occupied spatially segregated regions, apart from stromal, immune, and vascular populations (Supplementary Fig. S3). Together with the neighborhood control, this pattern makes simple transcript spillover an unlikely explanation for the B7-H3 and PSMA findings. The discovery tumor had low ESR1 and PGR expression and comparatively high ERBB2 . HER2 and TROP2 localization should therefore be interpreted within the context of their respective receptors rather than generalized across all breast cancer subtypes. Cross-specimen support was strongest for HER2 and TROP2. Their enrichment in tumor epithelium recurred in both Xenium specimens and on a second imaging platform. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient, but the public metadata did not establish patient-level independence for the reference block. The evidence therefore represents recurrence across three specimens and two platforms, not three independent patients. EGFR was highest in myoepithelial cells in both Xenium specimens, showing that tumor restriction cannot be assumed for every target. B7-H3 and PSMA were absent from the targeted panel, so their localization remains based on the discovery specimen. The survival analyses provide no evidence that any target is an independent prognostic marker. Nominal associations differed between the full cohort and the complete-covariate subset and did not survive correction for or adjustment for covariates. This null result should not be read as proof that the target expression has no prognostic relevance in any subgroup. The cohort was unselected, the number of events was limited, and we deliberately avoided exploratory analyses by subtype or alternative endpoints. Translating these transcript-level maps into clinical decisions will require protein-level measurement and direct correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity. We regard this as the central next step, rather than a peripheral caveat. A practical sequence would begin with multiplexed immunofluorescence or imaging mass cytometry on matched tissue sections, using the lineage markers applied here to reproduce the cell assignments alongside antibodies directed against the ectodomains engaged by ADCs. Simultaneous RNA and protein co-detection on the same section would then allow the transcript-to-protein relationship to be assessed cell-by-cell rather than assumed. Compartment-resolved quantitative scoring, as applied to PSMA in breast-cancer neovasculature [ 32 ], could subsequently convert localization into an estimate of antigen burden within each compartment. Clinical correlation would require complementary study designs. For efficacy, pretreatment tumor blocks from patients subsequently treated with a defined ADC could be scored separately for tumor-cell and microenvironmental target protein expression and related to objective response and progression-free survival. Assessment of toxicity would require additional evidence from relevant normal tissues and organ-specific adverse events in ADC-treated cohorts, because protein expression within the tumor microenvironment alone cannot establish on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Only outcome-linked studies of this kind can determine whether compartment-specific expression patterns such as those reported here for B7-H3 and PSMA have measurable clinical consequences. The spatial framework may also be relevant beyond ADCs. Nanoparticle and other tumor-directed delivery systems are influenced by vascular permeability, stromal barriers, and the organization of the tumor microenvironment [ 14 , 15 ]. Although these mechanisms differ from antigen-dependent ADC targeting, they reinforce the broader value of resolving delivery-relevant compartments within intact tissue. Until protein-level and outcome-linked data become available, however, the present findings should be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating guide to where such validation should be directed, not as evidence of ADC efficacy or safety. Limitations The whole-transcriptome discovery analysis is based on one tumor. HER2 and TROP2 were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens, but only one was clearly documented as a different patient. B7-H3 and PSMA were not present in the targeted validation panel. Their low-abundance stromal and vascular patterns, therefore, require confirmation in larger, patient-level cohorts across breast cancer subtypes. Cell annotations were marker-based rather than reviewed against matched histopathology. Differential expression tests also treated cells from a single specimen as independent units, which can inflate statistical confidence. Effect sizes and marker identity are more informative here than nominal cell-level P values. Public metadata did not consistently provide specimen-level sex and gender information, and these variables were not analyzed. Whole-transcriptome imaging was sparse for individual genes, limiting per-cell quantification. The bulk and survival analyses were based on a single cohort, and no signal of survival remained after adjustment. Most importantly, every target measurement was messenger RNA. ADC binding depends on the availability of an accessible cell-surface protein, whose RNA abundance cannot be measured directly. We did not assess protein localization, internalization, drug response, or toxicity. The findings are therefore descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Conclusion Single-cell spatial transcriptomics separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from targets expressed in stromal and vascular cells. HER2 and TROP2 showed the most consistent tumor enrichment across the three profiled specimens, whereas EGFR did not. These RNA-level findings should inform the design of protein-level, multi-patient validation studies. They cannot substitute for direct measurement of surface antigen or ADC activity. Compartment-resolved protein confirmation, followed by correlation with ADC response and toxicity in treated cohorts, is the necessary next step before any of these observations is applied clinically. Ethics approval and informed consent This study used only publicly available, de-identified datasets and involved no direct participant contact or new data collection. Ethical approval and informed-consent procedures for the source studies were reported in the original dataset publications. No additional ethics approval or informed consent was required for this secondary analysis. Funding This work was supported by the Ningxia Natural Science Foundation [grant numbers 2026AAC031176, 2026AAC031199 and 2025AAC030748], the National Natural Science Foundation of China [grant number 82260716], and the Regional Key Research and Development Program of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region [grant number 2026BEG02001]. The funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation, or the decision to submit the article for publication. Declaration of competing interest The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this article. Data and code availability All analyzed datasets are publicly available. The discovery dataset was the CosMx SMI Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (breast discovery release, sample S0; Bruker Spatial Biology; https://nanostring.com/products/cosmx-spatial-molecular-imager/ffpe-dataset/ ). The validation datasets were the Xenium Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma specimen (Xenium_V1_FFPE_Human_Breast_IDC_With_Addon) and the Human Breast Cancer reference block (Xenium_FFPE_Human_Breast_Cancer_Rep1) from the 10x Genomics Datasets portal ( https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets ). TCGA-BRCA gene expression and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub ( https://tcga.xenahubs.net ). Analysis scripts and package versions are provided in the Supplementary_Code.zip file. Supplementary Tables S1-S7 and Fig. source data are provided as machine-readable Excel workbooks.

EpiFoundation: A Foundation Model for Single-Cell ATAC-seq via Peak-to-Gene Alignment <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>
                  Foundation models exhibit strong capabilities for downstream tasks by learning generalized representations through self-supervised pre-training on large datasets. While several foundation models have been developed for single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data, there is still a lack of models specifically tailored for single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq), which measures epigenetic information in individual cells. The principal challenge in developing such a model lies in the vast number of scATAC peaks and the significant sparsity of the data, which complicates the formulation of peak-to-peak correlations. To address this challenge, we introduce
                  <jats:bold>EpiFoundation</jats:bold>
                  , a foundation model for learning cell representations from the high-dimensional and sparse space of peaks. Epi-Foundation relies on an innovative cross-modality pre-training procedure with two key technical innovations. First, EpiFoundation exclusively processes the non-zero peak set, thereby enhancing the density of cell-specific information within the input data. Second, EpiFoundation utilizes dense gene expression information to supervise the pretraining process, aligning peak-to-gene correlations. EpiFoundation can handle various types of downstream tasks, including cell-type annotation, batch correction, and gene expression prediction. To train and validate EpiFoundation, we curated
                  <jats:bold>MiniAtlas</jats:bold>
                  , a dataset of 100,000+ single cells with paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data, along with diverse test sets spanning various tissues and cell types for robust evaluation. EpiFoundation demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across multiple tissues and diverse downstream tasks.
                </jats:p>

evidence_text:
Artificial intelligence in thoracic surgery: a narrative review of clinical advances and applications in 2025.

Background and objective

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into thoracic surgery accelerated notably over the course of 2025, transitioning from isolated diagnostic aids toward comprehensive clinical pathway integration. The objective of this narrative review is to synthesize the latest evidence on AI applications across the entire thoracic surgical workflow, organized along the patient care continuum from preoperative assessment through intraoperative execution to postoperative management.

Methods

A PubMed/MEDLINE search was performed on March 6, 2026, and retrieved 378 English-language records published between January 1, 2025 and March 6, 2026. After title and abstract screening, potentially relevant articles underwent full-text review, and studies addressing the clinical applications of AI and related digital technologies across the thoracic surgical pathway were included in this narrative review.

Key content and findings

In the preoperative domain, large-scale foundation models and computational pathology systems have demonstrated strong performance in nodule risk stratification and noninvasive genomic prediction [area under the curve (AUC) >0.900]. Notably, dual-phase computed tomography (CT) systems such as NeoPred have achieved validation for predicting pathological response to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. Intraoperatively, augmented reality (AR) navigation has achieved randomized controlled trial (RCT)-level evidence outperforming conventional localization, while generative AI systems have attained expert-level anatomical recognition for surgical video analytics. Postoperatively, wearable continuous monitoring systems and digital therapeutics (DTx) entered prospective clinical validation. Furthermore, large language models (LLMs) emerged as increasingly important tools for automated surgical documentation. Despite these advances, most studies remain retrospective, and domain shift across institutions limits generalizability.

Conclusions

While AI has substantially affected thoracic surgery, important gaps persist regarding prospective validation and regulatory governance. Future priorities must focus on prospective multicenter interventional trials linking AI predictions to standardized clinical action protocols, federated learning architectures to overcome data silos, and the development of specialty-specific guidelines building upon the Artificial Intelligence Organization for Next Generation Surgeons (AIONS) 2025 consensus.

title: AI-augmented intraoperative decision-making workflows in diffuse midline glioma biopsy using cryosection pathology.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: AI-augmented intraoperative decision-making workflows in diffuse midline glioma biopsy using cryosection pathology. Cryosection pathology is essential for intraoperative diagnosis of diffuse midline gliomas, yet it often leads to diagnostic errors and may prompt unnecessary re-biopsies before completion of the formal molecular assessment. In this study, we propose an AI-augmented framework, CryoAID, for rapid molecular outcome prediction during surgery for patients with diffuse midline glioma. CryoAID integrates a generative model to correct cryosection artefacts and a pathology foundation model to predict molecular statuses directly from cryosection images. We validate CryoAID across multiple cohorts to predict tumoural molecular statuses in the internal (n = 326), external multi-centre (n = 52), and consecutive (n = 68) datasets. In particular, CryoAID accurately predicts major molecular statuses (e.g., ATRX, H3K27M, and TP53) using cryosection images that were previously deemed disqualified for molecular examinations. Beyond tumour cells, CryoAID reveals highly differential clinical features, including glial cell proliferation, abundant cytoplasm, and localised endothelial proliferation. In the retrospective analyses, CryoAID reduces re-biopsy rates by 26.4% and 26.6% in the internal and consecutive datasets, respectively. Our findings demonstrate that the AI-augmented pathology workflow can extract diagnostic value from specimens previously considered non-viable by traditional histopathology. This approach represents a shift towards real-time molecular pathology, potentially reducing re-biopsies and improving diagnostic precision for patients with diffuse midline glioma.

xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: DeepLNM: A Multimodal Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer. Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is critical for prognostic stratification and treatment selection in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet imaging and routine pathology can yield false-negative/false-positive results. We propose DeepLNM, a multi-center foundation model for LNM prediction in CRC, evaluated with retrospective, external, prospective, and user study evidence. A multimodal dataset was assembled from three hospitals, with matched hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSI), CT scans, and text. DeepLNM achieved a mean AUC of 0.922 in the internal cohort and AUCs of 0.872 and 0.848 in two external cohorts. In a prospective cohort from a registered clinical trial (NCT07239063), DeepLNM remained robust (AUC = 0.845). In a user study, DeepLNM improved diagnostic accuracy, especially for junior pathologists (95.0%-97.3%), while reducing diagnostic time and increasing confidence. To explore the model's generalizability, it was further validated in a gastric cancer cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.793. Finally, DeepLNM identified histopathological features associated with LNM, addressing the "black-box" concern of deep learning. Together, these results position DeepLNM as a clinically preliminarily validated multimodal model for predicting LNM status in CRC, potentially facilitating the clinical translation of AI pathology.

Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Analysis post- H&E staining:

For Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression analysis, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissues underwent deparaffinization, H&E staining, imaging and decrosslinking exactly according to the Visium HD FFPE Tissue Preparation Handbook (CG000684, 10x Genomics). After H&E staining, samples were imaged using the SLIDEVIEW VS200 slide scanner (Evident) at 20x magnification. Visium HD Gene Expression libraries were then generated using the Visium HD, Human Transcriptome, 6.5mm reagents (PN: 1000675, 10x Genomics) and following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide (CG000685, 10x Genomics). Quality control and molarity calculations of the libraries were performed with Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (#Q33216, Invitrogen) and 4200 Tapestation system (Agilent Technologies). Libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq X+ 10B at paired-end 100bp.

Sequential Immunofluorescence using COMET:

Sequential Immunofluorescence (SeqIF 
) staining was performed on FFPE tissue sections using COMET system from Lunaphore, according to standard protocol for proteomic applications (User manual – COMET 
, Revision: 006).
Briefly, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissue underwent deparaffinization and antigen retrieval using Dewax and HIER buffer, pH 9 (Epredia, #TA-999-DHBH) in the PT module (Epredia) at 102°C for 1h, with pre-heating temperature set to 85°C and cool-end temperature to 65°C. Following antigen retrieval, slides were rinsed and kept in the Multistaining Buffer (BU06, Lunaphore) until loading them on to the instrument for SeqIF. SeqIF staining was performed on the COMET 
 using the SPYRE 
 Immuno-oncology Core Panel (Lunaphore) supplemented with pan-Cytokeratin antibody. SeqIF 
 protocol was set up on the COMET 
 control software and sequential staining, imaging, and elution cycles were performed on the instrument as per manufacturer’s protocol. Imaging was performed with 12.5 x 12.5mm imaging area. 

Post- COMET Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Analysis:

For efficient preservation of RNA integrity to enable post-COMET Visium HD Gene expression analysis, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissues underwent deparaffinization and antigen retrieval according to the recommended pre-processing protocol for multiomics applications (User manual – COMET 
, Revision: 006).
Slides were baked at 60°C for 1h, followed by cooling down for 5 mins at RT. They were deparaffinized by incubating sequentially in two coplin jars of xylene (5 min each), two jars of 100% ethanol (2 mins each), and then dried for 2.5 min at 60°C. Antigen retrieval was performed using Dewax and HIER buffer pH 9 (Epredia, #TA-999-DHBH) in the PT module at 99°C for 1h, with 85°C and 65°C as the pre-heating and cool-end temperatures, respectively. After antigen retrieval, slides were rinsed and kept in Multistaining Buffer (BU06, Lunaphore) until loading them on to the COMET 
 instrument for SeqIF 
. The time between antigen retrieval and starting the SeqIF 
 run was kept as low as possible. SeqIF 
 staining was performed using the SPYRE 
 Immuno-oncology Core Panel (Lunaphore) supplemented with pan-Cytokeratin, with imaging area of 12.5 x 12.5mm exactly as per manufacturer’s protocol. Table1 provides the complete list of primary and secondary antibodies, and staining cycle details.
After the COMET 
 SeqIF 
 run was completed, slides were unloaded from the instrument and immersed in 1x PBS to keep them hydrated. They were air-dried for 5 min at RT and then assembled into the Visium HD slide cassette as per standard protocol (CG000684, 10x Genomics). Subsequent steps including pre-hybridization, probe hybridization and generation of Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression libraries were performed using the Visium HD, Human Transcriptome, 6.5mm reagents (PN: 1000675, 10x Genomics) and following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide (CG000685, 10x Genomics). Quality control and molarity calculations of the libraries were performed with Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (#Q33216, Invitrogen) and 4200 Tapestation system (Agilent Technologies). Libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq X+ 10B at paired-end 100bp, pooling 2-4 libraries per lane.

For the Xenium Prime In Situ workflow, Xenium slides with …. were processed for deparaffinization and decrosslinking according to the Demonstrated Protocol: Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue preparation Handbook (CG000578, 10x Genomics).
Subsequent steps including priming, RNase treatment and polishing, probe hybridization, post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, blocking, staining with Multi-Tissue Stain Mix  for multimodal cell segmentation, autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed using the Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides reagents (PN: 1000742, 10x Genomics), and following the Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression with optional Cell Segmentation User Guide (CG000760, 10x Genomics). Hybridization was carried out overnight at 50°C, in thermocycler, with the Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay Kit (PN: 1000671, 10x Genomics). Slides were imaged on the Xenium Analyzer with Xenium Prime 5K Decoding Reagents (PN: 1000740, 10x Genomics), Xenium Decoding Consumables v2 (PN: 1000726, 10x Genomics) and Xenium Reagent Bottles (PN: 1000740, 10x Genomics), and following the Xenium Analyzer User Guide (CG000584, 10x Genomics). In the overview scan performed by the instrument, ROIs were defined per slide, comprising all fields of view (FOVs) containing the tissue, while excluding the blank areas. Following the instrument run, the buffer on the slides was replaced with 0.05% PBST and slides were stored at 4°C. spec-3-w09g-removable Specimen Title tonsil_3 Sample preparation protocol Xenium In Situ workflow with Protein Staining and Cell Segmentation
For the Xenium in situ workflow with protein staining and multimodal cell segmentation, the processing of Xenium slides with tonsil tissue for deparaffinization, decrosslinking (CG000578, 10x Genomics) and subsequent steps of probe hybridization, ligation and amplification, autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining (CG000819, 10x Genomics) were exactly the same as for standard Xenium in situ workflow. Probe hybridization was carried out with the Xenium Human Immuno-oncology Profiling Panel (PN:1000654, 10x Genomics) overnight at 50°C in thermocycler. Following amplification and before autofluorescence quenching, tissue dehydration, secondary decrosslinking, blocking, protein and multimodal cell segmentation staining, and stain enhancement were performed using the Xenium Cell Segmentation Staining Reagents (PN: 1000661, 10x Genomics) and following the Xenium in situ Gene and Protein User Guide (CG000819, 10x Genomics). Staining was performed overnight at 4°C using a mix of Human Multi-tissue stain mix (PN: 1000661, 10x Genomics) and Xenium Protein Immune Cell Subpanels: A and B (PN: 1000833, PN: 1000834, 10x Genomics, respectively). Slides were imaged on the Xenium Analyzer with Xenium RNA and Protein Detection Reagents (PN: 1000884, 10x Genomics) and Xenium Decoding Consumables (PN: 1000487, 10x Genomics), and following the Xenium Analyzer User Guide (CG000584, 10x Genomics). In the overview scan performed by the instrument, a single ROI was defined per slide, comprising all FOVs containing the tissue, while excluding the blank areas. Following the instrument run, the buffer on the slides was replaced with 0.05% PBST and slides were stored at 4°C.

Antigen retrieval optimization for post-Xenium seqIF
To test and optimize antigen retrieval after Xenium for subsequent seqIFTM assays, FFPE tonsil sections mounted on SuperFrost Plus slides were mock Xenium processed as described above. Two different antigen retrieval conditions were tested using a PT module: 1) Dewax and HIER buffer pH9 (Epredia, #TA-999-DHBH) at 102°C for 1h and 2) DAKO Target Retrieval Solution, pH 9 (Agilent DAKO, #S2375) at 1x working concentration at 97°C for 40min. Pre-heating and cool-end temperatures were set to 85°C and 65°C, respectively, for both conditions. In addition, one mock Xenium processed slide received no antigen retrieval before seqIFTM. A previously untreated slide with tonsil tissue also underwent the standard antigen retrieval for seqIFTM with Dewax and HIER buffer pH9 at 102°C for 1h and served as a positive control. evidence_text:
Macrophage Signature-Based Prediction of Cancer Treatment Response Using Attention-Weighted Multiple Instance Learning

A bstract

Predicting immunotherapy response from single-cell data remains difficult due to patient-level labels, extreme class imbalance, and highly heterogeneous macrophage states. We present a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework that treats each patient as a bag of macrophage embeddings derived from a single-cell RNA foundation model. The architecture incorporates an attention-based pooling mechanism with reduced model complexity, dropout-enhanced regularization and explicit attention penalties to improve stability in small-sample regimes. To address imbalanced clinical datasets, MIL outputs are optimized with a combined focal loss and supervised contrastive objective that simultaneously sharpens class boundaries and improves representation clustering. Across three cancer datasets, this approach outperforms pseudobulk aggregation, embedding baselines and standard MIL variants. Attention-weighted attribution and transcriptional regulatory analysis reveal distinct macrophage programs, interferon and antigen-presentation networks in responders versus hypoxia-linked regulatory modules in non-responders. This shows the potential of MIL to uncover predictive and mechanistically interpretable immune states.

title: Performance of an Artificial Intelligence Foundation Model for Prostate Radiotherapy Segmentation.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text:
Performance of an Artificial Intelligence Foundation Model for Prostate Radiotherapy Segmentation.

Purpose

Radiation therapy is a major treatment modality for localized prostate cancer, and accurate target segmentation is a critical aspect of radiation delivery that can directly affect patient outcomes. We evaluated the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI) foundation model in target segmentation tasks for prostate radiotherapy planning.

Methods

AI segmentation using Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2) was evaluated from computed tomography images with varying levels of human intervention, ranging from intervals of every 2nd to every 10th ground truth slice provided as input. Segmentation accuracy was measured using dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) for intact and postoperative prostate target delineation.

Results

SAM 2 achieved performance similar to and, in some cases, worse than interpolation in DSC and HD95 for both intact and postoperative prostate cancer patient cases, and the AI segmentation accuracy was significantly better in the intact preoperative patient cases where anatomic boundaries were better defined than postoperative patient cases (P < .01† for intervals 5-10). When sparse ground truth was provided simulating lower levels of human intervention, DSC values decreased from 0.956 to 0.856 in the preoperative setting and from 0.952 to 0.751 in the postoperative setting when the interval between ground truth slices was increased from every 2nd to every 10th slice. Correspondingly, the HD95 increased from 1.817 to 4.436 in the preoperative setting and from 1.988 to 11.02 in the postoperative setting under the same conditions.

Conclusion

Current general-purpose AI foundation models do not outperform existing methods and are likely inadequate for prostate radiotherapy segmentation. Their clinical application will require further understanding of appropriate fine-tuning and task-specific performance.

title: Learning Discrete Cell and Niche Codes from Spatial Transcriptomics Using Dual Residual Vector Quantization
xenium_reason: Xenium is mentioned without evidence of dataset generation or reuse
evidence_text: Learning Discrete Cell and Niche Codes from Spatial Transcriptomics Using Dual Residual Vector Quantization Spatially-resolved transcriptomics (SRT) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution while preserving each cell’s spatial location, enabling the joint study of  cell identity and cellular  niche , the recurring microenvironment that organises tissue function. Existing representation-learning methods typically capture only one of these axes at a time. We present SQUINT, a graph vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) that learns  two disjoint codebooks per cell from a shared architecture: a  cell codebook quantising the per-cell embedding before neighbourhood aggregation, biased toward cell-intrinsic identity, and a  niche codebook quantising the embedding after graph neural network (GNN) aggregation, biased toward spatial context. Both use residual vector quantization, giving a coarse-to-fine discrete-token hierarchy. SQUINT is trained with per-branch negative-binomial reconstruction objectives and three domain-motivated components that we show are crucial: a within-section cosine adjacency loss that anchors the niche codes in the spatial graph, a cross-section contrastive loss on the cell latents that aligns transcriptomically matched cells, and a decoder section covariate that absorbs batch effects. Across three datasets spanning four spatial assays (STARmap, MERFISH, CosMx, Xenium) and four tasks – niche identification, cell-type identification, cross-section integration, and spatial gene-expression imputation in held-out regions – SQUINT outperforms or is competitive with strong baselines on identification and achieves the most faithful cross-section integration. The resulting discrete vocabulary makes tissues directly consumable by transformer-style foundation models and enables one-step query-to-reference atlas mapping via code-distribution similarity, which we demonstrate on a CosMx human non-small-cell lung cancer cohort.

title: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer. Cellular senescence, a stress-induced program causing stable cell-cycle arrest, is a hallmark of liver aging, fibrosis, and cancer. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms, spatial organization, and cancer-associated alterations in the liver remain unclear. We profiled 43 normal human livers spanning ages and fibrosis stages using a single-cell multiome, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX, complemented by fibrotic mouse models and 24 colorectal cancer liver metastases. We found CDKN1A+ senescent hepatocytes, fibroblasts, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells associated with age, liver disease, or cancer. Senescence differed between aged and fibrotic livers, with similar patterns in mice. Spatially, CDKN1A+ hepatocytes localized periportally, while SERPINE1+ aging-associated hepatocytes formed spatial clusters, potentially mediated by Claudins and THBS1. Fibrotic regions contained CXCL12+ senescent fibroblasts interacting with CXCR4+ immune cells. Chemotherapy intensified senescence in hepatocytes by 5-fold relative to aging and led to unique CDKN2A+ populations. Across conditions, senescent cells shared AP-1 activation, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and apoptosis resistance, suggesting therapeutic opportunities.

title: Applying Spatial Transcriptomics to the Human Heart: A Practical Guide for Translational Studies.

evidence_text: Applying Spatial Transcriptomics to the Human Heart: A Practical Guide for Translational Studies. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell methods are changing the questions we can ask about the human cardiovascular system. In this review, we share lessons learned from applying spatial profiling to human cardiovascular samples. We walk through experimental considerations, sampling, fixation, and ribonucleic acid quality control, then compare sequencing-based and imaging-based platforms within a 2-stage "discovery then validation" framework. We propose a heart-aware analytical pipeline: spatially informed quality control, normalization respecting the outsized transcriptome of cardiomyocytes, thoughtful segmentation, and honest assessment of reproducibility. We consider how spatial data can be woven together with single-cell, epigenomic, and proteomic layers, and look ahead to emerging frontiers including integration with cardiac imaging foundation models. Our hope is that spatially resolved molecular data will reveal new tissue niches to target for precision cardiovascular therapies.

xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Validation of histopathology-based deep learning algorithms for detection of actionable non-small cell lung cancer biomarkers. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patient management relies on molecular analysis to determine eligibility for targeted therapy. Furthermore, neoadjuvant immunotherapy is primarily suitable in the absence of specific genomic alterations. However, significant challenges remain, including suboptimal molecular testing and patients being assigned to non-optimal treatment strategies. Here, we present AI classifiers for the identification of EGFR, ALK, BRAF and MET alterations directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue using CanvOI 1.1, a digital pathology foundation model. Their performance was evaluated on an independent validation dataset of 968 NSCLC samples. The classifiers achieved AUCs of 0.87 for EGFR, 0.96 for ALK, 0.88 for BRAF and 0.83 for MET. Moreover, they demonstrated high accuracy in identifying cases lacking alterations. Our results highlight the potential of deep-learning tools for the detection of NSCLC biomarkers and specifically the identification of tumors without EGFR or ALK driver alterations, supporting more informed clinical decision-making.

evidence_text:
A pre-trained foundation model framework for multiplanar MRI classification of extramural vascular invasion and mesorectal fascia invasion in rectal cancer.

Objectives

Accurate MRI-based identification of extramural vascular invasion (EVI) and mesorectal fascia invasion (MFI) is crucial for risk-stratified rectal cancer treatment. However, subjective visual assessment and inter-institutional variability limit diagnostic consistency. This study developed and evaluated a multi-center, foundation model-driven framework that automatically classifies EVI and MFI on axial and sagittal MRI.

Materials and methods

A total of 331 pre-treatment rectal cancer T2-weighted MRI scans from three European hospitals were retrospectively recruited. A self-supervised frequency domain harmonization strategy was applied to reduce scanner variability. Three classifiers, SeResNet, the universal biomedical pretrained model (UMedPT) with a multilayer perceptron head, and a logistic-regression variant using frozen UMedPT features (UMedPT_LR), were trained (n = 265) and tested (n = 66). Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) visualized model predictions.

Results

UMedPT_LR achieved the best EVI performance with multiplanar fusion (AUC = 0.82, test set). For MFI, UMedPT trained on axial harmonized images yielded the highest performance (AUC = 0.77). Both tasks outperformed the CHAIMELEON 2024 benchmark (EVI: 0.82 vs 0.74; MFI: 0.77 vs 0.75). Harmonization enhanced MFI classification, and multiplanar fusion further boosted EVI performance. Grad-CAM confirmed biologically plausible attention on peritumoral regions (EVI) and mesorectal fascia margins (MFI).

Conclusion

The proposed foundation model-driven framework, leveraging frequency domain harmonization and multiplanar fusion, achieves state-of-the-art performance for automated EVI and MFI classification on MRI, demonstrating strong generalizability across multiple centers.

Critical relevance statement

Addressing inter-center inconsistencies in rectal cancer MRI, a multiplanar foundation model with cross-scanner harmonization significantly improves the detection of EVI and MFI, potentially standardizing staging and guiding therapy.

Key points

Among the first studies to investigate automated classification of both EVI and MFI using axial and sagittal T2-weighted MRI. Foundation model-derived features outperform conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for EVI and MFI classification. Frequency domain harmonization and multiplanar fusion selectively enhance diagnostic performance. Automated prediction of EVI and MFI may support more consistent staging and clinical decision-making across institutions.

title: A CT Lesion Foundation Model for Non-Invasive Assessment of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Aggressiveness and Prediction of Recurrence Risk.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: A CT Lesion Foundation Model for Non-Invasive Assessment of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Aggressiveness and Prediction of Recurrence Risk.  Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with high recurrence rates following curative resection. Accurate non-invasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and recurrence risk is critical for surgical decision-making and postoperative surveillance, yet remains challenging with conventional imaging modalities. Here, we developed a CT lesion foundation model (LFM), trained via self-supervised learning on 32,120 generic lesion and 6,387 HCC-specific CT patches to capture transferable intra-lesional imaging phenotypes. Across one internal and two external validation cohorts, the sequentially pretrained LFM (LFM-Seq) achieved area under the curve values of 0.916, 0.846, and 0.920 for microvascular invasion (MVI) assessment, and 0.833, 0.885 and 0.795 for pathological grade assessment. The model remained robust under scenarios of limited training data and tumor localization perturbations. Furthermore, LFM-Seq-derived risk scores stratified recurrence-free survival (RFS), yielding an externally validated C-index of 0.701, and remained independently associated with RFS after adjusting for clinicopathological factors. Exploratory biological interpretability analyses showed that LFM-Seq-derived risk phenotypes were associated with suppressed lymphocyte-related immune programs. These results suggest that CT lesion foundation models can support non-invasive and robust characterization of HCC aggressiveness, recurrence risk stratification and discovery of interpretable prognostic imaging biomarkers.

evidence_text: Artificial intelligence across the gastric cancer care continuum: Clinical evidence, multimodal integration, and translation Graphical abstract                     Health sciences     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Collection date 2026 Nov 20.       Introduction  Gastric cancer continues to impose a substantial global burden despite declining age-standardized incidence and mortality rates in some regions.  1   According to Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN) 2022, stomach cancer accounted for more than 968,000 new cases and nearly 660,000 deaths worldwide,  2   underscoring its status as one of the deadliest common malignancies.  2   The burden remains especially high in East Asia, where organized screening programs and high procedural volumes have made early detection a central clinical priority.  3   Nevertheless, many patients are still diagnosed at locally advanced or metastatic stages.  4   Early lesions may be endoscopically subtle, symptoms are often nonspecific, and the disease exhibits marked histologic, molecular, and spatial heterogeneities. Gastric cancer is, therefore, not only a high-burden disease but also one that is highly prone to error across the clinical pathway.  5    These clinical challenges align closely with the strengths of modern artificial intelligence (AI).  5   Over the past decade, the field has progressed from conventional machine learning models based on limited structured variables to deep neural networks capable of analyzing high-dimensional image data.  5   More recently, the field has moved toward multimodal and foundation model paradigms that learn transferable representations from large, weakly labeled, or unlabeled datasets.  6   In gastric cancer, this transition is especially consequential because management depends on integrating heterogeneous data streams, including white-light and image-enhanced endoscopy, computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), histopathology, immunophenotyping, molecular testing, laboratory findings, and treatment trajectories.  7   Few solid tumors illustrate the need for cross-modal clinical AI as clearly as gastric cancer.  8    Recent reviews suggest that gastric cancer is emerging as one of the most active areas in gastrointestinal oncology for AI translation.  9   A 2024 systematic review focused on gastric adenocarcinoma synthesized studies from PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library and concluded that AI is already reshaping the diagnostic and management pathways.  10   A 2023 systematic review of AI-assisted endoscopy identified 42 original studies and found that deep learning models frequently matched or outperformed endoscopists in tasks related to early gastric neoplasia.  11   The central question is no longer whether AI can recognize patterns in gastric cancer, but whether it can improve real-world decision-making as a trustworthy, equitable, and workflow integrated tool.  12    The present review, therefore, adopts a clinically oriented and translational perspective. Its distinct contribution is to examine AI across the complete gastric cancer care continuum, while explicitly comparing evidence maturity, clinical actionability, workflow compatibility, and regional transportability. It distinguishes near-term deployable systems, including real-time endoscopy and routine-slide pathology, from discovery-oriented technologies such as single-cell analysis, spatial transcriptomics, foundation models, and digital twins. Particular attention is given to multimodal integration, cross-regional generalization, clinician-AI interaction, regulatory governance, and medico-legal responsibility.  13    The scope includes AI applications in prevention and risk stratification, endoscopic detection and characterization, CT and PET/CT staging, digital pathology and biomarker prescreening, prognostic modeling, treatment-response prediction, surgical support, and longitudinal decision support. Four questions guide this review. Which applications currently have the strongest clinical evidence? How do imaging, pathology, multimodal, and omics-based approaches add value beyond endoscopic AI? Which methodological and geographic barriers limit reproducibility and equitable deployment? What validation, workflow, regulatory, and governance requirements are necessary before these systems can improve patient care? ( Figure 1 ).    Figure 1   AI across the gastric cancer care continuum  AI applications span prevention and screening prioritization, endoscopic detection and characterization, imaging-based staging, digital pathology and molecular prescreening, prognostic modeling, treatment allocation, and emerging multimodal decision support. Translational maturity is uneven: a real-time endoscopy CDSS retained external multicenter accuracies of 81.5% for four-class classification and 86.4% for invasion-depth assessment, whereas radiomics for peritoneal metastasis achieved a pooled AUC of 0.89 but substantial heterogeneity (I 2  = 88%).  AI, artificial intelligence; CDSS, clinical decision support system; CT, computed tomography; H&E, hematoxylin and eosin; PET/CT, positron emission tomography/computed tomography.                     Methods   Review design  This article was designed as a structured narrative review addressing the clinical and translational development of AI in gastric cancer. The narrative approach was selected because the evidence spans heterogeneous clinical tasks, data modalities, model architectures, outcome definitions, and study designs that are not suitable for a single pooled quantitative analysis. The conduct and reporting of the review were informed by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA).  This review was not prospectively registered and not designed as a formal systematic review. Accordingly, it does not claim full compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. Transparency was instead strengthened through a reproducible search description, explicit eligibility criteria, structured evidence characterization, and an adapted study-identification framework presented.    Information sources and search strategy  PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched for relevant studies published from January 1, 2022 through July 2026. Earlier landmark articles were retained when they established an important clinical or methodological foundation that remained relevant to recent developments. Backward citation searching of major reviews and forward citation tracking of influential original studies were also performed.  Searches used combinations of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to gastric cancer and AI. Representative terms included “gastric cancer,” “gastric adenocarcinoma,” “stomach neoplasm,” “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “neural network,” “radiomics,” “endoscopy,” “computed tomography,” “PET/CT,” “digital pathology,” “whole-slide image,” “multimodal,” “foundation model,” “prognosis,” “treatment response,” “immunotherapy,” “surgery,” and “clinical decision support.”    Eligibility and study selection  Eligible publications included peer-reviewed original clinical studies, prospective or retrospective validation studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical guidelines, methodological reporting guidelines, and regulatory documents relevant to AI applications in gastric adenocarcinoma.  Original studies were prioritized when they included multicenter recruitment, prospective evaluation, independent external validation, clinically actionable endpoints, comparison with clinicians or standard care, calibration analysis, decision curve analysis (DCA), or evaluation within a real or simulated clinical workflow. Studies were excluded from the principal synthesis when they did not report gastric cancer results separately, focused exclusively on non-human experiments without a clinical AI application, described an algorithm without patient-level evaluation or a clinically interpretable endpoint, were conference abstracts or non-peer-reviewed preprints, or lacked sufficient methodological information for critical interpretation.    Evidence appraisal and synthesis  Because of substantial heterogeneity across diagnostic, prognostic, therapeutic, surgical, and implementation studies, a single formal risk-of-bias instrument was not applied to all evidence. Representative studies were instead characterized according to study design, dataset and cohort size, internal and external validation, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, proximity to an actionable workflow, and implementation or patient-outcome evidence. These dimensions inform the qualitative evidence-maturity ratings in  Tables 1  and  2 . High model discrimination alone was not considered sufficient evidence of clinical maturity. Results were synthesized by stage of care and modality; no new meta-analysis was performed.
